\displaystyle d_{\text{min}}(\int_{0}^{\delta_{k}}f^{\prime}d\mu_{1})^{2}(\int_{0}^{\delta_{k}}d\mu_{1})^{-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle d_{\text{min}}\frac{(f(\delta_{k})-f(0))^{2}}{\delta_{k}}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle d_{\text{min}}\frac{(\epsilon\sqrt{\delta_{k}})^{2}}{\delta_{k}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle d_{\text{min}}\epsilon^{2}

Here, we use Jensen’s inequality.

Because
f^{\prime 2}
is integrable with respect to
\mathcal{D}
, we have
\int_{0}^{\delta_{0}}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\delta_{k}}^{\delta_{0}}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}
, so
0=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{0}^{\delta_{0}}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}-\int_{\delta_{k}}^{\delta_{0}}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{0}^{\delta_{k}}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}
. But
\int_{0}^{\delta_{k}}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}
is bounded away from zero. Contradiction. Hence, we have the lemma.

∎

10.4
Propositions

Proposition
1
.

Assume there exists an open set
S
where
\mathcal{D}
has a continuous, positive density function and
f
is not constant on
S
. Then
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})>0
.

Proof.

(For the purpose of this proof, naturally, we do not use assumption
3
.) Since
f
is non-constant on
S
, there are
x_{1},x_{2}\in S
with
f(x_{1})\neq f(x_{2})
. At least one of
f(x_{1}),f(x_{2})
is unequal to
\bar{f}
. WLOG,
f(x_{1})\neq\bar{f}
. Because
d_{x}
is continuous and positive on
S
, there exists an open set
S_{1}
and
\epsilon_{1}>0
such that
x_{1}\in S_{1}
and
d_{x}(x)>\epsilon_{1}
for all
x\in S_{1}
. Because
f
is continuous and
f(x_{1})\neq\bar{f}
, there exists an open set
S_{2}
and
\epsilon_{2}>0
such that
x_{1}\in S_{2}
and
||f(x)-\bar{f}||_{2}^{2}>\epsilon_{2}
for all
x\in S_{2}
. Let
S_{3}=S_{1}\cap S_{2}
. Because
S_{1}
and
S_{2}
are open, so is
S_{3}
. Because
x_{1}\in S_{1}
and
x_{1}\in S_{2}
,
S_{3}
is non-empty, we have
\int_{S_{3}}d\mu_{1}>0
. So we have

\displaystyle\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Tr(\mathbb{E}(f-\bar{f})^{T}(f-\bar{f}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}||f-\bar{f}||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{x}||f-\bar{f}||_{2}^{2}d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\int_{x\in S_{3}}||f-\bar{f}||_{2}^{2}d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{x\in S_{3}}||f-\bar{f}||_{2}^{2}d_{x}(x)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\int_{x\in S_{3}}\epsilon_{2}\epsilon_{1}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\epsilon_{2}\epsilon_{1}\int_{S_{3}}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle>

\displaystyle 0

∎

Proposition
2
.

Assume there exists a non-empty open set
S
where
\mathcal{D}
has a continuous, positive density function. Then
\mathrm{Cov}_{x}
is non-singular.

Proof.

(For the purpose of this proof, naturally, we do not use assumption
4
.) Assume
\mathrm{Cov}_{x}
is singular. Then there exists a non-zero vector
v\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}
such that
v\mathrm{Cov}_{x}=0
. Let
F(x)=xv^{T}
.
F
is not constant on any non-empty open set, so it is non-constant on
S
. Hence we can apply the proof of proposition
1
to obtain
\mathrm{Cov}_{F}>0
. We also have

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{F}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(F-\bar{F})^{T}(F-\bar{F})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}F^{T}F-\bar{F}^{T}\bar{F}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}vx^{T}xv^{T}-v\bar{x}^{T}\bar{x}v^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle v(\mathbb{E}x^{T}x-\bar{x}^{T}\bar{x})v^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle v(\mathbb{E}(x-\bar{x})^{T}(x-\bar{x}))v^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle v\mathrm{Cov}_{x}v^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

This is a contradiction, which completes the proof.

∎

Proposition
3
.

Let
f
be linear. Then
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})=1
.

Proof.

If
f:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}
is linear, we can write
f(x)=xA+b
for a fixed matrix
A
and vector
b
. Then we have

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Tr(A^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A)}{\Tr(\mathbb{E}_{x}(xA+b-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}(x^{\prime}A+b))^{T}(xA+b-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}(x^{\prime}A+b)))}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Tr(A^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A)}{\Tr(\mathbb{E}(xA-\bar{x}A)^{T}(xA-\bar{x}A))}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Tr(A^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A)}{\Tr(\mathbb{E}A^{T}(x-\bar{x})^{T}(x-\bar{x})A)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Tr(A^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A)}{\Tr(A^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1

∎

Proposition
4
.

Let
A
be an orthogonal matrix of size
d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{out}}
and
b
be a
d_{\text{out}}
-dimensional vector. Then
NLC(fA+b,\mathcal{D})=NLC(f,\mathcal{D})
.

Proof.

\displaystyle NLC(fA+b,\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}\Tr(A^{T}\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}^{T}(x)A)}{\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr((f(x)A+b-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}(f(x^{\prime})A+b))^{T}(f(x)A+b-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}(f(x^{\prime})A+b)))}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}}\Tr(A^{T}\mathcal{J}(x)(x^{\prime}-\bar{x})^{T}(x^{\prime}-\bar{x})\mathcal{J}(x)^{T}A)}{\mathbb{E}\Tr(A^{T}(f(x)-\bar{f})^{T}(f(x)-\bar{f})A)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}}||A^{T}\mathcal{J}(x)(x^{\prime}-\bar{x})^{T}||^{2}_{2}}{\mathbb{E}||A^{T}(f(x)-\bar{f})||^{2}_{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}}||\mathcal{J}(x)(x^{\prime}-\bar{x})^{T}||^{2}_{2}}{\mathbb{E}||f(x)-\bar{f}||^{2}_{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)(x^{\prime}-\bar{x})^{T}(x^{\prime}-\bar{x})\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})}{\mathbb{E}\Tr((f(x)-\bar{f})^{T}(f(x)-\bar{f}))}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

∎

Proposition
5
.

Let
A
be a matrix of size
d_{\text{in}}\times d_{\text{in}}
and
b
be a
d_{\text{in}}
-dimensional vector. Assume
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f(xA+b)})>0
. Then
NLC(f(xA+b),\mathcal{D})=NLC(f(x),\mathcal{D}A+b)
, where drawing
x
from
\mathcal{D}A+b
is equivalent to drawing
x
from
\mathcal{D}
and applying
xA+b
.

Proof.

\displaystyle NLC(f(xA+b),\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr(\frac{df(xA+b)}{dx}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\frac{df(xA+b)}{dx}^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f(xA+b)})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(xA+b)A^{T}(x^{\prime}-\bar{x})^{T}(x^{\prime}-\bar{x})A\mathcal{J}(xA+b)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f(xA+b)})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(xA+b)(x^{\prime}A+b-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime\prime}}(x^{\prime\prime}A+b))^{T}(x^{\prime}A+b-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime\prime}}(x^{\prime\prime}A+b))\mathcal{J}(xA+b)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathbb{E}_{x}(f(xA+b)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime\prime}}f(x^{\prime\prime}A+b))^{T}(f(xA+b)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime\prime}}f(x^{\prime\prime}A+b)))}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}A+b}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)(x^{\prime}-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}A+b}x^{\prime\prime})^{T}(x^{\prime}-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}A+b}x^{\prime\prime})\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}A+b}(f(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}A+b}f(x^{\prime\prime}))^{T}(f(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}A+b}f(x^{\prime\prime})))}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle NLC(f(x),\mathcal{D}A+b)^{2}

∎

Proposition
6
.

We have

1.

\mathbb{E}F^{T}\tilde{f}=0
and
\mathbb{E}F\tilde{f}^{T}=0
for any linear function
F:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}

2.

\mathbb{E}((x-\bar{x})A_{f})\tilde{f}^{T}=0
,
\mathbb{E}(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})\tilde{f}^{T}=0
and
\mathbb{E}((x-\bar{x})A_{f})(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})^{T}=0

3.

LAR + CAR + NAR = 1

Proof.

Since
F
is linear, it can be written as
xA+b
for some
A
,
b
. Let
\mathcal{A}
denote
\begin{pmatrix}A\\
b\end{pmatrix}
. The standard formula for the least squares linear fit yields
\begin{pmatrix}A_{f}\\
b_{f}\end{pmatrix}=(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f
, where
(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}
is valid by lemma
1
. Then we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}F^{T}\tilde{f}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(xA+b)^{T}(f-\chi\begin{pmatrix}A_{f}\\
b_{f}\end{pmatrix})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\chi\mathcal{A})^{T}(f-\chi(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathcal{A}^{T}(\chi^{T}f-\chi^{T}\chi(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{T}((\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f)-(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Since we have
F\tilde{f}^{T}=\Tr(F^{T}\tilde{f})
, we have
\mathbb{E}F\tilde{f}^{T}=0
. Hence, property 1.

(x-\bar{x})A_{f}
is linear, so by property 1 we have
\mathbb{E}((x-\bar{x})A_{f})\tilde{f}^{T}=0
.
b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f}
is linear, so by property 1 we have
\mathbb{E}(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})\tilde{f}^{T}=0
. Also we have
\mathbb{E}((x-\bar{x})A_{f})(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})^{T}=((\bar{x}-\bar{x})A_{f})(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})^{T}=0
. Hence, property 2. Finally, we have

\displaystyle 1

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})^{-1}\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})^{-1}\mathbb{E}ff^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})^{-1}\mathbb{E}(\tilde{f}+(x-\bar{x})A_{f}+(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f}))(\tilde{f}+(x-\bar{x})A_{f}+(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f}))^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})^{-1}\mathbb{E}\Big(\tilde{f}\tilde{f}^{T}+(x-\bar{x})A_{f}((x-\bar{x})A_{f})^{T}+(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})^{T}

\displaystyle+2((x-\bar{x})A_{f})\tilde{f}^{T}+2(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})\tilde{f}^{T}+2(x-\bar{x})A_{f}(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})^{T}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})^{-1}\mathbb{E}\Big(\tilde{f}\tilde{f}^{T}+(x-\bar{x})A_{f}((x-\bar{x})A_{f})^{T}+(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})(b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})^{T}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})^{-1}\mathbb{E}\Big(||\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}+||(x-\bar{x})A_{f}||_{2}^{2}+||b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f}||_{2}^{2}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}||\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2}}+\frac{\mathbb{E}||(x-\bar{x})A_{f}||_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2}}+\frac{\mathbb{E}||b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f}||_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle LAR+CAR+NAR

We have property 3.
∎

Proposition
7
.

Assume there exists an open set
S
where
\mathcal{D}
has a continuous, positive density function and
f
is not linear on
S
. Then
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}})>0
.

Proof.

We have
\tilde{f}=f-xA_{f}-b_{f}
. Assume
\tilde{f}
is linear on
S
. Then it can be written as
xA+b
. Then
f=x(A_{f}+A)+(b_{f}+b)
, so
f
is linear on
S
. Contradiction. So
\tilde{f}
is not linear on
S
. So
\tilde{f}
is not constant on
S
. Hence, by proposition
1
,
\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}}>0
.
∎

Proposition
8
.

Let
xA_{\tilde{f}}+b_{\tilde{f}}
be the least squares linear fit to
\tilde{f}
. Then
A_{\tilde{f}}=0
and
b_{\tilde{f}}=0
.

Proof.

The standard formula for the least squares linear fit yields
\begin{pmatrix}A_{f}\\
b_{f}\end{pmatrix}=(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f
and
\begin{pmatrix}A_{\tilde{f}}\\
b_{\tilde{f}}\end{pmatrix}=(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\tilde{f}
, where
(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}
is valid by lemma
1
. Then we have

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}A_{\tilde{f}}\\
b_{\tilde{f}}\end{pmatrix}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\tilde{f}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}(f-\chi\begin{pmatrix}A_{f}\\
b_{f}\end{pmatrix})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}(f-\chi(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\Big(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f-(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)(\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}\chi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\chi^{T}f\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Hence,
A_{\tilde{f}}=0
and
b_{\tilde{f}}=0
as required.

∎

Proposition
9
.

Let
\delta_{\text{in}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{Cov}_{x})
and
\delta_{\text{out}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{Cov}_{f})
be row vectors. Assume
NLC>0
. Then

\mathbb{E}_{x,\delta_{\text{in}}}||\frac{\delta_{\text{in}}}{NLC}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T}||_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{\delta_{\text{out}}}||\delta_{\text{out}}||_{2}^{2}

Proof.

We have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\delta_{\text{out}}}||\delta_{\text{out}}||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\delta_{\text{out}}}\sum_{j}\delta_{\text{out}}[j]\delta_{\text{out}}[j]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\delta_{\text{out}}}\sum_{j}(\delta_{\text{out}}^{T}\delta_{\text{out}})[j,j]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{j}(\mathbb{E}_{\delta_{\text{out}}}\delta_{\text{out}}^{T}\delta_{\text{out}})[j,j]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{j}\mathrm{Cov}_{f}[j,j]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})

Further, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x,\delta_{\text{in}}}||\delta_{\text{in}}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T}||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x,\delta_{\text{in}}}\sum_{j}\Big(\sum_{i}\delta_{\text{in}}[i]\mathcal{J}(x)[j,i]\Big)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x,\delta_{\text{in}}}\sum_{j}\Big((\sum_{i}\delta_{\text{in}}[i]\mathcal{J}(x)[j,i])(\sum_{i^{\prime}}\delta_{\text{in}}[i^{\prime}]\mathcal{J}(x)[j,i^{\prime}])\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x,\delta_{\text{in}}}\sum_{j}\Big(\mathcal{J}(x)\delta_{\text{in}}^{T}\delta_{\text{in}}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T}\Big)[j,j]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}\sum_{j}\Big(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathbb{E}_{\delta_{\text{in}}}(\delta_{\text{in}}^{T}\delta_{\text{in}})\mathcal{J}(x)^{T}\Big)[j,j]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}\sum_{j}\Big(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T}\Big)[j,j]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})

Finally, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x,\delta_{\text{in}}}||\frac{\delta_{\text{in}}}{NLC}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T}||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{NLC^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{x,\delta_{\text{in}}}||\delta_{\text{in}}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T}||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}{\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})}\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\delta_{\text{out}}}||\delta_{\text{out}}||_{2}^{2}

as required.
∎

10.5
Theorems

10.5.1
Theorem
1
:
NLC\geq 1
for Gaussian inputs

Theorem
1
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
be Gaussian. Then
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq 1
, where equality holds if and only if
f
is linear.

Proof.

In this proof, we will use theorems
2
and
3
. Since the proofs of those theorems are not dependent on this theorem, there is no circular reasoning.

By proposition
3
, we have
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})=1
if
f
is linear. So now assume
f
is not linear. By proposition
7
,
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}})>0
and so
NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})
is valid. We also have
\mathbb{E}||\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}||\tilde{f}-(\mathbb{E}\tilde{f})||_{2}^{2}+||\mathbb{E}\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}=\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}})+||\mathbb{E}\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}>0
and so
NAR(f,\mathcal{D})>0
. We have

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{LAR}{NAR+LAR}+\frac{NAR}{NAR+LAR}NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1+\frac{NAR}{NAR+LAR}(NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})^{2}-1)

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle 1+\frac{2NAR}{NAR+LAR}

\displaystyle>

\displaystyle 1

∎

Discussion and alternative proof sketch

Theorem
1
can be proven directly without relying on theorem
2
or
3
. In fact, we proved theorem
1
first and then developed the proof of theorem
2
as an extended version. Due to the length that this chapter already has, we will only give a quick summary of this direct proof here, thereby avoiding the near-duplication of tedious arguments present in the proof of theorem
2
.

Like the proof of theorem
2
, the direct proof of theorem
1
proceeds in stages. In the first stage, we examine odd, scalar
f
with unit Gaussian
\mathcal{D}
. Let
T>S>0
. Using integration by parts, we have

\displaystyle\int_{S}^{T}f^{2}d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{S}^{T}\frac{f^{2}}{x}(xd_{x})d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle[-\frac{f^{2}}{x}d_{x}]_{S}^{T}+\int_{S}^{T}\frac{2ff^{\prime}}{x}-\frac{f^{2}}{x^{2}}d_{x}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{f(S)^{2}}{S}n(S)-\frac{f(T)^{2}}{T}n(T)+\int_{S}^{T}\frac{2ff^{\prime}}{x}-\frac{f^{2}}{x^{2}}d\mu_{x}

and so

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2})-(\mathbb{E}f)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\big(\int_{0}^{\infty}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2}d\mu_{x}\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\big(\int_{0}^{S}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2}d\mu_{x}+\int_{S}^{T}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}-\int_{S}^{T}f^{2}d\mu_{x}+\int_{T}^{\infty}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2}d\mu_{x}\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\big(\int_{0}^{S}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2}d\mu_{x}+\int_{S}^{T}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle-\frac{f(S)^{2}}{S}n(S)+\frac{f(T)^{2}}{T}n(T)-\int_{S}^{T}\frac{2ff^{\prime}}{x}-\frac{f^{2}}{x^{2}}d\mu_{x}+\int_{T}^{\infty}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2}d\mu_{x}\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\int_{S}^{T}(f^{\prime}-\frac{f}{x})^{2}d\mu_{x}+

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\big(\int_{0}^{S}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2}d\mu_{x}+\int_{T}^{\infty}f^{\prime 2}-f^{2}d\mu_{x}-\frac{f(S)^{2}}{S}n(S)+\frac{f(T)^{2}}{T}n(T)\big)

The first term is strictly positive if
f
is not linear on
[S,T]
. Also, the first term increases as
S
decreases and
T
increases while the second term converges to zero as
S
converges to zero and
T
converges to infinity. Therefore, we can choose
S
and
T
such that the whole expression is strictly positive. This proves theorem
1
for odd, scalar
f
.

In the second stage, we generalize from odd, scalar
f
to arbitrary scalar
f
by observing that the NLC of such
f
is at least a weighted average between the NLC of an odd function that mirrors
f
on the negative quadrant and the NLC of an odd function that mirrors
f
on the positive quadrant. Next, we consider multi-dimensional unit Gaussian
\mathcal{D}
together with
d_{\text{out}}=1
. We use a simplified version of the argument from stage 4 of the proof of theorem
2
where we only need to define the
f_{i}
, but not the
t_{i,k}
or
p_{i,k}
. Finally, we extend to the general case via a series of trivial stages, analogously to the proof of theorem
2
.

10.5.2
Theorem
2
:
NLC\geq\sqrt{2}
when the least squares fit is zero

Theorem
2
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
be Gaussian and let the linear component of
f
be the zero function. Then we have

NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}

Proof.

This proof is quite long and will proceed in a number of stages. In each stage, we prove the statement
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
for a more general class of pairs
(f,\mathcal{D})
while building on the results from previous stages. The notation defined in any stage is local to that stage.

Stage 1
: The statement holds when
d_{\text{in}}=d_{\text{out}}=1
,
\mathcal{D}
has expectation zero and variance one,
f
is an even function and the constant component of
f
is the zero function.

We argue by contradiction. Assume
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})<\sqrt{2}
. Denote
\int_{S}^{T}x^{p}d\mu_{x}
by
I_{p}(S,T)
for any
S\leq T
and
p
. In this stage, we have
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}=\frac{\mathbb{E}f^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}f^{2}-(\mathbb{E}f)^{2}}=\frac{\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-X}^{X}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}}{\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-X}^{X}f^{2}d\mu_{x}-(\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-X}^{X}fd\mu_{x})^{2}}
. We have
\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}I_{0}(-X,X)=1
. So we have
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}=\frac{\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}}{I_{0}(-X,X)}}{\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}f^{2}d\mu_{x}}{I_{0}(-X,X)}-\Big(\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}fd\mu_{x}}{I_{0}(-X,X)}\Big)^{2}}
. Hence, there is an
X
with
\frac{\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}}{I_{0}(-X,X)}}{\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}f^{2}d\mu_{x}}{I_{0}(-X,X)}-\Big(\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}fd\mu_{x}}{I_{0}(-X,X)}\Big)^{2}}<2
and also
X>1
. For the remainder of stage 1, let
X
be this fixed value. We shorten the expression
I_{p}(-X,X)
to
I_{p}
. Rearranging, we obtain
\frac{1}{I_{0}}\int_{-X}^{X}f^{\prime 2}-2f^{2}d\mu_{x}+\frac{2}{I_{0}^{2}}(\int_{-X}^{X}fd\mu_{x})^{2}<0
. Let
\mathcal{T}
be
\mathcal{D}
restricted to
[-X,X]
. Then our formula becomes
(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f^{\prime 2})-2(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f^{2})+2(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f)^{2}<0
. Let
f_{K}
be the piecewise linear approximation of
f
on the interval
[-X,X]
with
K
linear segments as defined in section
10.1
. By lemma
4
, we can choose an
e>0
and
K_{e}
such that
(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f^{\prime 2}_{2K})-2(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f^{2}_{2K})+2(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f_{2K})^{2}<-e
for all
K>K_{e}
. We write
obj(f_{2K})<-e
.

The next step in the proof is to show that for each
\eta>0
, there is a
K_{\eta}>K_{e}
and an even quadratic function
q=ax^{2}+c
such that
obj(q)<obj(f_{2K_{\eta}})+\eta
. Because this step is quite long and tedious, we will first show how to complete stage 1 once we have shown the existence of this
K_{\eta}
and
q
. We have for arbitrary
q

\displaystyle obj(q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{I_{0}}\int_{-X}^{X}4a^{2}x^{2}-2a^{2}x^{4}-4acx^{2}-2c^{2}d\mu_{x}+\frac{2}{I_{0}^{2}}(\int_{-X}^{X}ax^{2}+cd\mu_{x})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{I_{0}}(4a^{2}I_{2}-2a^{2}I_{4}-4acI_{2}-2c^{2}I_{0})+\frac{2}{I_{0}^{2}}(a^{2}I_{2}^{2}+2acI_{2}I_{0}+c^{2}I_{0}^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2a^{2}}{I_{0}^{2}}(2I_{2}I_{0}-I_{4}I_{0}+I_{2}^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2a^{2}}{I_{0}^{2}}\Big(2(1-2N(-X)-2Xn(X))(1-2N(-X))-

\displaystyle(3-6N(-X)-2X(X^{2}+3)n(X))(1-2N(-X))+(1-2N(-X)-2Xn(X))^{2}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2a^{2}}{I_{0}^{2}}(-2Xn(X)+4Xn(X)N(-X)+4X^{2}n(X)^{2}+2n(X)X^{3}-4X^{3}n(X)N(X))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2a^{2}}{I_{0}^{2}}(2Xn(X)(X^{2}-1)(1-2N(-X))+4X^{2}n(X)^{2})

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle 0

In the last step, we used
X>1
. But if we choose
\eta<e
, then from
obj(f_{2K_{\eta}})<-e
and
obj(q)<obj(f_{2K_{\eta}})+\eta
we obtain
obj(q)<0
. This is the contradiction that would complete stage 1. So we are left to show the following.

Claim 1:
For each
\eta>0
, there is a
K_{\eta}>K_{e}
and an even quadratic function
q=ax^{2}+c
such that
obj(q)<obj(f_{2K_{\eta}})+\eta
.

For each
K
, we define the even quadratic function
q_{K}=a_{K}x^{2}+c_{K}
. We choose the parameters
a_{K}
and
c_{K}
to satisfy the following equalities:
f_{2K}(X)=q_{K}(X)
and
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}f_{2K}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}q_{K}
. It is clear that for each pair of values of
f_{2K}(X)
and
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}f_{2K}
, there exist unique values for
a_{K}
and
c_{K}
. Because
f
, and hence
f_{2K}
, is even, we also have
f_{2K}(-X)=q_{K}(-X)
.

Let
objdiff(K)=obj(f_{2K})-obj(q_{K})
. The remainder of the proof of claim 1 will proceed as follows. In step 1, we will fix
K
and derive an alternative formula for
objdiff
. In step 2, we will break down that formula into a sum of terms where each term is either positive or arbitrarily close to zero for large
K
. This will then allow us to pick a
K>K_{e}
with
objdiff(K)>-\eta
for arbitrary
K_{e}
and
\eta
, and then we will have claim 1.

Step 1: Fix
K
. Define
F_{k}
,
0\leq k\leq K
as follows. On
[-X,-\frac{k}{K}X]
and
[\frac{k}{K}X,X]
,
F_{k}
is equal to
f_{2K}
. On
[-\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k}{K}X]
,
F_{k}
is an even quadratic that connects with
f_{2K}
at
-\frac{k}{K}X
and
\frac{k}{K}X
and has
\mathbb{E}_{x\in[-\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k}{K}X]}F_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{x\in[-\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k}{K}X]}f_{2K}
, which is equivalent to
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}F_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}f_{2K}
, to
\int_{-X}^{X}F_{k}d\mu_{x}=\int_{-X}^{X}f_{2K}d\mu_{x}
and to
\int_{0}^{\frac{k}{K}X}F_{k}d\mu_{x}=\int_{0}^{\frac{k}{K}X}f_{2K}d\mu_{x}
because both functions are even. Then
F_{0}=f_{2K}
and
F_{K}=q_{K}
. So
objdiff=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}obj(F_{k})-obj(F_{k+1})
. As
\int_{-X}^{X}F_{k}d\mu_{x}
is the same for all
k
, we have
objdiff=\frac{1}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\int_{-X}^{X}(F^{\prime 2}_{k}-2F^{2}_{k})-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-2F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}
. Because all functions are even, we then have
objdiff=\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\int_{0}^{X}(F^{\prime 2}_{k}-2F^{2}_{k})-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-2F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}
. Finally, we can eliminate sections of the integral where consecutive
F
’s are equal. Then we obtain
objdiff=\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\int_{0}^{\frac{(k+1)}{K}X}(F^{\prime 2}_{k}-2F^{2}_{k})-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-2F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}
. Denote the
k
’th term of this sum by
D_{k}
.

Let’s look at a specific
D_{k}
. For now, we will omit most
k
and
K
subscripts because
k
and
K
are considered fixed. Instead, we introduce some additional notation. Let
\epsilon=\frac{X}{K}
,
y=k\epsilon
,
z=(k+1)\epsilon
and let
bx+d
be the line segment in
f_{2K}
between
k\epsilon
and
(k+1)\epsilon
. Let
ax^{2}+r
be the equation of the even square in
F_{k}
between 0 and
k\epsilon
. Let
Ax^{2}+R
be the even quadratic in
F_{k+1}
between 0 and
(k+1)\epsilon
. Then the 6 parameters
a,r,A,R,b,d
satisfy the following constraints, which arise from
F_{k}(y)=f_{2K}(y)
,
F_{k+1}(z)=f_{2K}(z)
and
\int_{0}^{z}F_{k}d\mu_{x}=\int_{0}^{z}F_{k+1}d\mu_{x}
respectively.

\displaystyle ay^{2}+r

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle by+d

\displaystyle Az^{2}+R

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle bz+d

\displaystyle aI_{2}(0,y)+rI_{0}(0,y)+bI_{1}(y,z)+dI_{0}(y,z)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle AI_{2}(0,z)+RI_{0}(0,z)

And we have

\displaystyle D_{k}(a,r,A,R,b,d)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(b^{2}-2d^{2})I_{0}(y,z)-2b^{2}I_{2}(y,z)-4bdI_{1}(y,z)+4a(a-r)I_{2}(0,y)-2a^{2}I_{4}(0,y)

\displaystyle-2r^{2}I_{0}(0,y)-4A(A-R)I_{2}(0,z)+2A^{2}I_{4}(0,z)+2R^{2}I_{0}(0,z)

It is easy to check that simultaneously adding a constant to
F_{k}
and
F_{k+1}
neither alters
D_{k}
nor affects the validity of the constraints. Hence WLOG we can subtract
d
from
r
and
R
and then set
d=0
within the constraints and
D_{k}
. We then use the first two constraints to substitute values for
r
and
R
into the third constraint and
D_{k}
. We thus obtain a single constraint.

A=\frac{aI_{2}(0,y)+(by-ay^{2})I_{0}(0,y)+bI_{1}(y,z)-bzI_{0}(0,z)}{I_{2}(0,z)-z^{2}I_{0}(0,z)}

The denominator is
h(z)
where
h
is defined as in lemma
5
. By that lemma,
z>0
implies
h(z)<0
, so the above ratio is valid.

Both
N
and
n
are continuously differentiable with a Lipschitz derivative. Therefore, we have
N(z)=N(y)+\epsilon N^{\prime}(y)+\epsilon^{2}\nabla(y,\epsilon)=N(y)+\epsilon n(y)+\epsilon^{2}\nabla(y,\epsilon)
and
n(z)=n(y)+\epsilon n^{\prime}(y)+\epsilon^{2}\nu(y,\epsilon)=n(y)-\epsilon yn(y)+\epsilon^{2}\nu(y,\epsilon)
for some
\nu
and
\nabla
which are bounded for
y,\epsilon\in[0,X]
. Substituting the above expressions for
A
,
n(z)
,
N(z)
and
z=y+\epsilon
into
D_{k}
we obtain

D_{k}(a,b)=n(y)(2ya-b)^{2}\frac{h^{2}(y)}{h^{2}(y+\epsilon)}\epsilon+\frac{P^{(2)}b^{2}+P^{(1)}b+P^{(0)}}{h^{2}(y+\epsilon)}\epsilon^{2}

Here
P^{(2)}
,
P^{(1)}
and
P^{(0)}
are polynomials composed of
\epsilon
,
y
,
n(y)
,
N(y)
,
\nu(y,\epsilon)
,
\nabla(y,\epsilon)
and
a
terms. Importantly, the symbolic expression of these polynomials is not dependent on
K
or
k
.

Now, we re-introduce the
k
subscripts as we aggregate the values of the
D_{k}
for our fixed
K
. We obtain

objdiff=\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}D_{k}=\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}n(y_{k})(2y_{k}a_{k}-b_{k})^{2}\frac{h^{2}(y_{k})}{h^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)}\epsilon+\frac{P^{(2)}b_{k}^{2}+P^{(1)}b_{k}+P^{(0)}}{h^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)}\epsilon^{2}

Again, we note that the three polynomials do not have
k
subscripts because their symbolic expression does not depend on
k
. This is the alternative expression of
objdiff
we were looking for in step 1.

Step 2: Now
K
is no longer considered fixed. Let
C
be a positive integer and assume that
K
is a multiple of
C
. Then we break down
objdiff(K)
into
\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{\frac{K}{C}-1}D_{k}
and
\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}D_{k}
.

Let’s look at
\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}D_{k}
first, and let’s do so for a fixed value of
C
. We have
y_{k}>\frac{X}{C}
, so by lemma
5
,
h(y_{k}+\epsilon)
is bounded away from zero across all
K
and
k\geq\frac{K}{C}
. All terms that make up the polynomials
P^{(0)},P^{(1)},P^{(2)}
are bounded, except possibly
a_{k}
. Hence, if we can show that
a_{k}
is also bounded, then the polynomials are bounded.
a_{k}
and
r_{k}
are determined via the system

\begin{pmatrix}I_{2}(0,y_{k})&I_{0}(0,y_{k})\\
y_{k}^{2}&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_{k}\\
r_{k}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\int_{0}^{y_{k}}f_{2K}(x)d\mu_{x}\\
f_{2K}(y_{k})\end{pmatrix}

Since
f
is continuous,
f
is bounded on
[0,X]
, so the right-hand side is bounded. Since
y_{k}
is bounded, all entries in the 2 by 2 matrix are bounded. So, if the determinant of the matrix is bounded away from zero, then
a_{k}
and
r_{k}
are bounded. The determinant is
I_{2}(0,y_{k})-y_{k}^{2}I_{0}(0,y_{k})=h(y_{k})
. Since
y_{k}\geq\frac{X}{C}
is bounded away from zero, so is
h(y_{k})
by lemma
5
. Hence
a_{k}
is indeed bounded. So we have for some constants
B_{2},B_{1},B_{0}

\displaystyle\Big|\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\frac{P^{(2)}b_{k}^{2}+P^{(1)}b_{k}+P^{(0)}}{h^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)}\epsilon^{2}\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}(b_{k}^{2}B_{2}+|b_{k}|B_{1}+B_{0})\epsilon^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2B_{2}\epsilon}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon+\frac{2B_{1}\epsilon}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}|b_{k}|\epsilon+\frac{2B_{0}\epsilon}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\epsilon

We will now investigate each of the 3 terms in the above sum one after the other.

1.

Remember that
b_{k}
is defined to be the slope of
f_{2K}
on
[\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k+1}{K}X]
. By the intermediate value principle,
f^{\prime}
takes a value at least as large as
b_{k}
and a value at least as small as
b_{k}
on
[\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k+1}{K}X]
. Hence,
f^{\prime 2}
takes a value at least as large as
b_{k}^{2}
in
[\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k+1}{K}X]
. Let such a value be
\beta_{k}^{2}
. Because
f^{\prime 2}
is integrable over the unit Gaussian measure over any finite interval, it is also integrable over the canonical Lebesgue measure over any finite interval. Hence we have
\int_{\frac{X}{C}}^{X}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{1}=\lim_{K\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\beta_{k}^{2}\epsilon
. So
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\beta_{k}^{2}\epsilon
is bounded for sufficiently large
K
, so
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon
is bounded for sufficiently large
K
. And since
\epsilon
converges to zero as
K
converges to infinity,
\frac{2B_{2}\epsilon}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon
converges to zero.

2.

Since
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon
is bounded for sufficiently large
K
, so is
\sqrt{\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon}
, so is
(\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}|b_{k}|\epsilon)(\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\epsilon)^{-\frac{1}{2}}
by Jensen’s inequality, so is
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}|b_{k}|\epsilon
. And since
\epsilon
converges to zero as
K
converges to infinity,
\frac{2B_{1}\epsilon}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}|b_{k}|\epsilon
converges to zero.

3.

\frac{2B_{0}\epsilon}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\epsilon=\frac{2B_{0}\epsilon(X-\frac{X}{C})}{I_{0}}
also converges to zero.

So in summary, we have that, for a fixed
C
and
K
restricted to multiples of
C
,
\Big|\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\frac{P^{(2)}b_{k}^{2}+P^{(1)}b_{k}+P^{(0)}}{h^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)}\epsilon^{2}\Big|
converges to zero as
K
converges to infinity.

Now let’s look at
\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{\frac{K}{C}-1}D_{k}
. We have
\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{\frac{K}{C}-1}D_{k}=\frac{2}{I_{0}}\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}(F^{\prime 2}_{0}-2F^{2}_{0})-(F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}-2F^{2}_{\frac{K}{C}})d\mu_{x}=\frac{2}{I_{0}}\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{\prime 2}_{0}+2F^{2}_{\frac{K}{C}}-2F^{2}_{0}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}
. The first two out of those four terms are non-negative. Since
f
is bounded on
[0,X]
, so is
F_{0}
. So
\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}-2F^{2}_{0}d\mu_{x}
converges to zero as
C
converges to infinity. Finally, we turn to the
\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}
term. On
[0,\frac{X}{C}]
,
F_{\frac{K}{C}}
is an even quadratic. Denote it by
ax^{2}+r
. Setting
\delta=\frac{X}{C}
,
a
and
r
are determined via the system

\begin{pmatrix}I_{2}(0,\delta)&I_{0}(0,\delta)\\
\delta^{2}&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a\\
r\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\int_{0}^{\delta}f_{2K}(x)d\mu_{x}\\
f_{2K}(\delta)\end{pmatrix}

Thus we obtain

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\delta}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-4a^{2}I_{2}(0,\delta)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-4I_{2}(0,\delta)\Big(\frac{\int_{0}^{\delta}f_{2K}(x)d\mu_{x}-I_{0}(0,\delta)f_{2K}(\delta)}{I_{2}(0,\delta)-\delta^{2}I_{0}(0,\delta)}\Big)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-4I_{2}(0,\delta)I_{0}(0,\delta)^{2}\Big(\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\in[0,\delta]}f_{2K}(x)-f_{2K}(\delta)}{I_{2}(0,\delta)-\delta^{2}I_{0}(0,\delta)}\Big)^{2}

The denominator is clearly non-zero. By lemma
7
, we have that all values of
f
are within
o(\delta^{\frac{1}{2}})
of
f(0)
on the interval
[0,\delta]
. Since
K
is a multiple of
C
, we have
\frac{X}{K}\leq\frac{X}{C}=\delta
. Therefore, if the domain of a line segment in
f_{2K}
intersects
[0,\delta]
, that domain is contained in
[0,2\delta]
. Therefore,
f_{2K}
can only take values in
[0,\delta]
that
f
takes in
[0,2\delta]
. Therefore, all values of
f_{2K}
are also within
o(\delta^{\frac{1}{2}})
of
f(0)
on the interval
[0,\delta]
, uniformly over
K
. Hence,
\mathbb{E}_{x\in[0,\delta]}f_{2K}(x)-f_{2K}(\delta)=o(\delta^{\frac{1}{2}})
. It is easy to check that
I_{2}(0,\delta)=\Theta(\delta^{3})
,
I_{0}(0,\delta)=\Theta(\delta)
and
I_{2}(0,\delta)-\delta^{2}I_{0}(0,\delta)=\Theta(\delta^{3})
. This yields that
\int_{0}^{\delta}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}=o(1)
, so
\int_{0}^{\delta}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}
converges to zero as
\delta
converges to zero, i.e. as
C
converges to infinity.

This was the last piece of the puzzle. Now we put it all together. For some
C
and
K
a multiple of
C
we have

\displaystyle objdiff(K)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2}{I_{0}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\int_{0}^{\frac{(k+1)}{K}X}(F^{\prime 2}_{k}-2F^{2}_{k})-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-2F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2}{I_{0}}\Bigg(\Big(\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{\prime 2}_{0}d\mu_{x}\Big)-2\Big(\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{2}_{0}d\mu_{x}\Big)-\Big(\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}\Big)+2\Big(\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}\Big)

\displaystyle+\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}n(y_{k})(2y_{k}a_{k}-b_{k})^{2}\frac{h^{2}(y_{k})}{h^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)}\epsilon+\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\frac{P^{(2)}b_{k}^{2}+P^{(1)}b_{k}+P^{(0)}}{h^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)}\epsilon^{2}\Bigg)

Out of the six terms, the first, fourth and fifth are non-negative. We have shown that as
C
converges to infinity, the second and third terms converge to zero. And we have shown that for a fixed
C
as
K
converges to infinity, the sixth term converges to zero. Therefore, no matter the value of
\eta
, we can first choose a
C
and then a
K>K_{e}
which is a multiple of
C
such that
objdiff(K)
is greater than
-\eta
, as required. The constant
\frac{2}{I_{0}}
has no influence on the analysis. Step 2 is complete. Hence, we have claim 1. Hence, stage 1 is complete.

Stage 2
: The statement holds when
d_{\text{in}}=d_{\text{out}}=1
,
\mathcal{D}
has expectation zero and variance one,
f
is an odd function and the constant component of
f
is the zero function.

We proceed largely analogously to stage 1.

Again, we argue by contradiction. However, as opposed to stage 1, we assume
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})<\sqrt{3}
. If we can use this to derive a contradiction, we will have proven the strictly stronger statement
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{3}
. Denote
\int_{S}^{T}x^{p}d\mu_{x}
by
I_{p}(S,T)
for any
S\leq T
and
p
. We have
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}=\frac{\mathbb{E}f^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}f^{2}-(\mathbb{E}f)^{2}}
. Because
f
is odd, we have
\mathbb{E}f=0
. Since the linear and constant component of
f
are both the zero function, we have
f=\tilde{f}
. By proposition
6
part 1, we have
\mathbb{E}x\tilde{f}=\mathbb{E}xf=0
and so
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}=\frac{\mathbb{E}f^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}f^{2}-\frac{2}{3}(\mathbb{E}xf)^{2}}=\frac{\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-X}^{X}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}}{\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-X}^{X}f^{2}d\mu_{x}-\frac{2}{3}(\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-X}^{X}xfd\mu_{x})^{2}}
. We have
\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}I_{2}(-X,X)=1
. So we have
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}=\frac{\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}}{I_{2}(-X,X)}}{\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}f^{2}d\mu_{x}}{I_{2}(-X,X)}-\frac{2}{3}\Big(\lim_{X\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}xfd\mu_{x}}{I_{2}(-X,X)}\Big)^{2}}
. Hence, there is an
X
with
\frac{\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{x}}{I_{2}(-X,X)}}{\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}f^{2}d\mu_{x}}{I_{2}(-X,X)}-\frac{2}{3}\Big(\frac{\int_{-X}^{X}fd\mu_{x}}{I_{2}(-X,X)}\Big)^{2}}<3
and also
X>100
. For the remainder of stage 2, let
X
be this fixed value. We shorten the expression
I_{p}(-X,X)
to
I_{p}
. Rearranging, we obtain
\frac{1}{I_{2}}\int_{-X}^{X}f^{\prime 2}-3f^{2}d\mu_{x}+\frac{2}{I_{2}^{2}}(\int_{-X}^{X}xfd\mu_{x})^{2}<0
. Let
\mathcal{T}
be
\mathcal{D}
restricted to
[-X,X]
. Then our formula becomes
\frac{I_{0}}{I_{2}}(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f^{\prime 2})-\frac{3I_{0}}{I_{2}}(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f^{2})+\frac{2I_{0}^{2}}{I_{2}^{2}}(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}xf)^{2}<0
. Let
f_{K}
be the piecewise linear approximation of
f
on the interval
[-X,X]
with
K
linear segments as defined in section
10.1
. By lemma
4
, we can choose an
e>0
and
K_{e}
such that
\frac{I_{0}}{I_{2}}(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f^{\prime 2}_{2K})-\frac{3I_{0}}{I_{2}}(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}f^{2}_{2K})+\frac{2I_{0}^{2}}{I_{2}^{2}}(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{T}}xf_{2K})^{2}<-e
for all
K>K_{e}
. We write
obj(f_{2K})<-e
.

The next step in the proof is to show that for each
\eta>0
, there is a
K_{\eta}>K_{e}
and an odd cubic function
q=ax^{3}+cx
such that
obj(q)<obj(f_{2K_{\eta}})+\eta
. Because this step is quite long and tedious, we will first show how to complete stage 2 once we have shown the existence of this
K_{\eta}
and
q
. We have for arbitrary
q

\displaystyle obj(q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{I_{2}}\int_{-X}^{X}9a^{2}x^{4}+6acx^{2}+c^{2}-3a^{2}x^{6}-6acx^{4}-3c^{2}x^{2}d\mu_{x}+\frac{2}{I_{2}^{2}}(\int_{-X}^{X}ax^{4}+cx^{2}d\mu_{x})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{I_{2}}(9a^{2}I_{4}+6acI_{2}+c^{2}I_{0}-3a^{2}I_{6}-6acI_{4}-3c^{2}I_{2})+\frac{2}{I_{2}^{2}}(a^{2}I_{4}^{2}+2acI_{4}I_{2}+c^{2}I_{2}^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{I_{2}}((9I_{4}-3I_{6}+2\frac{I_{4}^{2}}{I_{2}})a^{2}+(6I_{2}-2I_{4})ac+(I_{0}-I_{2})c^{2})

If
a=0
, this becomes
\frac{(I_{0}-I_{2})c^{2}}{I_{2}}
, which is non-negative so
obj(q)\geq 0
. If
a\neq 0
, then

obj(q)=\frac{a^{2}}{I_{2}}\Big((9I_{4}-3I_{6}+2\frac{I_{4}^{2}}{I_{2}})+(6I_{2}-2I_{4})(\frac{c}{a})+(I_{0}-I_{2})(\frac{c}{a})^{2}\Big)

Inside the large parentheses, we have a quadratic in
\frac{c}{a}
. The coefficient of the quadratic term is positive. The discriminant is
\frac{32n(X)^{2}X^{4}(-3+6n(X)X+X^{2}-2N(-X)(X^{2}-3))}{-1+2N(-X)+2n(X)X}
. Since
X>100
,
X^{2}
dominates the sum in the numerator and
-1
dominates the sum in the denominator. Hence, the discriminant is negative. Therefore, the quadratic is positive everywhere, so
obj(q)>0
.

So no matter the value of
a
we have
obj(q)\geq 0
. But if we choose
\eta<e
, then from
obj(f_{2K_{\eta}})<-e
and
obj(q)<obj(f_{2K_{\eta}})+\eta
we obtain
obj(q)<0
. This is the contradiction that would complete stage 2. So we are left to show the following.

Claim 1
: For each
\eta>0
, there is a
K_{\eta}>K_{e}
and an odd cubic function
q=ax^{3}+cx
such that
obj(q)<obj(f_{2K_{\eta}})+\eta
.

We define for each
K
the odd cubic function
q_{K}=a_{K}x^{3}+c_{K}x
. We choose the parameters
a_{K}
and
c_{K}
to satisfy the following two constraints:
f_{2K}(X)=q_{K}(X)
and
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}xf_{2K}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}xq_{K}
. It is clear that for each pair of values of
f_{2K}(X)
and
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}xf_{2K}
, there exist unique values for
a_{K}
and
c_{K}
. Because
f
and hence
f_{2K}
is odd, we also have
f_{2K}(-X)=q_{K}(-X)
.

Let
objdiff(K)=obj(f_{2K})-obj(q_{K})
. The remainder of the proof of claim 1 will proceed as follows. In step 1, we will fix
K
and derive an alternative formula for
objdiff
. In step 2, we will break down that formula into a sum of terms where each term is either positive or arbitrarily close to zero for large
K
. This will then allow us to pick a
K>K_{e}
with
objdiff(K)>-\eta
for arbitrary
K_{e}
and
\eta
, and then we will have claim 1.

Step 1: Fix
K
. Define
F_{k}
,
0\leq k\leq K
as follows. On
[-X,-\frac{k}{K}X]
and
[\frac{k}{K}X,X]
,
F_{k}
equals
f_{2K}
. On
[-\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k}{K}X]
,
F_{k}
is an odd cubic that connects with
f_{2K}
at
-\frac{k}{K}X
and
\frac{k}{K}X
and has
\mathbb{E}_{x\in[-\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k}{K}X]}xF_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{x\in[-\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k}{K}X]}xf_{2K}
, which is equivalent to
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}xF_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}xf_{2K}
, to
\int_{-X}^{X}xF_{k}d\mu_{x}=\int_{-X}^{X}xf_{2K}d\mu_{x}
and to
\int_{0}^{\frac{k}{K}X}xF_{k}d\mu_{x}=\int_{0}^{\frac{k}{K}X}xf_{2K}d\mu_{x}
because both functions are odd. Then
F_{0}=f_{2K}
and
F_{K}=q_{K}
. So
objdiff=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}obj(F_{k})-obj(F_{k+1})
. As
\int_{-X}^{X}xF_{k}d\mu_{x}
is the same for all
k
, we have
objdiff=\frac{1}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\int_{-X}^{X}(F^{\prime 2}_{k}-3F^{2}_{k})-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-3F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}
. Because all functions are odd, we then have
objdiff=\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\int_{0}^{X}(F^{\prime 2}_{k}-3F^{2}_{k})-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-3F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}
. Finally, we can eliminate sections of the integral where consecutive
F
’s are equal. Then we obtain
objdiff=\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\int_{0}^{\frac{(k+1)}{K}X}(F^{\prime 2}_{k}-3F^{2}_{k})-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-3F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}
. Denote the
k
’th term of this sum by
D_{k}
.

Let’s look at a specific
D_{k}
where
k\geq 1
. For now, we will omit most
k
and
K
subscripts because
k
and
K
are considered fixed. Instead, we introduce some additional notation. Let
\epsilon=\frac{X}{K}
,
y=k\epsilon
,
z=(k+1)\epsilon
and let
bx+d
be the line segment in
f_{2K}
between
k\epsilon
and
(k+1)\epsilon
. Let
ax^{3}+rx
be the odd cubic in
F_{k}
between 0 and
k\epsilon
. Let
Ax^{3}+Rx
be the equation of the odd cubic in
F_{k+1}
between 0 and
(k+1)\epsilon
.

Then the 6 parameters
a,r,A,R,b,d
satisfy the following constraints, which arise from
F_{k}(y)=f_{2K}(y)
,
F_{k+1}(z)=f_{2K}(z)
and
\int_{0}^{z}xF_{k}d\mu_{x}=\int_{0}^{z}xF_{k+1}d\mu_{x}
respectively.

\displaystyle ay^{3}+ry

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle by+d

\displaystyle Az^{3}+Rz

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle bz+d

\displaystyle aI_{4}(0,y)+rI_{2}(0,y)+bI_{2}(y,z)+dI_{1}(y,z)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle AI_{4}(0,z)+RI_{2}(0,z)

And we have

\displaystyle D_{k}(a,r,A,R,b,d)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(b^{2}-3d^{2})I_{0}(y,z)-3b^{2}I_{2}(y,z)-6bdI_{1}(y,z)-3a^{2}I_{6}(0,y)+(9a^{2}-6ar)I_{4}(0,y)

\displaystyle+(6ar-3r^{2})I_{2}(0,y)+r^{2}I_{0}(0,y)+3A^{2}I_{6}(0,z)-(9A^{2}-6AR)I_{4}(0,z)

\displaystyle-(6AR-3R^{2})I_{2}(0,z)-R^{2}I_{0}(0,z)

We also have

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}F^{\prime}_{k}-F^{\prime}_{k+1}d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}(F^{\prime}_{k}-F^{\prime}_{k+1})d_{x}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle[(F_{k}-F_{k+1})d_{x}]_{0}^{z}-\int_{0}^{z}(F_{k}-F_{k+1})\frac{dd_{x}}{dx}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle[(F_{k}-F_{k+1})d_{x}]_{0}^{z}+\int_{0}^{z}x(F_{k}-F_{k+1})d_{x}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0+\int_{0}^{z}x(F_{k}-F_{k+1})d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Here, we use that
F_{k}
and
F_{k+1}
are odd and hence
F_{k}(0)=F_{k+1}(0)=0
. We use that
F_{k}
and
F_{k+1}
are equal to
f_{2K}
on
[z,X]
and hence
F_{k}(z)=F_{k+1}(z)
. We use that
\int_{0}^{z}xF_{k}d\mu_{x}=\int_{0}^{z}xF_{k+1}d\mu_{x}
. We also use integration by parts. This is allowed because the probability density function
d_{x}
is absolutely continuous and
F^{\prime}_{k}-F^{\prime}_{k+1}
is integrable.

Let
c
be an arbitrary constant. Then we have

\displaystyle D_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}F^{\prime 2}_{k}-3F^{2}_{k}-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-3F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}(F_{k}-cx+cx)^{\prime 2}-3(F_{k}-cx+cx)^{2}

\displaystyle-((F_{k+1}-cx+cx)^{\prime 2}-3(F_{k+1}-cx+cx)^{2})d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}(F_{k}-cx)^{\prime 2}+2c(F^{\prime}_{k}-c)+c^{2}-3(F_{k}-cx)^{2}-6(F_{k}-cx)cx-3c^{2}x^{2}

\displaystyle-((F_{k+1}-cx)^{\prime 2}+2c(F^{\prime}_{k+1}-c)+c^{2}-3(F_{k+1}-cx)^{2}-6(F_{k+1}-cx)cx-3c^{2}x^{2})d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}(F_{k}-cx)^{\prime 2}-3(F_{k}-cx)^{2}-((F_{k+1}-cx)^{\prime 2}-3(F_{k+1}-cx)^{2})

\displaystyle+2c(F^{\prime}_{k}-c)-6(F_{k}-cx)cx-2c(F^{\prime}_{k+1}-c)+6(F_{k+1}-cx)cxd\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}(F_{k}-cx)^{\prime 2}-3(F_{k}-cx)^{2}-((F_{k+1}-cx)^{\prime 2}-3(F_{k+1}-cx)^{2})d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle+2c\int_{0}^{z}F^{\prime}_{k}-F^{\prime}_{k+1}d\mu_{x}-6c\int_{0}^{z}F_{k}x-F_{k+1}xd\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}(F_{k}-cx)^{\prime 2}-3(F_{k}-cx)^{2}-((F_{k+1}-cx)^{\prime 2}-3(F_{k+1}-cx)^{2})d\mu_{x}

So subtracting a constant multiple of
x
from
F_{k}
and
F_{k+1}
simultaneously does not alter
D_{k}
. It also does not affect the validity of the constraints. Hence, WLOG, we may subtract
b
from
r
and
R
and then set
b=0
within the constraints and
D_{k}
. We then use the first two constraints to substitute values for
r
and
R
into the third constraint and
D_{k}
. We thus obtain a single constraint.

A=\frac{aI_{4}(0,y)+(\frac{d}{y}-ay^{2})I_{2}(0,y)+dI_{1}(y,z)-\frac{d}{z}I_{2}(0,z)}{I_{4}(0,z)-z^{2}I_{2}(0,z)}

The large denominator is
H(z)
where
H
is defined as in lemma
6
. By that lemma,
z>0
implies
H(z)<0
, so the large ratio is valid. Since
z>0
,
\frac{d}{z}
is valid. Since we set
k\geq 1
, we have
y>0
and so
\frac{d}{y}
is valid.

Both
N
and
n
are continuously differentiable with a Lipschitz derivative. Therefore, we have
N(z)=N(y)+\epsilon N^{\prime}(y)+\epsilon^{2}\nabla(y,\epsilon)=N(y)+\epsilon n(y)+\epsilon^{2}\nabla(y,\epsilon)
and
n(z)=n(y)+\epsilon n^{\prime}(y)+\epsilon^{2}\nu(y,\epsilon)=n(y)-\epsilon yn(y)+\epsilon^{2}\nu(y,\epsilon)
for some
\nu
and
\nabla
which are bounded for
y,\epsilon\in[0,X]
. Substituting the above expressions for
A
,
n(z)
,
N(z)
and
z=y+\epsilon
into
D_{k}
we obtain

D_{k}(a,d)=n(y)\frac{(2y^{3}a+d)^{2}}{(y+\epsilon)^{2}}\frac{H^{2}(y)}{H^{2}(y+\epsilon)}\epsilon+\frac{P^{(2)}d^{2}+P^{(1)}d+P^{(0)}}{H^{2}(y+\epsilon)y^{2}(y+\epsilon)^{2}}\epsilon^{2}

Here
P^{(2)}
,
P^{(1)}
and
P^{(0)}
are polynomials composed of
\epsilon
,
y
,
n(y)
,
N(y)
,
\nu(y,\epsilon)
,
\nabla(y,\epsilon)
and
a
terms. Importantly, the symbolic expression of these polynomials is not dependent on
K
or
k
.

Now, we re-introduce the
k
subscripts as we aggregate the values of the
D_{k}
for our fixed
K
. We obtain

objdiff=\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}D_{k}=\frac{2}{I_{2}}\Big(D_{0}+\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}n(y_{k})\frac{(2y_{k}^{3}a_{k}+d_{k})^{2}}{(y_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}\frac{H^{2}(y_{k})}{H^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)}\epsilon+\frac{P^{(2)}d_{k}^{2}+P^{(1)}d_{k}+P^{(0)}}{H^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)y_{k}^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}\epsilon^{2}\Big)

Again, we note that the three polynomials do not have
k
subscripts because their symbolic expression does not depend on
k
. This is the alternative expression of
objdiff
we were looking for in step 1.

Step 2: Now
K
is no longer considered fixed. Let
C
be a positive integer and assume that
K
is a multiple of
C
. Then we break down
objdiff(K)
into
\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\frac{K}{C}-1}D_{k}
and
\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}D_{k}
.

Let’s look at
\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}D_{k}
first, and let’s do so for a fixed value of
C
. We have
y_{k}>\frac{X}{C}
, so by lemma
6
,
H(y_{k}+\epsilon)
is bounded away from zero across all
K
and
k\geq\frac{K}{C}
, and so is
y_{k}
and
y_{k}+\epsilon
. All terms that make up the polynomials
P^{(0)},P^{(1)},P^{(2)}
are bounded except possibly
a_{k}
. Hence, if we can show that
a_{k}
is also bounded, then the polynomials are bounded.
a_{k}
and
r_{k}
are determined via the system

\begin{pmatrix}I_{4}(0,y_{k})&I_{2}(0,y_{k})\\
y_{k}^{3}&y_{k}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_{k}\\
r_{k}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\int_{0}^{y_{k}}xf_{2K}(x)d\mu_{x}\\
f_{2K}(y_{k})\end{pmatrix}

Since
f
is continuous,
f
is bounded on
[0,X]
, so the right-hand side is bounded. Since
y_{k}
is bounded, all entries in the 2 by 2 matrix are bounded. So if the determinant of the matrix is bounded away from zero, then
a_{k}
and
r_{k}
are bounded. The determinant is
y_{k}I_{4}(0,y_{k})-y_{k}^{3}I_{2}(0,y_{k})=y_{k}H(y_{k})
. Since
y_{k}\geq\frac{X}{C}
is bounded away from zero, so are both terms in this product by lemma
6
. Hence
a_{k}
is indeed bounded. So we have for some constants
B_{2},B_{1},B_{0}

\displaystyle\Big|\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\frac{P^{(2)}d_{k}^{2}+P^{(1)}d_{k}+P^{(0)}}{H^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)y_{k}^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}\epsilon^{2}\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}(d_{k}^{2}B_{2}+|d_{k}|B_{1}+B_{0})\epsilon^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2B_{2}\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}d_{k}^{2}\epsilon+\frac{2B_{1}\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}|d_{k}|\epsilon+\frac{2B_{0}\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\epsilon

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2B_{2}\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}(f(x_{k})-b_{k}x_{k})^{2}\epsilon+\frac{2B_{1}\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}|f(x_{k})-b_{k}x_{k}|\epsilon+\frac{2B_{0}\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\epsilon

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\frac{2\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}B_{2}x_{k}^{2}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon+\frac{2\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}(2B_{2}|f(x_{k})|x_{k}+B_{1}x_{k})|b_{k}|\epsilon

\displaystyle+\frac{2\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}(B_{2}f(x_{k})^{2}+B_{1}|f(x_{k})|+B_{0})\epsilon

Here we use
f(x_{k})=f_{2K}(x_{k})=b_{k}x_{k}+d_{k}
. We will now investigate each of the 3 terms in the above sum one after the other.

1.

Remember that
b_{k}
is defined to be the slope of
f_{2K}
on
[\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k+1}{K}X]
. By the intermediate value principle,
f^{\prime}
takes a value at least as large as
b_{k}
and a value at least as small as
b_{k}
on
[\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k+1}{K}X]
. Hence,
f^{\prime 2}
takes a value at least as large as
b_{k}^{2}
in
[\frac{k}{K}X,\frac{k+1}{K}X]
. Let such a value be
\beta_{k}^{2}
. Because
f^{\prime 2}
is integrable over the unit Gaussian measure over any finite interval, it is also integrable over the canonical Lebesgue measure over any finite interval. Hence we have
\int_{\frac{X}{C}}^{X}f^{\prime 2}d\mu_{1}=\lim_{K\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\beta_{k}^{2}\epsilon
. So
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\beta_{k}^{2}\epsilon
is bounded for sufficiently large
K
, so
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon
is, so
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}B_{2}x_{k}^{2}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon
is as
x_{k}^{2}<X^{2}
. And since
\epsilon
converges to zero as
K
converges to infinity,
\frac{2\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}B_{2}x_{k}^{2}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon
converges to zero.

2.

Since
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon
is bounded for sufficiently large
K
, so is
\sqrt{\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}b_{k}^{2}\epsilon}
, so is
(\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}|b_{k}|\epsilon)(\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\epsilon)^{-\frac{1}{2}}
by Jensen’s inequality, so is
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}|b_{k}|\epsilon
.
f
is bounded on
[0,X]
as
f
is continuous. Since also
x_{k}<X
,
\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}(2B_{2}|f(x_{k})|x_{k}+B_{1}x_{k})|b_{k}|\epsilon
is bounded for sufficiently large
K
. And since
\epsilon
converges to zero as
K
converges to infinity,
\frac{2\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}(2B_{2}|f(x_{k})|x_{k}+B_{1}x_{k})|b_{k}|\epsilon
converges to zero.

3.

Again,
f
is bounded on
[0,X]
and
x_{k}<X
. So
\frac{2\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}(B_{2}f(x_{k})^{2}+B_{1}|f(x_{k})|+B_{0})\epsilon<\frac{2\epsilon}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}B\epsilon=\frac{2\epsilon}{I_{2}}B(X-\frac{X}{C})
for some
B
, which converges to zero.

So in summary, we have that for a fixed
C
and
K
restricted to multiples of
C
,
\Big|\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=\frac{K}{C}}^{K-1}\frac{P^{(2)}d_{k}^{2}+P^{(1)}d_{k}+P^{(0)}}{H^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)y_{k}^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}\epsilon^{2}\Big|
converges to zero as
K
converges to infinity.

Now let’s look at
\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\frac{K}{C}-1}D_{k}
. We have
\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\frac{K}{C}-1}D_{k}=\frac{2}{I_{2}}\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}(F^{\prime 2}_{0}-3F^{2}_{0})-(F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}-3F^{2}_{\frac{K}{C}})d\mu_{x}=\frac{2}{I_{2}}\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{\prime 2}_{0}+3F^{2}_{\frac{K}{C}}-3F^{2}_{0}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}
. The first two out of these four terms are non-negative. Since
f
is bounded on
[0,X]
, so is
F_{0}
. So
\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}-3F^{2}_{0}d\mu_{x}
converges to zero as
C
converges to infinity. Finally, we turn to the
\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}
term. On
[0,\frac{X}{C}]
,
F_{\frac{K}{C}}
is an odd cubic. Denote it by
ax^{3}+rx
. Setting
\delta=\frac{X}{C}
,
a
and
r
are determined via the system

\begin{pmatrix}I_{4}(0,\delta)&I_{2}(0,\delta)\\
\delta^{3}&\delta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a\\
r\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\int_{0}^{\delta}xf_{2K}(x)d\mu_{x}\\
f_{2K}(\delta)\end{pmatrix}

So we have

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\delta}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-9a^{2}I_{4}(0,\delta)-6acI_{2}(0,\delta)-c^{2}I_{0}(0,\delta)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{-9(\delta\int_{0}^{\delta}xf_{2K}d\mu_{x}-I_{2}(0,\delta)f_{2K}(\delta))^{2}I_{4}(0,\delta)...}{(I_{4}(0,\delta)\delta-I_{2}(0,\delta)\delta^{3})^{2}}

\displaystyle\frac{...-(-\delta^{3}\int_{0}^{\delta}xf_{2K}d\mu_{x}+I_{4}(0,\delta)f_{2K}(\delta))^{2}I_{0}(0,\delta)...}{(I_{4}(0,\delta)\delta-I_{2}(0,\delta)\delta^{3})^{2}}

\displaystyle\frac{...-6(\delta\int_{0}^{\delta}xf_{2K}d\mu_{x}-I_{2}(0,\delta)f_{2K}(\delta))(-\delta^{3}\int_{0}^{\delta}xf_{2K}d\mu_{x}+I_{4}(0,\delta)f_{2K}(\delta))I_{2}(0,\delta)}{(I_{4}(0,\delta)\delta-I_{2}(0,\delta)\delta^{3})^{2}}

The denominator is clearly non-zero. By lemma
7
, we have that all values of
f
are within
o(\delta^{\frac{1}{2}})
of
f(0)
on the interval
[0,\delta]
. Since
K
is a multiple of
C
, we have
\frac{X}{K}\leq\frac{X}{C}=\delta
. Therefore, if the domain of a line segment in
f_{2K}
intersects
[0,\delta]
, that domain is contained in
[0,2\delta]
. Therefore,
f_{2K}
can only take values in
[0,\delta]
that
f
takes in
[0,2\delta]
. Therefore, all values of
f_{2K}
are also within
o(\delta^{\frac{1}{2}})
of
f(0)
on the interval
[0,\delta]
, uniformly over
K
. Because
f
is odd,
f(0)=0
and hence
f_{2K}(0)=0
. Hence,
f_{2K}(\delta)=o(\delta^{\frac{1}{2}})
and
\int_{0}^{\delta}xf_{2K}(x)d\mu_{x}=o(\delta^{\frac{5}{2}})
. We can write
I_{0}(0,\delta)
,
I_{2}(0,\delta)
and
I_{4}(0,\delta)
in terms of
\delta
,
n(\delta)
and
N(\delta)
and then replace
n
and
N
by their Taylor expansion about zero including terms up to
\delta^{7}
, using that both
n
and
N
are Lipschitz differentiable on
[0,X]
arbitrarily many times. This yields that the numerator of the big ratio is
o(\delta^{12})
and the denominator
\Theta(\delta^{12})
. So
\int_{0}^{\delta}-F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}
converges to zero as
\delta
converges to zero, i.e. as
C
converges to infinity.

This is the last piece of the puzzle. Now we put it all together. For some
C
and
K
a multiple of
C
we have

\displaystyle objdiff(K)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2}{I_{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\int_{0}^{\frac{(k+1)}{K}X}(F^{\prime 2}_{k}-3F^{2}_{k})-(F^{\prime 2}_{k+1}-3F^{2}_{k+1})d\mu_{x}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{2}{I_{2}}\Bigg(\Big(\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{\prime 2}_{0}d\mu_{x}\Big)-3\Big(\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{2}_{0}d\mu_{x}\Big)-\Big(\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{\prime 2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}\Big)+3\Big(\int_{0}^{\frac{X}{C}}F^{2}_{\frac{K}{C}}d\mu_{x}\Big)

\displaystyle+n(y_{k})\frac{(2y_{k}^{3}a_{k}+d_{k})^{2}}{(y_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}\frac{H^{2}(y_{k})}{H^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)}\epsilon+\frac{P^{(2)}d_{k}^{2}+P^{(1)}d_{k}+P^{(0)}}{H^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)y_{k}^{2}(y_{k}+\epsilon)^{2}}\epsilon^{2}\Bigg)

Out of the six terms, the first, fourth and fifth are non-negative. We have shown that as
C
converges to infinity the second and third terms converge to zero. And we have shown that for a fixed
C
as
K
converges to infinity, the sixth term converges to zero. Therefore, no matter the value of
\eta
, we can first choose a
C
and then a
K>K_{e}
which is a multiple of
C
such that
objdiff(K)
is greater than
-\eta
, as required. The constant
\frac{2}{I_{2}}
has no influence on the analysis. Step 2 is complete. Hence, we have claim 1. Hence, stage 2 is complete.

Stage 3
: The statement holds when
d_{\text{in}}=d_{\text{out}}=1
,
\mathcal{D}
has expectation zero and variance one and the constant component of
f
is the zero function.

Since the linear and constant component of
f
are both the zero function, we have
f=\tilde{f}
. By proposition
6
part 1, we have
\mathbb{E}f=0
and
\mathbb{E}xf=0
.

Let
g(x)=\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}
and
h(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}
. Then
g
is even,
h
is odd and
f=g+h
. Because
h
is odd,
\mathbb{E}h=0
, so also
\mathbb{E}g=0
. Because
g
is even,
\mathbb{E}xg=0
, so also
\mathbb{E}xh=0
. So by lemma
3
, we have
A_{g}=A_{h}=0
and
b_{g}=b_{h}=0
.

Assume
g
is not the zero function. Because
\mathbb{E}g=0
,
g
is not the constant function. So by proposition
1
,
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{g})>0
. So we can apply stage 1 to
g
and obtain
NLC(g,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
. Similarly, if
h
is not the zero function,
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{h})>0
and
NLC(h,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
.

If either
g
or
h
is the zero function,
f
is equal to
g
or
h
, so we have
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
as desired. So now assume neither
g
nor
h
is the zero function. Because
g
is even and
h
is odd, we have
\mathbb{E}gh=\mathbb{E}g^{\prime}h^{\prime}=0
. So we have

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}f^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}f^{2}+(\mathbb{E}f)^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}f^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}f^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}(g+h)^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}(g+h)^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}g^{\prime 2}+2\mathbb{E}g^{\prime}h^{\prime}+\mathbb{E}h^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}g^{2}+2\mathbb{E}gh+\mathbb{E}h^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}g^{\prime 2}+\mathbb{E}h^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}g^{2}+\mathbb{E}h^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}g^{\prime 2}+\mathbb{E}h^{\prime 2}}{\mathbb{E}g^{2}-(\mathbb{E}g)^{2}+\mathbb{E}h^{2}-(\mathbb{E}h)^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{NLC(g,\mathcal{D})^{2}\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{g})+NLC(h,\mathcal{D})^{2}\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{h})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{g})+\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{h})}

So
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}
is a weighted average of two values which are greater or equal to 2. Therefore
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
.

Stage 4
: The statement holds when
d_{\text{out}}=1
,
\mathcal{D}
has expectation zero and identity covariance and the constant component of
f
is the zero function.

We will proceed by induction on
d_{\text{in}}
. The case
d_{\text{in}}=1
is equivalent to stage 3. Now fix
d_{\text{in}}>1
and assume that the statement holds for all lower input dimensionalities. In this stage only, the letters
i
,
j
,
k
,
r
and
s
are all used to index input dimensions and range from 0 to
d_{\text{in}}-1
.

Since the linear and constant component of
f
are both the zero function, we have
f=\tilde{f}
. By proposition
6
part 1, we have
\mathbb{E}f=0
and
\mathbb{E}x[i]f=0
for all
i
. Because
\mathcal{D}
is the unit Gaussian, we have
\mathbb{E}x[i]=0
and
\mathbb{E}x[i]^{2}=1
for all
i
. These formulas will be used repeatedly throughout this stage.

Define
f_{i}(x[i])=\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}f
,
T_{i,k}(x[i])=(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[k])-(\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[k])x[i]
,
t_{i,k}(x[i],x[k])=T_{i,k}x[k]
,
P_{i,k}=\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[k]
,
p_{i,k}(x[i],x[k])=P_{i,k}x[i]x[k]
,
\hat{f}=f-\sum_{i}f_{i}-\sum_{i\neq k}t_{i,k}-\sum_{i>k}p_{i,k}
and
F_{i}=\hat{f}+\sum_{j\neq i}f_{j}+\sum_{j\neq i,k\neq j}t_{j,k}
.

Claim 1
:
\mathbb{E}T_{i,k}x[j]=0

If
i\neq j
, we have
\mathbb{E}T_{i,k}x[j]=(\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}T_{i,k})(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}x[j])=0
. So now assume
i=j
. We have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}T_{i,k}x[j]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}((\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[k])-(\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[k])x[i])x[i]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[k]x[i])-(\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[k])\mathbb{E}x[i]^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[k]-\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[k]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Claim 2:

\hat{f}
, the
f_{i}
, the
t_{i,k}
with
i\neq k
and the
p_{i,k}
with
i>k
form an orthogonal decomposition of
f
under
\mathcal{D}
.

We will verify that each pair of distinct components is indeed orthogonal.

Claim 2a
:
\mathbb{E}f_{i}f_{k}=0
when
i\neq k

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}f_{i}f_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}f)(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq k}f)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}f)(\mathbb{E}f)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Claim 2b
:
\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}t_{j,l}=0
when
i\neq k
,
j\neq l
and
(i,k)\neq(j,l)

Assume
k\neq j
and
k\neq l
. Then we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}t_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}T_{i,k}x[k]T_{j,l}x[l]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq k}T_{i,k}T_{j,l}x[l])(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}x[k])

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

We obtain the same result with
l\neq i
and
l\neq k
.

Now assume
k=l
and
i\neq j
. We have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}t_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}T_{i,k}x[k]T_{j,k}x[k]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}T_{i,k})(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,k})(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}x[k]^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}((\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[k])-(\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[k])x[i]))(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,k})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle((\mathbb{E}fx[k])-(\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[k])(\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}x[i]))(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,k})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Finally, assume
k=j
and
i=l
. We have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}t_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}T_{i,k}T_{k,i}x[i]x[k]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}T_{i,k}x[i])(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}T_{k,i}x[k])

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

using claim 1.

Claim 2c
:
\mathbb{E}p_{i,k}p_{j,l}=0
when
i>k
,
l>j
and
(i,k)\neq(j,l)

Because of the constraints on
i
,
j
,
k
and
l
, at least one of the four indices must have a value unequal to the other 3. Assume
i
has a unique value.

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}p_{i,k}p_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle P_{i,k}P_{j,l}\mathbb{E}x[i]x[j]x[k]x[l]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle P_{i,k}P_{j,l}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}x[j]x[k]x[l])(\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}x[i])

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

If
j
,
k
or
l
has a unique value, the derivation is analogous.

Claim 2d
:
\mathbb{E}f_{j}t_{i,k}=0
when
i\neq k

If
j\neq k
, we have
\mathbb{E}f_{j}t_{i,k}=(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq k}f_{j}T_{i,k})(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}x[k])=0
. If
j=k
, we have
\mathbb{E}f_{j}t_{i,k}=\mathbb{E}f_{k}T_{i,k}x[k]=(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}f_{k}x[k])(\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}T_{i,k})=(\mathbb{E}fx[k])(\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}T_{i,k})=0
.

Claim 2e
:
\mathbb{E}f_{j}p_{i,k}=0
when
i\neq k

We have either
j\neq i
or
j\neq k
. By symmetry, WLOG,
j\neq k
. Then
\mathbb{E}f_{j}p_{i,k}=P_{i,k}\mathbb{E}f_{j}x[i]x[k]=P_{i,k}(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}x[k])(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq k}f_{j}x[i])=0
.

Claim 2f
:
\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}p_{j,l}=0
when
i\neq k
,
j\neq l
.

Assume
k\neq j
and
k\neq l
. Then
\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}p_{j,l}=P_{j,l}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq k}T_{i,k}x[j]x[l])(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}x[k])=0
. Now assume
k=j
or
k=l
. By symmetry, WLOG,
k=l
. Then
\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}p_{j,l}=P_{j,k}(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}x[k]^{2})(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq k}T_{i,k}x[j])=P_{j,k}\mathbb{E}T_{i,k}x[j]=0
by claim 1.

Claim 2g
:
\mathbb{E}\hat{f}f_{j}=0

Going forward, we utilize claims 2a through 2f.

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\hat{f}f_{j}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(f-\sum_{i}f_{i}-\sum_{i\neq k}t_{i,k}-\sum_{i>k}p_{i,k})f_{j}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}ff_{j}-\sum_{i\neq j}\mathbb{E}f_{i}f_{j}-\mathbb{E}f_{j}^{2}-\sum_{i\neq k}\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}f_{j}-\sum_{i>k}\mathbb{E}p_{i,k}f_{j}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}ff_{j}-\mathbb{E}f_{j}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq j}f)f_{j}-\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}f_{j}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}f_{j}^{2}-\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}f_{j}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Claim 2h
:
\mathbb{E}\hat{f}t_{j,l}=0
when
j\neq l

Claim 1 yields
\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}x[j]=0
. So we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\hat{f}t_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(f-\sum_{i}f_{i}-\sum_{i\neq k}t_{i,k}-\sum_{i>k}p_{i,k})t_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}ft_{j,l}-\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}f_{i}t_{j,l}-\sum_{i\neq k,(i,k)\neq(j,l)}\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}t_{j,l}-\mathbb{E}t_{j,l}^{2}-\sum_{i>k}\mathbb{E}p_{i,k}t_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}ft_{j,l}-\mathbb{E}t_{j,l}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}ft_{j,l}-(\mathbb{E}fx[l]x[j])(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}x[j])-\mathbb{E}t_{j,l}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}fT_{j,l}x[l]-\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}(\mathbb{E}fx[l]x[j])x[j]-\mathbb{E}T_{j,l}^{2}x[l]^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq j}fx[l])-\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}(\mathbb{E}fx[l]x[j])x[j]-(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}^{2})(\mathbb{E}_{x[l]}x[l]^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}((\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq j}fx[l])-(\mathbb{E}fx[l]x[j])x[j])-(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}^{2})-(\mathbb{E}_{x[j]}T_{j,l}^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Claim 2i
:
\mathbb{E}\hat{f}p_{j,l}=0
when
j>l

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\hat{f}p_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(f-\sum_{i}f_{i}-\sum_{i\neq k}t_{i,k}-\sum_{i>k}p_{i,k})p_{j,l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}fp_{j,l}-\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}f_{i}p_{j,l}-\sum_{i\neq k}\mathbb{E}t_{i,k}p_{j,l}-\sum_{i>k,(i,k)\neq(j,l)}\mathbb{E}p_{i,k}p_{j,l}-\mathbb{E}p_{j,l}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}fp_{j,l}-\mathbb{E}p_{j,l}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle P_{j,l}(\mathbb{E}fx[j]x[l])-P_{j,l}^{2}\mathbb{E}x[j]^{2}x[l]^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle P_{j,l}^{2}-P_{j,l}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Claims 2a through 2i together yield Claim 2.

Let
d_{r}
be the conditional density function of
x[r]
given
x[i^{\prime}]
,
i^{\prime}\neq r
. Because
\mathcal{D}
is the unit Gaussian,
d_{r}
is the density function of the one-dimensional unit Gaussian.

Claim 3
:
\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[r]}x[s]=0
when
r\neq s

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[r]}x[s]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq r}\Big(\int_{x[r]=-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[r]}d_{r}d\mu_{1}\Big)x[s]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq r}\Big([F_{i}d_{r}]_{x[r]=-\infty}^{\infty}-\int_{x[r]=-\infty}^{\infty}F_{i}\frac{dd_{r}}{dx[r]}d\mu_{1}\Big)x[s]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq r}\Big(\int_{x[r]=-\infty}^{\infty}F_{i}x[r]d_{r}d\mu_{1}\Big)x[s]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}F_{i}x[r]x[s]

Here, we use integration by parts on a 1-dimensional subspace. This is allowed because
d_{r}
is absolutely continuous and
\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[r]}
is integrable. Because
r\neq s
, either
i\neq r
or
i\neq s
. Assume

. Continuing the above chain of equations, we have

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}F_{i}x[r]x[s]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(f-f_{i}-\sum_{k\neq i}T_{i,k}x[k]-\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}x[j]x[k])x[r]x[s]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}fx[r]x[s]-(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq r}f_{i}x[s])(\mathbb{E}_{x[r]}x[r])-\sum_{k\neq i,k\neq r}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq r}T_{i,k}x[k]x[s])(\mathbb{E}_{x[r]}x[r])

\displaystyle-(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq r}T_{i,r}x[s])(\mathbb{E}_{x[r]}x[r]^{2})

\displaystyle-\sum_{j>k,\{j,k\}\neq\{r,s\}}P_{j,k}\mathbb{E}x[j]x[k]x[r]x[s]-P_{r,s}(\mathbb{E}_{x[r]}x[r]^{2})(\mathbb{E}_{x[s]}x[s]^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}fx[r]x[s]-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq r}T_{i,r}x[s]-P_{r,s}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}T_{i,r}x[s]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

The last step uses claim 1. If
i\neq s
, the derivation is analogous.

Claim 4
:
\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}F_{i}
is the zero function of
x[i]

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}F_{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}f-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}f_{i}-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\sum_{k\neq i}T_{i,k}x[k]-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}x[j]x[k]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}f-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}f-\sum_{k\neq i}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i,k}T_{i,k})(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}x[k])-\sum_{j>k}P_{i,k}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}x[j]x[k])
