\displaystyle 0

Claim 5:

\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}F_{i}x[r]
is the zero function of
x[i]
when
r\neq i

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}F_{i}x[r]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[r]-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}f_{i}x[r]

\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\sum_{k\neq i}T_{i,k}x[k]x[r]-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}x[j]x[k]x[r]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[r]-(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}f)(\mathbb{E}_{x[r]}x[r])

\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\sum_{k\neq i,k\neq r}T_{i,k}x[k]x[r]-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}T_{i,r}x[r]^{2}

\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\sum_{j>k,\{j,k\}\neq\{i,r\}}P_{j,k}x[j]x[k]x[r]-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}P_{i,r}x[i]x[r]^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[r]-\sum_{k\neq i,k\neq r}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i,k}T_{i,k}x[r])(\mathbb{E}_{x[k]}x[k])-T_{i,r}

\displaystyle-\sum_{j>k,\{j,k\}\neq\{i,r\}}P_{j,k}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}x[j]x[k]x[r])-P_{i,r}x[i]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[r]-T_{i,r}-P_{i,r}x[i]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[r]-\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}fx[r]+(\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[r])x[i]-(\mathbb{E}fx[i]x[r])x[i]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Let
F_{i}|x[i]
and
\mathcal{D}|x[i]
denote the function
F_{i}
and distribution
\mathcal{D}
restricted to the subspace corresponding to a specific value of
x[i]
respectively. Since
\mathcal{D}
is the unit Gaussian of dimensionality
d_{\text{in}}
,
\mathcal{D}|x[i]
is the unit Gaussian of dimensionality
d_{\text{in}}-1
. Claim 4 and 5, together with lemma
3
, yield that the least squares linear fit of
F_{i}|x[i]
under
\mathcal{D}|x[i]
is the zero function. Then proposition
1
and the induction hypothesis yield
NLC(F_{i}|x[i],\mathcal{D}|x[i])\geq\sqrt{2}
and hence
\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}F_{i}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\Big(\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}\Big)^{2}
for all
x[i]
where
F_{i}|x[i]
is not the zero function. Of course, this inequality holds trivially for any
x[i]
where
F_{i}|x[i]
is the zero function, so the inequality holds regardless.

Because
\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}x[j]=0
for all
j\neq i
and values of
x[i]
, we can further apply lemma
2
to
F_{i}|x[i]
and
\mathcal{D}|x[i]
to obtain
\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[j]}=0
for all
j\neq i
.

Now we put all our results from throughout this stage together. Because
\mathcal{D}
is the unit Gaussian, we have
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}=\frac{\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{df}{dx[i]})^{2}}{\mathbb{E}f^{2}}
. For the numerator, we have

\displaystyle\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{df}{dx[i]})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{d\hat{f}}{dx[i]}+\sum_{j}\frac{df_{j}}{dx[i]}+\sum_{j\neq k}\frac{dt_{j,k}}{dx[i]}+\sum_{j>k}\frac{dp_{j,k}}{dx[i]})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{d\hat{f}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{j}\frac{df_{j}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{j\neq k}\frac{dt_{j,k}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{j>k}\frac{dp_{j,k}}{dx[i^{\prime}]})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{d\hat{f}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{df_{j}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{j\neq k}\frac{dt_{j,k}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{j>k}\frac{dp_{j,k}}{dx[i^{\prime}]})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{k\neq i}\frac{dt_{i,k}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{j>k}\frac{dp_{j,k}}{dx[i^{\prime}]})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\frac{dt_{i,i^{\prime}}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}\frac{dp_{j,i^{\prime}}}{dx[i^{\prime}]})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}+T_{i,i^{\prime}}+\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}x[j])^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}\Big(\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}^{2}+T_{i,i^{\prime}}^{2}+\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}^{2}x[j]^{2}+2\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}T_{i,i^{\prime}}

\displaystyle+2\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}x[j]+2T_{i,i^{\prime}}\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}x[j]+2\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime},k\neq i^{\prime},j\neq k}P_{j,i^{\prime}}x[j]P_{k,i^{\prime}}x[k]\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\Big(\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}^{2}+\mathbb{E}T_{i,i^{\prime}}^{2}+\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}^{2}\mathbb{E}x[j]^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}T_{i,i^{\prime}}

\displaystyle+2\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}x[j]+2\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}T_{i,i^{\prime}}x[j]+2\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime},k\neq i^{\prime},j\neq k}P_{j,i^{\prime}}P_{k,i^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}x[j]x[k]\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\Big(\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}^{2}+\mathbb{E}T_{i,i^{\prime}}^{2}+\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}^{2}+2\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime\prime}],i^{\prime\prime}\neq i}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]})T_{i,i^{\prime}}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\Big(\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}^{2}+\mathbb{E}T_{i,i^{\prime}}^{2}+\sum_{j\neq i^{\prime}}P_{j,i^{\prime}}^{2}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}(\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}^{2}+T_{i,i^{\prime}}^{2})+2\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}^{2}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}^{2}+2\sum_{j>k}P^{2}_{j,k}

For the denominator, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}f^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\hat{f}+\sum_{j}f_{j}+\sum_{j\neq k}t_{j,k}+\sum_{j>k}p_{j,k})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\hat{f}^{2}+\sum_{j}f_{j}^{2}+\sum_{j\neq k}t_{j,k}^{2}+\sum_{j>k}p_{j,k}^{2})

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}(\hat{f}^{2}+\sum_{j}f_{j}^{2}+\sum_{j\neq k}t_{j,k}^{2}+\sum_{j>k}p_{j,k}^{2}+\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\hat{f}^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}(\hat{f}^{2}+\sum_{j\neq i}f_{j}^{2}+\sum_{j\neq k,j\neq i}t_{j,k}^{2})+\mathbb{E}\sum_{j>k}p_{j,k}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}(\hat{f}+\sum_{j\neq i}f_{j}+\sum_{j\neq k,j\neq i}t_{j,k})^{2}+\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}F_{i}^{2}+\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}F_{i}^{2})+\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}_{x[i]}\Big(\mathbb{E}_{x[i^{\prime}],i^{\prime}\neq i}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}^{2}\Big)+\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2(d_{\text{in}}-1)}\sum_{i}\sum_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbb{E}\frac{dF_{i}}{dx[i^{\prime}]}^{2}+\sum_{j>k}P_{j,k}^{2}

Hence the numerator is at least twice the denominator. Hence
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}\geq 2
and
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
as required.

Stage 5
: The statement holds when
\mathcal{D}
has expectation zero and identity covariance, and the constant component of
f
is the zero function.

As in previous stages, we have
f=\tilde{f}
and
\mathbb{E}f=0
. Because the least squares linear fit to
f
is the zero function, by definition, for each
j
, the least squares linear fit to
f[j]
is the zero function. Also, by proposition
1
,
f[j]
is either the zero function or
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f[j]})>0
and hence
\mathbb{E}f[j]^{2}>0
. If
f[j]
is not the zero function, we can apply stage 4 to
f[j]
to obtain
NLC(f[j],\mathcal{D})^{2}=\frac{\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}\mathcal{J}[j,i]^{2}}{\mathbb{E}f[j]^{2}}\geq 2
. If
f[j]
is the zero function, then
\mathcal{J}[j,i]
is also the zero function for all
i
.

We have

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i,j}\mathbb{E}\mathcal{J}[j,i]^{2}}{\sum_{j}\mathbb{E}f[j]^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{j:\text{$f[j]$ not the zero function}}(\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}\mathcal{J}[j,i]^{2})}{\sum_{j:\text{$f[j]$ not the zero function}}\mathbb{E}f[j]^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{j:\text{$f[j]$ not the zero function}}NLC(f[j],\mathcal{D})^{2}\mathbb{E}f[j]^{2}}{\sum_{j:\text{$f[j]$ not the zero function}}\mathbb{E}f[j]^{2}}

So
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}
is simply the weighted average of the
NLC(f[j],\mathcal{D})^{2}
values corresponding to non-zero
f[j]
, all of which are at least 2. Note that at least one
f[j]
is non-zero because we have
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})>0
by assumption
3
. Hence,
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}\geq 2
, and so
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
.

Stage 6
: The statement holds when
\mathcal{D}
has expectation zero and the constant component of
f
is the zero function.

Since the linear and constant component of
f
are both the zero function, we have
f=\tilde{f}
. By proposition
6
part 1, we have
\mathbb{E}f=0
and
\mathbb{E}x^{T}f=0
. Let

, which is valid by assumption

. Consider

\mathcal{D}

. We have

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}f^{\prime}(xC^{-T})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}f(xC^{-T}C^{T})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}f(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

and

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}x^{T}f^{\prime}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}C^{-1}x^{T}f^{\prime}(xC^{-T})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}C^{-1}x^{T}f(xC^{-T}C^{T})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle C^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}x^{T}f(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

and

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}x

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}xC^{-T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}x)C^{-T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

and

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}x^{T}x

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(xC^{-T})^{T}(xC^{-T})

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}C^{-1}x^{T}xC^{-T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle C^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}C^{-T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle I

and

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{f^{\prime}(x),x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}(f^{\prime}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}f^{\prime}(x^{\prime}))^{T}(f^{\prime}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}f^{\prime}(x^{\prime}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}f^{\prime}(x)^{T}f^{\prime}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}f(xC^{-T}C^{T})^{T}f(xC^{-T}C^{T})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{f}

Further, we have
\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)=\mathcal{J}(xC^{T})C
. Then we have

\displaystyle NLC(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f^{\prime}(x),x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(xC^{-T}C^{T})CC^{T}\mathcal{J}(xC^{-T}C^{T})^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

Because

, the least squares linear fit to

Stage 7

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}x

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(x-\bar{x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(x-\bar{x})^{T}(x-\bar{x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{x}

Further, we have

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f^{\prime}(x),x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}})}

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

Because
\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}f^{\prime}=0
,
\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}x^{T}f^{\prime}=0
and lemma
3
, the least squares linear fit to
f^{\prime}
under
\mathcal{D^{\prime}}
is the zero function. Also, we have
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f^{\prime}(x),x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}})=\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})>0
and
\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}x=0
. So we can use stage 6 to obtain
NLC(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})\geq\sqrt{2}
, and thus
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
.

Stage 8
: The statement holds under the general conditions of theorem
2
.

We can write
f=\tilde{f}+b_{f}
. By lemma
6
, we have
\mathbb{E}\tilde{f}=\mathbb{E}x^{T}\tilde{f}=0
. By lemma
3
, the least squares linear fit to
\tilde{f}
is the zero function. We also have

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{f}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}(\tilde{f}(x)+b_{f}-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}(\tilde{f}(x^{\prime})+b_{f}))^{T}(\tilde{f}(x)+b_{f}-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}(\tilde{f}(x^{\prime})+b_{f}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}(\tilde{f}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}\tilde{f}(x^{\prime}))^{T}(\tilde{f}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}\tilde{f}(x^{\prime}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}}

and hence
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}})>0
. So we can apply stage 7 to
\tilde{f}
and obtain
NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
. Because the Jacobian of
f
and
\tilde{f}
are equal and we have
\mathrm{Cov}_{f}=\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}}
as shown above,
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})=NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})
and so
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})\geq\sqrt{2}
.

∎

Remark.
We used the Wolfram Mathematica Software to obtain the formula for
objdiff
given at the end of step 1 in claim 1 in stages 1 and 2.

10.5.3
Theorem
3
: NLC depends on the least squares fit

Theorem
3
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
be Gaussian and assume
f
is not linear. Then we have

NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}=\frac{LAR}{NAR+LAR}+\frac{NAR}{NAR+LAR}NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})^{2}

Proof.

Because
f
is not linear, by proposition
7
,
\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}})>0
, and so
NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})
is valid. By proposition
6
part 1, we have
\mathbb{E}x^{T}\tilde{f}=0
and
\mathbb{E}\tilde{f}=0
, and so
\mathbb{E}||\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}||\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}-||\mathbb{E}\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}=\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}})
. Assume
\bar{x}=0
. Then proposition
8
followed by lemma
2
yields
\mathbb{E}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}=0
, where
\tilde{\mathcal{J}}
is the Jacobian of
\tilde{f}
. Using these statements we have

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}\Tr(\mathcal{J}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}\Tr(\frac{d}{dx}(\tilde{f}+xA_{f}+b_{f})\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\frac{d}{dx}(\tilde{f}+xA_{f}+b_{f})^{T})}{\text{\scalebox{0.85}{$\Tr(\mathbb{E}_{x}(\tilde{f}(x)+xA_{f}+b_{f}-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}(\tilde{f}(x^{\prime})+x^{\prime}A_{f}+b_{f}))^{T}(\tilde{f}(x)+xA_{f}+b_{f}-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}(\tilde{f}(x^{\prime})+x^{\prime}A_{f}+b_{f}))$}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}\Tr((\tilde{\mathcal{J}}+A_{f}^{T})\mathrm{Cov}_{x}(\tilde{\mathcal{J}}+A_{f}^{T})^{T})}{\Tr(\mathbb{E}(\tilde{f}+xA_{f})^{T}(\tilde{f}+xA_{f}))}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\Tr(\mathbb{E}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{T}+\mathbb{E}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A_{f}+\mathbb{E}A_{f}^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{T}+\mathbb{E}A_{f}^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A_{f})}{\Tr(\mathbb{E}\tilde{f}^{T}\tilde{f}+\mathbb{E}(xA_{f})^{T}\tilde{f}+\mathbb{E}\tilde{f}^{T}xA_{f}+\mathbb{E}(xA_{f})^{T}xA_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}\Tr(\tilde{\mathcal{J}}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{T})+\Tr((\mathbb{E}\tilde{\mathcal{J}})\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A_{f})+\Tr(A_{f}^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathbb{E}(\tilde{\mathcal{J}})^{T})+\Tr(A_{f}^{T}\mathrm{Cov}_{x}A_{f})}{\mathbb{E}\Tr(\tilde{f}^{T}\tilde{f})+\Tr(A_{f}^{T}(\mathbb{E}x^{T}\tilde{f}))+\Tr((A_{f}^{T}(\mathbb{E}x^{T}\tilde{f}))^{T})+\mathbb{E}\Tr((xA_{f})^{T}xA_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})^{2}\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}})+\mathbb{E}||(x-\bar{x})A_{f}||_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}||\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}||xA_{f}||_{2}^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})^{2}\mathbb{E}||\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}||(x-\bar{x})A_{f}||_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}||\tilde{f}||_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}||(x-\bar{x})A_{f}||_{2}^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})^{2}(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})NAR+(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})LAR}{(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})NAR+(\mathbb{E}||f||_{2}^{2})LAR}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{LAR}{NAR+LAR}+\frac{NAR}{NAR+LAR}NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})^{2}

So now assume
\bar{x}\neq 0
. Define
f^{\prime}
and
\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
, where
f^{\prime}(x)=f(x+\bar{x})
and drawing
x
from
\mathcal{D}^{\prime}
is equivalent to drawing
x
from
\mathcal{D}
and then subtracting
\bar{x}
. Then we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}f^{\prime}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}f^{\prime}(x-\bar{x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}f(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}f(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bar{f}

and

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}x

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(x-\bar{x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

and

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}(x-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}x^{\prime})^{T}(x-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}x^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}x^{T}x

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(x-\bar{x})^{T}(x-\bar{x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{x}

and

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{f^{\prime}(x),x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}(f^{\prime}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}f^{\prime}(x^{\prime}))^{T}(f^{\prime}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}f^{\prime}(x^{\prime}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}(f^{\prime}(x)-\bar{f})^{T}(f^{\prime}(x)-\bar{f})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(f(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})-\bar{f})^{T}(f(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})-\bar{f})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(f(x)-\bar{f})^{T}(f(x)-\bar{f})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{f}

Further, we have
\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)=\mathcal{J}(x+\bar{x})
, where
\mathcal{J}^{\prime}
is the Jacobian of
f^{\prime}
. Then we have

\displaystyle NLC(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f^{\prime}(x),x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\Tr(\mathcal{J}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\mathcal{J}(x)^{T})}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

Let
xA_{f^{\prime}}+b_{f^{\prime}}
be the least squares linear fit to
f^{\prime}
and let
\tilde{f}^{\prime}=f^{\prime}-xA_{f^{\prime}}+b_{f^{\prime}}
. Then we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||f-(xA_{f}+b_{f})||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||f^{\prime}-((x+\bar{x})A_{f}+b_{f})||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||f^{\prime}-(xA_{f^{\prime}}+b_{f^{\prime}})||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||f-((x-\bar{x})A_{f^{\prime}}+b_{f^{\prime}})||_{2}^{2}

But by definition of the least squares linear fit, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||f-(xA_{f}+b_{f})||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||f-((x-\bar{x})A_{f^{\prime}}+b_{f^{\prime}})||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||f^{\prime}-(xA_{f^{\prime}}+b_{f^{\prime}})||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||f^{\prime}-((x+\bar{x})A_{f}+b_{f})||_{2}^{2}

Therefore, all four terms are equal. We obtain
A_{f^{\prime}}=A_{f}
,
b_{f^{\prime}}=b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f}
and

\displaystyle\tilde{f}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle f^{\prime}-(xA_{f^{\prime}}+b_{f^{\prime}})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle f^{\prime}-(xA_{f}+b_{f}+\bar{x}A_{f})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle f(x+\bar{x})-((x+\bar{x})A_{f}+b_{f})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\tilde{f}(x+\bar{x})

and hence
\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime}=\tilde{\mathcal{J}}(x+\bar{x})
, where
\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime}
is the Jacobian of
\tilde{f}^{\prime}
. This yields

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||\tilde{f}^{\prime}(x)||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||\tilde{f}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||\tilde{f}(x)||_{2}^{2}

and

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||f^{\prime}(x)||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||f(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||f(x)||_{2}^{2}

and

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||(x-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}x^{\prime})A_{f^{\prime}}||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||xA_{f^{\prime}}||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}||xA_{f}||_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}||(x-\bar{x})A_{f}||_{2}^{2}

and

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}^{\prime}(x),x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}(\tilde{f}^{\prime}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}\tilde{f}^{\prime}(x^{\prime}))^{T}(\tilde{f}^{\prime}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D^{\prime}}}\tilde{f}^{\prime}(x^{\prime}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(\tilde{f}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}}\tilde{f}(x^{\prime}-\bar{x}+\bar{x}))^{T}(\tilde{f}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}}\tilde{f}(x^{\prime}-\bar{x}+\bar{x}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}(\tilde{f}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}}\tilde{f}(x^{\prime}))^{T}(\tilde{f}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}}\tilde{f}(x^{\prime}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}_{\tilde{f}}

and

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\Tr(\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime}(x)^{T})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\Tr(\tilde{\mathcal{J}}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}(x-\bar{x}+\bar{x})^{T})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\Tr(\tilde{\mathcal{J}}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{x}\tilde{\mathcal{J}}(x)^{T})

and hence
LAR(f,\mathcal{D})=LAR(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})
,
NAR(f,\mathcal{D})=NAR(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})
and
NLC(f,\mathcal{D})=NLC(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})
.

Putting it all together, using
\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}x=0
and the fact that we proved the theorem for the case
\bar{x}=0
, we have

\displaystyle NLC(f,\mathcal{D})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle NLC(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D^{\prime}})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{LAR(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})}{NAR(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})+LAR(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})}+\frac{NAR(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})}{NAR(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})+LAR(f^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})}NLC(\tilde{f}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{LAR(f,\mathcal{D})}{NAR(f,\mathcal{D})+LAR(f,\mathcal{D})}+\frac{NAR(f,\mathcal{D})}{NAR(f,\mathcal{D})+LAR(f,\mathcal{D})}NLC(\tilde{f},\mathcal{D})^{2}

∎

Chapter 11
Mean field nonlinearity theory

In this chapter, we prove the theorems and propositions stated in chapter
5
concerning constructs such as activation functions, mean field architectures and A-architectures. As opposed to chapter
10
, a neural architecture in this chapter is a directed, acyclic graph where each node corresponds to a layer that uses one of a small number of operations. Each layer is a function from one real vector space to another, and therefore can be viewed as a “mini-architecture” or “mini-network” in the sense of chapter
10
. Of course, the space of functions representable by a layer graph of specific operations is much more constrained than the space of all differentiable functions considered in chapter
10
. On the other side of this tradeoff, we get to make specific predictions about metric values and layer (meta-)distributions in this chapter, and we get to enumerate all possible behaviors across activation functions.

11.1
Notation, terminology and conventions

From a notation, terminology and convention (NTC) standpoint, this chapter is a continuation of chapter
5
and therefore uses the NTCs of chapter
5
as well as chapter
2
, which are summarized in section
2.7
. Of course, we do not make use of all NTCs from those chapters. A basic understanding of prior material of this thesis should make it possible to read this chapter while referring back to section
2.7
and the
definition
environments of chapter
5
as necessary. We outline the most important constructs and give definitions that are unique to this chapter below.

11.1.1
Neural architectures

A ‘neural architecture’
f
is a function of a trainable real ‘parameter’ vector
\theta
and a real ‘input’ vector. It is also a directed, acyclic graph of ‘layers’
f_{l}
,
0\leq l\leq L
. Each layer
f_{l}
takes as input the outputs of its dependencies, which are its parents in the layer graph, as well as the parameter sub-vector
\theta_{l}
belonging to
f_{l}
.
\theta_{1}
through
\theta_{L}
make up
\theta
. A source in the graph is an ‘input layer’ and a sink is an ‘output layer’. We write
f_{k_{l}[1]}
, ..,
f_{k_{l}[\kappa_{l}]}
, ..
f_{k_{l}[K_{l}]}
for the dependencies of a layer
f_{l}
with
K_{l}\geq 1
dependencies, through we usually write
f_{k[1]}
, ..,
f_{k[\kappa]}
, ..
f_{k[K]}
as
l
is clear from context. We also write
f_{k_{l}}
for the dependency of a layer
f_{l}
with a single dependency, though we usually write
f_{k}
as
l
is clear from context.

We detail our NTCs surrounding neural architectures in section
2.3.4
. In this chapter, we consider specifically two types of architectures that we also consider in chapter
5
: A-architectures and mean field architectures. A-architectures defined in section
5.3.1
represent fully-connected architectures built from popular building blocks and design strategies, and mean field architectures defined in section
5.1.1
represent abstract templates which are used to prove results for practical architectures like A-architectures. A layer in a mean field architecture corresponds to a line in a NETSOR program in
Yang 2019
;
Yang 2020b
;
Yang 2020a
. Mean field architectures can have ‘finite input layers’, ‘readin layers’ and ‘readout layers’ as defined in sections
5.1.3
and
5.1.4
.

Both mean field and A-architectures differ slightly from the framework of section
2.3.4
, as described in their definitions. Both types have layers whose width can vary via the parameter
d_{\text{MF}}
, which is used to take the limit of infinite width. Mean field architectures can have multiple input and output layers. An A-architecture has a single input layer
f_{0}
to which the input
x
is assigned and a single output layer
f_{L}
which returns the ‘output’
f(\theta,x)
.

11.1.2
Multi-activation functions

Mean field architectures use ‘elementwise layers’ as defined in section
5.1.1
. An elementwise layer
f_{l}
uses a ‘multi-activation function’
\rho_{l}
, which is applied elementwise to the ‘elementwise dependencies’
f_{\dot{k}_{l}[1]}
, ..,
f_{\dot{k}_{l}[\dot{\kappa}_{l}]}
, ..,
f_{\dot{k}_{l}[\dot{K}_{l}]}
of
f_{l}
and applied to the ‘layer means’ of the ‘mean dependencies’
f_{\hat{k}_{l}[1]}
, ..,
f_{\hat{k}_{l}[\hat{\kappa}_{l}]}
, ..,
f_{\hat{k}_{l}[\hat{K}_{l}]}
of
f_{l}
. This yields

f_{l}=\rho_{l}.(f_{\dot{k}_{l}[1]},..,f_{\dot{k}_{l}[\dot{K}_{l}]},\mathbb{E}_{i}f_{\hat{k}_{l}[1]}[i],..,\mathbb{E}_{i}f_{\hat{k}_{l}[\hat{K}_{l}]}[i])

When considering
\rho_{l}
as a function of its inputs, we term the inputs corresponding to elementwise dependencies the ‘elementwise inputs’ and the inputs corresponding to mean dependencies the ‘mean inputs’. We denote an elementwise input corresponding to a dependency on layer
f_{l^{\prime}}
by
e_{l^{\prime}}
and a mean input corresponding to a dependency on layer
f_{l^{\prime}}
by
m_{l^{\prime}}
. This yields

\rho_{l}(e_{\dot{k}_{l}[1]},..,e_{\dot{k}_{l}[\dot{K}_{l}]},m_{\hat{k}_{l}[1]},..,m_{\hat{k}_{l}[\hat{K}_{l}]})

We usually omit the
l
subscript as it is clear from context. Note that in this chapter as in chapter
5
, when the letter
m
is used as a subscript as in
\mathcal{J}_{l,m}
, it denotes a layer index instead of a mean input.

As in table
5.1
and the definition of ‘parameter-control’ in section
5.1.2
, we usually write a multi-activation function simply as
\rho_{l}(e,m)
, where
e
and
m
are placeholders that refer to the tuples
(e_{\dot{k}_{l}[1]},..,e_{\dot{k}_{l}[\dot{K}_{l}]})
and
(m_{\hat{k}_{l}[1]},..,m_{\hat{k}_{l}[\hat{K}_{l}]})
respectively. When we use
\mathfrak{m}
or
m^{*}
as specific assignments to
m
, those terms also function as placeholders. So we write e.g.
\rho(e,m^{*})
for
\rho(e_{\dot{k}_{l}[1]},..,e_{\dot{k}_{l}[\dot{K}_{l}]},m^{*}_{\hat{k}_{l}[1]},..,m^{*}_{\hat{k}_{l}[\hat{K}_{l}]})
.

In addition to denoting the
\dot{\kappa}_{l}
’th elementwise input by
e_{\dot{k}_{l}[\dot{\kappa}_{l}]}
, we also use the vector notation
e[\dot{\kappa}_{l}]
, and similarly
m[\hat{\kappa}_{l}]
. We do this especially when we consider a multi-activation function
\rho
“in a vacuum” without reference to an architecture or layer, such as in lemmas
12
,
13
and
14
. In that case, we write
\dot{K}
for the number of components of
e
ad
\hat{K}
for the number of components of
m
. However, even then
e
and
m
still behave as placeholders. For example, in lemma
14
, the
\rho^{(n)}
do not necessarily have to have identical inputs. The components of
e
and
m
for some
\rho^{(n)}
can match up in any way with the components of
e
and
m
for any other
\rho^{(n^{\prime})}
, though there is no crossover between elementwise and mean inputs.

We sometimes reference the distribution of one or more
e
values. In that case, we consider
(e_{0},e_{1},..,e_{L})
to form a Gaussian vector with moments given by
\mathbb{E}e_{l}=\mathfrak{m}_{l}
and
\mathbb{E}e_{l}e_{m}=\mathfrak{c}_{l;m}
as defined in table
5.1
. Note that
\mathfrak{c}_{l;m}
is only defined when
f_{l}
and
f_{m}
have the same width. At any point where we reference the distribution of
e
values, the well-definedness of the
\mathfrak{m}_{l}
and
\mathfrak{c}_{l;m}
values required to specify the distribution has already been guaranteed by applying background theorem
1
to a sub-architecture in the context of an induction. Usually, the distribution of the value of a multi-activation function
\rho_{l}
is induced by its elementwise inputs.

11.1.3
Other NTCs

•

Throughout this work, we consider an activation function
\tau:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
to be an arbitrary scalar function. Conditions on
\tau
are discussed below.

•

\mu_{1}
denotes the canonical Lebesgue measure.

•

n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)
denotes the probability density function of the Gaussian with mean
\mu
and (co)variance
\sigma^{2}
evaluated at
s
.
n(\sigma^{2},s)
is short for
n(0,\sigma^{2},s)
and
n(s)
is short for
n(0,1,s)
. Note that the letter
n
can also refer to a sequence or tuple index when it is not used as a function. For example,
n(s_{n})
would refer to the unit Gaussian density evaluated at the
n
’th scalar in some sequence.

•

a_{\tau}s+b_{\tau}
denotes the least squares linear fit to
\tau(s)
under
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
and
\tilde{\tau}(s)=\tau(s)-a_{\tau}s-b_{\tau}
. LAR, CAR and NAR are defined as in section
4.4.7
.

•

c
is overloaded to refer to both the co-mean parameter of e.g. an elem-like
(q,c)
input distribution as well as a generic constant.

•

\mathcal{C}^{d}
for a positive integer
d
is the class of functions
F(\chi)=c||\chi||_{2}^{d}+c^{\prime}
for
c,c^{\prime}>0
and
\chi
of any dimensionality.

•

We say a function class
\mathcal{C}
is ‘linearly closed’ if any finite linear combination of members of
\mathcal{C}
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}
.

•

We say a multi-activation function
\rho(e,m)
is ‘elem-poly(
d
)’ if …

–

…it is a weighted sum of products of expressions that are of form (i)
e[\dot{\kappa}]^{c}
for some positive integer constant
c
, (ii)
m[\hat{\kappa}]^{c}
for some positive integer constant
c
or (iii)
(m[\hat{\kappa}]+c)^{-c^{\prime}}
for some positive real constants
c
,
c^{\prime}
.

–

… the total power of
e[\kappa]
terms in any product is at most
d
.

For example, consider

\displaystyle\rho(e,m)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e[1]^{2}e[4]^{3}m[2]m[0]m[5]^{2}(m[1]+c_{1})^{-\frac{1}{4}}(m[2]+c_{2})^{-4}

\displaystyle-e[3]^{2}e[0]e[1](m[6]+c_{3})^{-\frac{1}{2}}(m[9]+c_{4})^{-\frac{5}{2}}+e[3]m[4]

This
\rho
would be elem-poly(
d
) for any
d\geq\max(2+3,2+1+1,1)=5

•

T_{2}(s)=\max_{|s^{\prime}|\leq|s|}|\tau^{\prime\prime}(s^{\prime})|
and
T_{3}(s)=\max_{|s^{\prime}|\leq|s|}|\tau^{\prime\prime\prime}(s^{\prime})|

•

We often shorten
\lim_{\mathsf{quantity}\rightarrow\mathsf{value}}
to
\lim_{\mathsf{quantity}}
when
\mathsf{value}
is clear from context.

•

We use the notation and terminology of section
2.4.1
for our layer operations.

•

A valid logical ordering of results in this chapter is as follows: lemmas
8
through
17
, propositions
10
,
11
,
17
,
12
through
16
, theorems
4
through
7
, and propositions
18
,
19
. The proof of a result may depend on another result that comes before it but not on a result that comes after it in this ordering.

11.2
General assumptions

In contrast to chapter
10
, we do not assume differentiability for all results in this chapter. Differentiability and continuity conditions are always stated explicitly in the results of this chapter or come along with the definition of an A-architecture given in section
5.3.1
.

We only make the following assumption throughout.

Assumption 6
.

Simple expressions involving
\tau
, its derivatives, its left and right derivative, as well as
\max
operators such as those involved in
T_{2}
and
T_{3}
defined above or those used in lemma
18
, are integrable with respect to any Gaussian measure, where we use the term “integrable” as defined in section
2.6.2
. For example, expressions like
\tau(s)
,
\tau^{\prime}(s)^{2}
and
sT_{3}(s)\tau^{\prime\prime\prime}(t)
are assumed to be integrable, assuming the higher derivatives are valid. We assume that any integral of such an expression over a multi-dimensional Gaussian measure can be broken down into a sequence of 1-dimensional integrals. We assume that such simple expressions, when multiplied with a Gaussian density, converge to zero along any direction.

This assumption is mild, as we argue in section
2.6.2
. Gaussian distributions are very light-tailed. When
\tau
is at least continuous, which we assume in most results, it is integrable over any bounded set with respect to the canonical Lebesgue measure or any Gaussian measure.

Whenever we consider an expectation or integral involving a multi-activation function
\rho
, the validity of that integral is guaranteed by background theorem
1
or background corollary
2
. We did not check which implicit integrability assumptions were present in
Yang 2019
. The parameter-control assumption is clearly related to integrability, though it is also clearly not enough as the function that assigns 1 to rational numbers and 0 to non-rational numbers is controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{\text{E2}}
but not integrable. It is possible that continuous
\tau
and
\rho
that are (parameter-)controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{\text{E2}}
fulfill all integrability requirements of this chapter and
Yang 2019
, though we did not check this. Note that if
\tau
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{\text{E2}}
, so is e.g.
T_{2}
and
T_{3}
.

11.3
Lemmas

Lemma 8
.

Let
F:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
be a continuous, non-negative function that is integrable with respect to
d\mu_{1}
and not zero everywhere. Then
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}}Fd\mu_{1}>0
.

Proof.

Let
\chi\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}
be such that
F(\chi)>0
. Because
F
is continuous, there exists an open set
S
containing
\chi
and
\epsilon>0
such that
F>\epsilon
in
S
. Becasue
S
is open,
\mu_{1}(S)>0
. Since
F
is non-negative,
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}}Fd\mu_{1}\geq\int_{S}Fd\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{1}(S)\epsilon>0
as required.
∎

Lemma 9
.

Let
p\geq 0
be an integer,
\lambda>0
and let
F:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
be a function that is right-continuous at zero. Assume
s^{p}F(s)n(\lambda^{2},s)
is integrable with respect to
d\mu_{1}
on
[0,\infty)
for all
\lambda>0
. Then

\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow 0}\lambda^{-p}\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}F(s)n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}=F(0)\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}n(1,s)d\mu_{1}

Proof.

Let
D(s)=F(s)-F(0)
. Because
\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}<\infty
for all
\lambda>0
, we have
\int_{0}^{\infty}|D(s)|s^{p}n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}(|F(s)|+|F(0)|)s^{p}n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}<\infty
. Let
D_{\text{int}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}|D(s)|s^{p}n(1,s)d\mu_{1}
and
P_{\text{int}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}n(1,s)d\mu_{1}
. Because
F
is right-continuous at 0,
F
is bounded in
[0,\delta]
for some
\delta>0
. Let
\lambda<\min(\delta^{2},1)
and
B(\lambda)=\max_{0\leq s\leq\sqrt{\lambda}}|D(s)|
. Then we have

\displaystyle|\lambda^{-p}\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}F(s)n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}-F(0)\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}n(1,s)d\mu_{1}|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle|\lambda^{-p}\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}F(s)n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}-F(0)\int_{0}^{\infty}\lambda^{-p}s^{p}n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle|\lambda^{-p}\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}D(s)n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\lambda^{-p}\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}|D(s)|n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lambda^{-p}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\lambda}}s^{p}|D(s)|n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}+\lambda^{-p}\int_{\sqrt{\lambda}}^{\infty}s^{p}|D(s)|n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle B(\lambda)\lambda^{-p}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\lambda}}s^{p}n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}+\lambda^{-p}\int_{\sqrt{\lambda}}^{\infty}s^{p}|D(s)|\frac{n(\lambda^{2},\sqrt{\lambda})}{n(1,\sqrt{\lambda})}n(1,s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle B(\lambda)\lambda^{-p}\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}+\lambda^{-p}\frac{n(\lambda^{2},\sqrt{\lambda})}{n(1,\sqrt{\lambda})}D_{\text{int}}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle B(\lambda)\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{p}n(1,s)d\mu_{1}+\lambda^{-p}\frac{n(\lambda^{2},\sqrt{\lambda})}{n(1,\sqrt{\lambda})}D_{\text{int}}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle B(\lambda)P_{\text{int}}+\lambda^{-p}\frac{n(\lambda^{2},\sqrt{\lambda})}{n(1,\sqrt{\lambda})}D_{\text{int}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle B(\lambda)P_{\text{int}}+\lambda^{-p}\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\lambda^{2}}}e^{-\frac{\lambda}{2\lambda^{2}}}}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{\lambda}{2}}}D_{\text{int}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle B(\lambda)P_{\text{int}}+\lambda^{-p-1}e^{-\frac{1}{2\lambda}+\frac{\lambda}{2}}D_{\text{int}}

B(\lambda)
converges to 0 as
\lambda
converges to 0 from the right due to the right-continuity of
F
.
\lambda^{-p-1}e^{-\frac{1}{2\lambda}+\frac{\lambda}{2}}
converges to zero exponentially as
\lambda
converges to zero.

∎

Lemma 10
.

Let
F(s):\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
be a non-negative function which is bounded on any bounded interval and integrable with respect to any Gaussian measure. Let
\mu_{\text{max}}
and
\sigma_{\text{max}}
be positive constants. Then
\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})}F(s)
is bounded over
-\mu_{\text{max}}\leq\mu\leq\mu_{\text{max}}
and
0\leq\sigma\leq\sigma_{\text{max}}
, where
\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,0)}F(s)
is defined as
F(\mu)
.

Proof.

Since
F
is non-negative,
\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})}F(s)
is bounded below by zero for all
\mu
,
\sigma
. Hence, for the rest of this proof we will concern ourselves only with upper bounds. Throughout this proof, we assume
-\mu_{\text{max}}\leq\mu\leq\mu_{\text{max}}
and
0\leq\sigma\leq\sigma_{\text{max}}
.

First consider the case
\sigma=0
. Then
\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})}F(s)
is equal to a value taken by
F
in
[-\mu_{\text{max}},\mu_{\text{max}}]
.
F
is bounded there, so
\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})}F(s)
is bounded as well. Let this bound be
B_{4}
.

Going forward, we assume
0<\sigma\leq\sigma_{\text{max}}
holds.

Consider some
s\leq-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}}
. Then
n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)\leq n(-\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma^{2},s)
. On the interval
(0,\sigma_{\text{max}}]
,
n(-\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma^{2},s)
is differentiable as a function of
\sigma
. We have

\displaystyle\frac{dn(-\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma^{2},s)}{d\sigma}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}(-\sigma^{-2}+(s+\mu_{\text{max}})^{2}\sigma^{-4})e^{-\frac{(s+\mu_{\text{max}})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}(-\sigma^{-2}+(-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}}+\mu_{\text{max}})^{2}\sigma^{-4})e^{-\frac{(s+\mu_{\text{max}})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\frac{\sigma^{-4}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}(\sigma_{\text{max}}^{2}-\sigma^{2})e^{-\frac{(s+\mu_{\text{max}})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle 0

Therefore,
n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)\leq n(-\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma^{2},s)\leq(-\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma_{\text{max}}^{2},s)
. Similarly, when we consider
s\geq\mu_{\text{max}}+\sigma_{\text{max}}
we obtain
n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)\leq n(\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma_{\text{max}}^{2},s)
.

Because
F
is integrable with respect to any Gaussian measure, we can set

B_{1}=\int_{s=-\infty}^{-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}}}F(s)n(-\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma_{\text{max}}^{2},s)d\mu_{1}<\infty

and

B_{2}=\int_{s=\mu_{\text{max}}+\sigma_{\text{max}}}^{\infty}F(s)n(\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma_{\text{max}}^{2},s)d\mu_{1}<\infty

Also,
F
is bounded on
[-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}},\mu_{\text{max}}+\sigma_{\text{max}}]
. Let this bound be
B_{3}
. Finally, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})}F(s)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{s=-\infty}^{-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}}}F(s)n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)d\mu_{1}+\int_{s=-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}}}^{\mu_{\text{max}}+\sigma_{\text{max}}}F(s)n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle+\int_{s=\mu_{\text{max}}+\sigma_{\text{max}}}^{\infty}F(s)n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int_{s=-\infty}^{-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}}}F(s)n(-\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma_{\text{max}}^{2},s)d\mu_{1}+\int_{s=-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}}}^{\mu_{\text{max}}+\sigma_{\text{max}}}B_{3}n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle+\int_{s=\mu_{\text{max}}+\sigma_{\text{max}}}^{\infty}F(s)n(\mu_{\text{max}},\sigma_{\text{max}}^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle B_{1}+B_{2}+B_{3}\int_{s=-\mu_{\text{max}}-\sigma_{\text{max}}}^{\mu_{\text{max}}+\sigma_{\text{max}}}n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle B_{1}+B_{2}+B_{3}\int_{s=-\infty}^{\infty}n(\mu,\sigma^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle B_{1}+B_{2}+B_{3}

So
\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})}F(s)
is bounded by
B_{1}+B_{2}+B_{3}
.

Therefore, no matter whether
\sigma=0
, we have that
\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})}F(s)
is bounded by the maximum of
B_{4}
and
B_{1}+B_{2}+B_{3}
, as required.

∎

Lemma 11
.

Let
a_{\tau}s+b_{\tau}
be the least squares linear fit to
\tau(s)
under
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
. Let
\tilde{\tau}=\tau-a_{\tau}s-b_{\tau}
. Let
a_{\tilde{\tau}}s+b_{\tilde{\tau}}
be the least squares linear fit to
\tilde{\tau}(s)
under
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
. Let
s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
. Then
a_{\tau}=\mathbb{E}s\tau(s)
,
b_{\tau}=\mathbb{E}\tau(s)
,
a_{\tilde{\tau}}=\mathbb{E}s\tilde{\tau}(s)=0
and
b_{\tilde{\tau}}=\mathbb{E}\tilde{\tau}(s)=0
.

Proof.

The standard formula for the least squares linear fit yields

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}a_{\tau}\\
b_{\tau}\end{pmatrix}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{E}s^{2}&\mathbb{E}s\\
\mathbb{E}s&1\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{E}s\tau\\
\mathbb{E}\tau\end{pmatrix}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{E}s\tau\\
\mathbb{E}\tau\end{pmatrix}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{E}s\tau\\
\mathbb{E}\tau\end{pmatrix}

Similarly,
a_{\tilde{\tau}}=\mathbb{E}s\tilde{\tau}=\mathbb{E}s(\tau-a_{\tau}s-b_{\tau})=a_{\tau}-a_{\tau}\mathbb{E}s^{2}-b_{\tau}\mathbb{E}s=0
and
\tilde{b}=\mathbb{E}\tilde{\tau}=\mathbb{E}(\tau-a_{\tau}s-b_{\tau})=b_{\tau}-b_{\tau}=0
.
∎

Lemma 12
.

Let
\rho(e,m)
be a multi-activation function. Let
m^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{\hat{K}}
be a fixed assignment to its mean inputs and let
M^{*}
be an open set containing
m^{*}
. Let
\mathcal{C}
be some function class. Assume:

•

\mathcal{C}
is linearly closed.

•

\rho(e,m^{*})
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}
as a function of
e
.

•

\rho(e,m)
is differentiable for
m\in M^{*}
.

•

For each
1\leq\hat{\kappa}\leq\hat{K}
,
\max_{m\in M^{*}}\Big|\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm[\hat{\kappa}]}\Big|
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}
as a function of
e
.

Then
\rho
is parameter-controlled by
\mathcal{C}
at
m^{*}
.

Proof.

We will look at the conditions of parameter-control in turn.
\rho(e,m^{*})
being controlled by
\mathcal{C}
is a condition of this proposition. Let
\rho^{\text{mean}}(m)=||m-m^{*}||_{2}
when
m\in M^{*}
and
\infty
otherwise. This yields that
\rho^{\text{mean}}(m^{*})=0
and that
\rho^{\text{mean}}
is continuous at
m^{*}
. Let
\rho^{\text{elem}}=\sum_{\hat{\kappa}=1}^{\hat{K}}\max_{m\in M^{*}}\Big|\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm[\hat{\kappa}]}\Big|
. By assumption, it is the sum of functions controlled by
\mathcal{C}
, which is controlled by
\mathcal{C}
as
\mathcal{C}
is linearly closed. If
m\not\in M^{*}
, clearly we have
|\rho(e,m)-\rho(e,m^{*})|\leq\rho^{elem}(e)\rho^{mean}(m)=\infty
. Otherwise, we have

\displaystyle\Big|\rho(e,m)-\rho(e,m^{*})\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle||m-m^{*}||_{2}\max_{m\in M^{*}}\Big|\Big|\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm}\Big|\Big|_{2}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle||m-m^{*}||_{2}\max_{m\in M^{*}}\Big|\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm}\Big|_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle||m-m^{*}||_{2}\sum_{\hat{\kappa}=1}^{\hat{K}}\max_{m\in M^{*}}\Big|\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm[\hat{\kappa}]}\Big|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\rho^{\text{mean}}(m)\rho^{\text{elem}}(e)

as required.

∎

Lemma 13
.

Let
\rho(e,m)
be a multi-activation function that is elem-poly
(d)
. Let
m^{*}
be a fixed assignment to
m
such that
m^{*}[\hat{\kappa}]\geq 0
for any
\hat{\kappa}
for which an
(m[\hat{\kappa}]+c)^{c^{\prime}}
expression appears in
\rho
. Let
M(m^{*})
be the open hypercube with center
m^{*}
and side length equal to the least
c
among
(m[\hat{\kappa}]+c)^{-c^{\prime}}
expressions that appear in
\rho
.

Then:

1.

For each
1\leq\hat{\kappa}\leq\hat{K}
,
\max_{m\in M(m^{*})}\Big|\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm[\hat{\kappa}]}\Big|
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{d}
as a function of
e
.

2.

\rho
is parameter-controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{d}
at
m^{*}
.

Proof.

Polynomials of degree at most
d
are controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{d}
, so
\rho(e,m^{*})
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{d}
. If
\rho
has no mean dependencies, that is all that needs to be checked for statement 2, and statement 1 is trivial. So now assume that
\rho
does have one or more mean dependencies. We note that, by construction, for each
m\in M(m^{*})
, the base of each
(m[\hat{\kappa}]+c)^{-c^{\prime}}
expression that appears in
\rho
is positive, so
\rho
is both well-defined and differentiable with respect to any
m[\hat{\kappa}]
.

Let
s
be the side length of
M(m^{*})
. Let
\lceil\rho\rceil
be a function of
e
that is derived from
\rho
by (i) fixing each expression
m[\hat{\kappa}]
that appears to
|m^{*}[\hat{\kappa}]|+\frac{s}{2}
, (ii) fixing each
(m[\hat{\kappa}]+c)^{-c^{\prime}}
that appears to
(m^{*}[\hat{\kappa}]-\frac{s}{2}+c)^{-c^{\prime}}
and (iii) changing each minus in front of a term into a plus. It is easy to check that
\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm[\hat{\kappa}]}
for any
\hat{\kappa}
is also elem-poly(
d
). Finally, it is easy to check that
\max_{m\in M^{*}}\Big|\frac{d\rho}{dm[\hat{\kappa}]}\Big|\leq\Big\lceil\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm[\hat{\kappa}]}\Big\rceil
. But
\Big\lceil\frac{d\rho(e,m)}{dm[\hat{\kappa}]}\Big\rceil
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{d}
, as it is a polynomial of degree at most
d
. This yields statement 1.

For statement 2, we use lemma
12
.
\mathcal{C}^{d}
is linearly closed, and we already showed the other three conditions of the lemma.
∎

Lemma 14
.

Let all
\rho^{(1)}
, ..,
\rho^{(N)}
be multi-activation functions which do not have to have the same elementwise or mean inputs as detailed in section
11.1.2
. Let them all be parameter-controlled by
\mathcal{C}
for some linearly closed class
\mathcal{C}
at some
m^{*}
. Then any linear combination
\rho=\sum_{n=1}^{N}w^{(n)}\rho^{(n)}
is also parameter-controlled by
\mathcal{C}
at
m^{*}
.

Proof.

Since the
\rho^{(n)}
are parameter-controlled, there exist corresponding functions
\rho^{(n)\text{elem}}
and
\rho^{(n)\text{mean}}
. WLOG
\rho^{(n)\text{elem}}\geq 0
for all
n
. We will check the 5 conditions of the parameter-control property for
\rho
using
\rho^{\text{elem}}=\sum_{n}\sqrt{|w^{(n)}|}\rho^{(n)\text{elem}}
and
\rho^{\text{mean}}=\sum_{n}\sqrt{|w^{(n)}|}\rho^{(n)\text{mean}}
.

For each
n
, we have
|\rho^{(n)}(e,m^{*})|\leq F^{(n)}
for some
F^{(n)}\in\mathcal{C}
, so
|\rho(e,m^{*})|\leq\sum_{n}|w^{(n)}|F^{(n)}
.
\sum_{n}|w^{(n)}|F^{(n)}
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}
because
\mathcal{C}
is linearly closed, so
\rho(e,m^{*})
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}
. Analogously,
\rho^{\text{elem}}
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}
.

If the
\rho^{(n)\text{mean}}
are zero and continuous at
m^{*}
, so is any linear combination of them. Finally, we have

\displaystyle|\rho(e,m)-\rho(e,m^{*})|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}|w^{(n)}||\rho^{(n)}(e,m)-\rho^{(n)}(e,m^{*})|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}|w^{(n)}|\rho^{(n)\text{elem}}\rho^{(n)\text{mean}}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\Big(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sqrt{|w^{(n)}|}\rho^{(n)\text{elem}}\Big)\Big(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sqrt{|w^{(n)}|}\rho^{(n)\text{mean}}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\rho^{\text{elem}}\rho^{\text{mean}}

as required.

∎

Lemma 15
.

Let
F:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
be integrable with respect to any Gaussian measure. Let
\hat{\Sigma}
be a positive definite symmetric matrix. Then

\lim_{\Sigma\rightarrow\hat{\Sigma}}\mathbb{E}_{\chi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)}F(\chi)=\mathbb{E}_{\chi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\hat{\Sigma})}F(\chi)

Proof.

We argue by contradiction. Assume there is an
\epsilon
such that
|\mathbb{E}_{\chi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)}F(\chi)-\mathbb{E}_{\chi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\hat{\Sigma})}F(\chi)|>\epsilon
for
\Sigma
arbitrarily close to
\hat{\Sigma}
. Let
s
be the largest eigenvalue of
\hat{\Sigma}
. Then there exists a constant
C
such that, for any
\chi
with
||\chi||_{2}>C
and any positive definite symmetric matrix
\Sigma
with eigenvalues less than
2s
, we have
n(3sI,\chi)>n(\Sigma,\chi)
. So for any such
\Sigma
and
c>C
we have

\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}_{\chi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)}F(\chi)-\mathbb{E}_{\chi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\hat{\Sigma})}F(\chi)|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}_{d_{\text{in}}}}F(\chi)(n(\Sigma,\chi)-n(\hat{\Sigma},\chi))d\mu_{1}\Big|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big|\int_{||\chi||_{2}>c}F(\chi)(n(\Sigma,s)-n(\hat{\Sigma},\chi))d\mu_{1}+\int_{||\chi||_{2}\leq c}F(\chi)(n(\Sigma,s)-n(\hat{\Sigma},\chi))d\mu_{1}\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int_{||\chi||_{2}>c}|F(\chi)|n(\Sigma,X)d\mu_{1}+\int_{||\chi||_{2}>c}|F(\chi)|n(\hat{\Sigma},\chi)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle+\Big|\int_{||\chi||_{2}\leq c}F(\chi)(n(\Sigma,s)-n(\hat{\Sigma},\chi))d\mu_{1}\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int_{||\chi||_{2}>c}|F(\chi)|n(3sI,\chi)d\mu_{1}+\int_{||\chi||_{2}>c}|F(\chi)|n(3sI,\chi)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle+\Big|\int_{||\chi||_{2}\leq c}F(\chi)(n(\Sigma,s)-n(\hat{\Sigma},\chi))d\mu_{1}\Big|

Because
F
is integrable with respect to any Gaussian measure, the first two terms converge to zero as
c
converges to infinity. So we can choose
c
large enough that they sum to less than
\frac{1}{2}\epsilon
. Now consider
c
fixed to that value. Then the third term is a product between a function that is bounded on the bounded set
||\chi||_{2}\leq c
because it is controlled and a function that converges to zero uniformly as
\Sigma
converges to
\hat{\Sigma}
. So the third term converges to zero, so it is eventually less than
\frac{1}{2}\epsilon
. Also, as
\Sigma
converges to
\hat{\Sigma}
, its eigenvalues are eventually less than
2s
. But that means that
|\mathbb{E}_{\chi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)}F(\chi)-\mathbb{E}_{\chi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\hat{\Sigma})}F(\chi)|
is eventually less than
\epsilon
. Contradiction.
∎

Lemma 16
.

Let
A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\
b&d\end{pmatrix}
and
A^{\prime}=\begin{pmatrix}a^{\prime}&b^{\prime}\\
b^{\prime}&d^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}
be two full rank matrices with non-negative diagonal entries and equal off-diagonal entries. Let
c>0
and
c^{\prime}>0
. Then
cA+c^{\prime}A^{\prime}
is full rank, has non-negative diagonal entries and equal off-diagonal entries.

Proof.

We have

cA+c^{\prime}A^{\prime}=\begin{pmatrix}ca+c^{\prime}a^{\prime}&cb+c^{\prime}b^{\prime}\\
cb+c^{\prime}b^{\prime}&cd+c^{\prime}d^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}

Clearly, the diagonal entries are non-negative and off-diagonal elements are equal.
A
and
A^{\prime}
having full rank corresponds to
ad-b^{2}>0
and
a^{\prime}d^{\prime}-b^{\prime 2}>0
respectively. We have

\displaystyle(ca+c^{\prime}a^{\prime})(cd+c^{\prime}d^{\prime})-(cb+c^{\prime}b^{\prime})^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c^{2}(ad-b^{2})+c^{\prime 2}(a^{\prime}d^{\prime}-b^{\prime 2})+cc^{\prime}(ad^{\prime}+a^{\prime}d-2bb^{\prime})

\displaystyle>

\displaystyle cc^{\prime}(ad^{\prime}+a^{\prime}d-2bb^{\prime})

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle cc^{\prime}(2\sqrt{ad^{\prime}a^{\prime}d}-2bb^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2cc^{\prime}(\sqrt{ad}\sqrt{a^{\prime}d^{\prime}}-bb^{\prime})

\displaystyle>

\displaystyle 2cc^{\prime}(\sqrt{b^{2}}\sqrt{b^{\prime 2}}-bb^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

as required. Here, we use that the arithmetic mean is larger than the geometric mean for non-negative reals.

∎

Lemma 17
.

Let
(A)_{n}
be an infinite sequence of independent random matrices. Let
(u)_{n}
be the infinite sequence of unit Gaussian random vectors where the dimensionality of
u_{n}
is equal to the right dimension of
A_{n}
. Assume that
||A_{n}u_{n}||_{2}
converges to some limit
\Lambda
almost surely. Then
||A_{n}||_{F}
converges to
\Lambda
almost surely.

Proof.

We argue by contradiction. Assume
||A_{n}||_{F}
does not converge almost surely to
\Lambda
. Then
||A_{n}||_{F}^{2}
does not converge almost surely to
\Lambda^{2}
. By the Borel-Cantelli lemma, there exists an
\epsilon
such that
\sum_{n}P(\big|||A_{n}||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|>\epsilon)=\infty
, where
P(\mathsf{event})
denotes the probability of an event.

We make the following additional definitions.

•

A
is some fixed matrix of size
D^{\text{left}}\times D^{\text{right}}
with
\big|||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|>\epsilon
.

•

UCV^{T}
is the singular value decomposition of
A
.

•

D=\min(D^{\text{left}},D^{\text{right}})

•

c_{1}
, ..,
c_{D}
are the singular values of
A
.

•

u
/
u^{D}
is the unit Gaussian vector of dimensionality
D^{\text{right}}
/
D
.

For now, we study our fixed
A
. Because vector length and the unit Gaussian are rotation invariant, we have that the distribution of
||Au||_{2}^{2}=||UCV^{T}u||_{2}^{2}
is the same as that of
||Cu^{D}||_{2}^{2}=\sum_{d=1}^{D}c_{d}^{2}u[d]^{2}
. So
\mathbb{E}_{u}||Au||_{2}^{2}=\sum_{d=1}^{D}c_{d}^{2}
and
\mathbb{V}_{u}||Au||_{2}^{2}=2\sum_{d=1}^{D}c_{d}^{4}
and hence
2(\mathbb{E}_{u}||Au||_{2}^{2})^{2}\geq\mathbb{V}_{u}||Au||_{2}^{2}
.
\mathbb{V}
is the variance operator. Also, it is well-known that
||A||_{F}^{2}=\sum_{d=1}^{D}c_{d}^{2}
holds.

Since
\big|||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|>\epsilon
, we have either
||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}>\epsilon
or
||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}<-\epsilon
. Assume for now
||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}>\epsilon
. Let
E_{1}
be the event that
\big|||Au||_{2}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}
. Let
E_{2}
be the event that
||Au||_{2}^{2}>||A||_{F}^{2}
. Let
E_{3}
be the complementary event. Denote the expectation of
||Au||_{2}^{2}-||A||_{F}^{2}
under the three events also by
E_{1}
through
E_{3}
and denote the probabilities of the events as
P_{1}
through
P_{3}
. Then

0=\mathbb{E}_{u}||Au||_{2}^{2}-||A||_{F}^{2}=P_{1}E_{1}+P_{2}E_{2}+P_{3}E_{3}\leq P_{2}E_{2}-P_{1}\Big(||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\Big)

Assume
P_{1}\geq\frac{1}{2}
. Then we must also have
P_{2}>0
and so
E_{2}\geq\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}\Big(||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\Big)
. Also we have

2(||A||_{F}^{2})^{2}=2(\mathbb{E}_{u}||Au||_{2}^{2})^{2}\geq\mathbb{V}_{u}||Au||_{2}^{2}\geq P_{1}E_{1}^{2}+P_{2}E_{2}^{2}+P_{3}E_{3}^{2}\geq P_{2}E_{2}^{2}

\geq\frac{P_{1}^{2}}{P_{2}}\Big(||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\Big)^{2}\geq\frac{\frac{1}{2}^{2}}{1-P_{1}}\Big(||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\Big)^{2}

So we obtain

P_{2}+P_{3}=1-P_{1}\geq\frac{\Big(||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\Big)^{2}}{8(||A||_{F}^{2})^{2}}\geq\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{32(\Lambda^{2}+\epsilon)^{2}}

If
P_{1}<\frac{1}{2}
, we obtain
P_{2}+P_{3}\geq\frac{1}{2}
. So across both cases we obtain
P_{2}+P_{3}\geq\min(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{32(\Lambda^{2}+\epsilon)^{2}})>0
. Let this lower bound be
B
.

If we have
||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}<-\epsilon
instead of
||A||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}>\epsilon
, there is an analogous argument. We define
E_{2}
as
||Au||_{2}^{2}<||A||_{F}^{2}
and obtain
P_{2}(-E_{2})\geq P_{1}\Big(\Lambda^{2}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}-||A||_{F}^{2}\Big)
which also leads to
P_{2}+P_{3}\geq B
.

Now we return to our random sequence
(A)_{n}
. We have

\displaystyle\sum_{n}P\Big(\big|||A_{n}u_{n}||_{2}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|>\frac{\epsilon}{2}\Big)

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\sum_{n}P\Big(\big|||A_{n}u_{n}||_{2}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|>\frac{\epsilon}{2}\Big|\big|||A_{n}||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|>\epsilon\Big)P\Big(\big|||A_{n}||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|>\epsilon\Big)

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle B\sum_{n}P\Big(\big|||A_{n}||_{F}^{2}-\Lambda^{2}\big|>\epsilon\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\infty

So by the second Borel-Cantelli lemma,
||A_{n}u_{n}||_{2}^{2}
does not converge to
\Lambda^{2}
almost surely, so
||A_{n}u_{n}||_{2}
does not converge to
\Lambda
almost surely. Contradiction, as required.

∎

11.4
Propositions

Proposition
10
.

Let
\mathcal{M}_{1}
be a meta-distribution over distributions
\mathcal{X}_{1}
over scalars
s
. For each
d>0
, let
\mathcal{M}_{d}
be the elementwise meta-distribution over distributions
\mathcal{X}_{d}
over vectors
\chi_{d}
of dimensionality
d
that is generated by
\mathcal{M}_{1}
. Let
q=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}\sim\mathcal{M}_{1},s\sim\mathcal{X}_{1}}s^{2}
and
c=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}\sim\mathcal{M}_{1}}(\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{X}_{1}}s)^{2}
. Let
\chi_{d}
and
\chi^{\prime}_{d}
be drawn from the same
\mathcal{X}_{d}
, which is drawn from
\mathcal{M}_{d}
. Then

\lim_{d\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}_{i}\chi_{d}[i]^{2}=q\text{ a.s.}

\lim_{d\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}_{i}\chi_{d}[i]\chi^{\prime}_{d}[i]=c\text{ a.s.}

Proof.

Because
\mathcal{M}_{d}
is elementwise, for each
d
, the
x_{d}[i]^{2}
are independent and the
x_{d}[i]x^{\prime}_{d}[i]
are independent. So the strong law of large numbers applies to the average. Hence, we have
\lim_{d\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}_{i}\chi_{d}[i]^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}\sim\mathcal{M}_{1},s\sim\mathcal{X}_{1}}s^{2}=q
and

\displaystyle\lim_{d\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}_{i}\chi_{d}[i]\chi^{\prime}_{d}[i]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}\sim\mathcal{M}_{1},s,s^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{X}_{1}}ss^{\prime}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}\sim\mathcal{M}_{1}}(\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{X}_{1}}s)(\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{X}_{1}}s^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}_{1}\sim\mathcal{M}_{1}}(\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{X}_{1}}s)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c

∎

Proposition
11
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
be a data distribution using a finite set of labels in the form of one-hot vectors. Let
p_{1},..,p_{C}>0
be the probabilities of each of the
C>1
classes occurring. Let the input of
\mathcal{D}
be elem-like
(q,c)
for some
q>c\geq 0
.

Then
PNLCD(\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}}}
with probability
1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}
and 0 with probability
\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}
.

Proof.

We have

\displaystyle\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Tr((\mathbb{E}_{x}(x-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}x^{\prime})^{T}(x-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}x^{\prime}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}(x-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}x^{\prime})(x-\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}}x^{\prime})^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}xx^{T}-\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}}x^{\prime}x^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle d_{\text{in}}(q-c)

Further, we have

\displaystyle\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{y})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y}yy^{T}-\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}}y^{\prime}y^{T}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}

Let
E_{1}
be the event under which
y\neq y^{\prime}
,
\mathbb{E}_{i}x[i]x[i]=q
,
\mathbb{E}_{i}x^{\prime}[i]x^{\prime}[i]=q
and
\mathbb{E}_{i}x[i]x^{\prime}[i]=c
. Let
E_{2}
be the event under which
y=y^{\prime}
,
\mathbb{E}_{i}x[i]x[i]=q
,
\mathbb{E}_{i}x^{\prime}[i]x^{\prime}[i]=q
and
\mathbb{E}_{i}x[i]x^{\prime}[i]=c
. Under
E_{1}
we have

\displaystyle PNLCD

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{||y-y^{\prime}||_{2}^{2}\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{x})}{||x-x^{\prime}||_{2}^{2}\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{y})}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{2d_{\text{in}}(q-c)}{(xx^{T}+x^{\prime}x^{\prime T}-2x^{\prime}x^{T})(1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2})}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{2d_{\text{in}}(q-c)}{(2d_{\text{in}}q-2d_{\text{in}}c)(1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2})}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}}}

Under
E_{2}
, we have
PNLCD=0
. Since
C>1
and the
p_{\zeta}
are positive and sum to 1, we have
\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}}}>0
. The probability of
E_{1}
is
1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}
and the probability of
E_{2}
is
\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}
. Since both probabilities sum to 1,
PNLCD=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}}}
indeed holds with probability
1-\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}
and
PNLCD=0
holds with probability
\sum_{\zeta=1}^{C}p_{\zeta}^{2}
, as required.
∎

Proposition
12
.

Assume
\tau
is continuous, non-constant and
q>c>-q
. Then

\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,q)>\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,c)

Proof.

Let
\begin{pmatrix}s\\
t\end{pmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)
where
\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}q&c\\
c&q\end{pmatrix}
. Then

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,q)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,c)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau(s)^{2}-\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\tau(t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau(s)^{2}-2\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\tau(t)+\mathbb{E}_{t}\tau(t)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(\tau(s)-\tau(t))^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{s,t\in\mathbb{R}^{2}}n\bigg(0,\Sigma,\begin{pmatrix}s\\
t\end{pmatrix}\bigg)(\tau(s)-\tau(t))^{2}d\mu_{1}

n\bigg(0,\Sigma,\begin{pmatrix}s\\
t\end{pmatrix}\bigg)(\tau(s)-\tau(t))^{2}
is continuous because
\tau
is continuous. It is clearly non-negative. It is not zero everywhere because
\tau
is non-constant. And by assumption
6
, it is integrable. Hence, by lemma
8
, its integral is positive, and so
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,q)>\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,c)
.
∎

Proposition
13
.

For any
\tau
and
q\geq c\geq 0
, we have

\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,c)\geq 0

Proof.

By proposition
17
, we have
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,c)=\mathfrak{B}_{\tau}(q,c)=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,c)}(\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q-c)}\tau(t+s))^{2}\geq 0
.
∎

Proposition
14
.

Assume
\tau
is continuous, not the zero function and
q>0
. Then

\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,q)>0

Proof.

We have
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,q)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q)}\tau(s)^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}n(q,s)d\mu_{1}
. By lemma
8
, this is positive.
∎

Proposition
15
.

Let
f
be an A-architecture. Let
\mathfrak{q}_{l}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l}
and
\mathfrak{g}_{l}
be defined according to table
5.3
where
q>c\geq 0
. Then
\mathfrak{q}_{l}>\mathfrak{c}_{l}\geq 0
and
\mathfrak{g}_{l}>0
for all
l
.

Proof.

As with theorem
5
, we prove this proposition by induction on
l
. Hence, in each calculation rule in table
5.3
, we can assume the statement of the proposition holds for the dependencies. Considering that
\sigma_{l}^{2}>0
for fully-connected (FC) layers by property
22.5
, the only calculation rules that do not obviously yield
\mathfrak{q}_{l}>\mathfrak{c}_{l}\geq 0
and
\mathfrak{g}_{l}>0
are those for the activation operation. For an activation layer
f_{l}
we have

\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}_{l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})

\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{c}_{k})

\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{l}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{k}\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})

Because
\tau
is continuous and non-constant by property
22.2
, and because
\mathfrak{q}_{k}>\mathfrak{c}_{k}\geq 0
, we have
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})>\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{c}_{k})
and hence
\mathfrak{q}_{l}>\mathfrak{c}_{l}
by proposition
12
. By proposition
13
, we have
\mathfrak{c}_{l}=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{c}_{k})\geq 0
. Because
\tau
is non-constant,
\tau^{\prime}
is not the zero function. Because
\tau
is twice differentiable by property
22.2
,
\tau^{\prime}
is continuous. So by proposition
14
, we have
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})>0
and hence
\mathfrak{g}_{l}=\mathfrak{g}_{k}\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})>0
as required.

∎

Proposition
16
.

Let
\mathfrak{q}_{l}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l}
and
\mathfrak{g}_{l}
be defined according to table
5.3
. Let
0\leq m\leq l\leq L
and let
f_{m}
be a bottleneck for
f_{l}
in the A-architecture
f
. Then

\mathfrak{n}_{l,m}(f,q,c)=\sqrt{\sum_{p\in P_{m,l}}w(p)\prod_{f_{l^{\prime}}\in p}\mathfrak{n}_{\tau_{l^{\prime}}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k^{\prime}},\mathfrak{c}_{k^{\prime}})^{2}}

where
P_{m,l}
is the set of directed paths from
f_{m}
to
f_{l}
, the product is over all activation layers
f_{l^{\prime}}
on path
p
excluding its starting point and
f_{k^{\prime}}
is the dependency of
f_{l^{\prime}}
.

Proof.

Denote the right-hand side of the equation by
RHS_{l,m}
. All denominators that arise in this proof are non-zero by proposition
15
.

As with theorem
5
, we prove this proposition by induction on
l
. Fix
m
throughout the remainder of the proof. The base case of our induction is
l=m
. In that case, we have a single path from
f_{m}
to
f_{l}
containing only one vertex that is also its starting point. Hence, that path contains no activation or addition layers outside of its starting point and so its weight is 1 and so
RHS_{l,m}=1
. We also have
\mathfrak{n}_{l,m}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}}=1
, as required.

Now we proceed based on layer operation for the induction step based on
l
. Note that we now have
l>m
, so
l\neq 0
so
f_{l}
is not an input layer.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an FC, bias, LN or BN layer. Then
P_{m,l}
is the same as
P_{m,k}
, except that one vertex is added to each path. Also, since this new vertex is neither an addition nor activation layer,
RHS_{l,m}=RHS_{k,m}
. Further,

\mathfrak{n}_{l,m}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k})}}\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k})}{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}

By substituting the values from table
5.3
for
\mathfrak{g}_{l}
,
\mathfrak{q}_{l}
and
\mathfrak{c}_{l}
, we find that
\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k})}{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}=1
, and hence
\mathfrak{n}_{l,m}=\mathfrak{n}_{k,m}
. Since
\mathfrak{n}_{k,m}=RHS_{k,m}
, we have
\mathfrak{n}_{l,m}=RHS_{l,m}
.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an activation layer. Then
P_{m,l}
is the same as
P_{m,k}
, except that one vertex is added to each path. Since this new vertex is an activation layer, one value is added to the product for each path, but the weights remain the same. Hence

\displaystyle RHS_{l,m}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle RHS_{k,m}\mathfrak{n}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{c}_{k})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{n}_{k,m}\mathfrak{n}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{c}_{k})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k})}}\sqrt{\frac{(\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k})\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{c}_{k})}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k})}}\sqrt{\frac{(\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k})\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}}{\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{n}_{l,m}

as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an addition layer. Then
P_{m,l}
is the union of the distinct sets
P_{m,k[\kappa]}
for
1\leq\kappa\leq K
, where each path also has the vertex
f_{l}
added. The product for each path is still the same, but the weight is multiplied by
w_{\kappa}^{2}\frac{\mathfrak{q}_{k[\kappa]}-\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa]}}{\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l}}
. So we have

\displaystyle RHS_{l,m}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\frac{\mathfrak{q}_{k[\kappa]}-\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa]}}{\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l}}\sum_{p\in P_{m,k[\kappa]}}w(p)\prod_{f_{l^{\prime}}\in p}\mathfrak{n}_{\tau_{l^{\prime}}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k^{\prime}},\mathfrak{c}_{k^{\prime}})^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\frac{\mathfrak{q}_{k[\kappa]}-\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa]}}{\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l}}\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k[\kappa]}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{k[\kappa]}-\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa]})}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\mathfrak{g}_{k[\kappa]}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}

as required.

∎

Proposition
17
.

For any
\tau
and
q\geq c\geq 0
, we have

\mathfrak{B}_{\tau}(q,c)=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,c)

Proof.

Let
u
be a 3-dimensional unit Gaussian column vector. Then
\sqrt{q}u[0]
and
\frac{c}{\sqrt{q}}u[0]+\sqrt{q-\frac{c^{2}}{q}}u[1]
are jointly Gaussian with mean zero and covariance
\begin{pmatrix}q&c\\
c&q\end{pmatrix}
, and so
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,c)=\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau(\sqrt{q}u[0])\tau(\frac{c}{\sqrt{q}}u[0]+\sqrt{q-\frac{c^{2}}{q}}u[1])
. Let

A=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\frac{c}{q}}&\sqrt{\frac{q-c}{q}}&0\\
\sqrt{\frac{c(q-c)}{q(q+c)}}&-\sqrt{\frac{c^{2}}{q(q+c)}}&\sqrt{\frac{q}{q(q+c)}}\\
\sqrt{\frac{q-c}{q+c}}&-\sqrt{\frac{c}{q+c}}&-\sqrt{\frac{c}{q+c}}\end{pmatrix}

Because
A
is orthogonal and the distribution of
u
is spherically symmetric,
u
and
Au
have the same distribution. So we have

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(q,c)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{q}&0&0\end{pmatrix}u\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{c}{\sqrt{q}}&\sqrt{q-\frac{c^{2}}{q}}&0\end{pmatrix}u\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{q}&0&0\end{pmatrix}Au\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{c}{\sqrt{q}}&\sqrt{q-\frac{c^{2}}{q}}&0\end{pmatrix}Au\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{c}&\sqrt{q-c}&0\end{pmatrix}u\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{c}&0&\sqrt{q-c}\end{pmatrix}u\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t,r\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\tau(\sqrt{c}s+\sqrt{q-c}t)\tau(\sqrt{c}s+\sqrt{q-c}r)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}(\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\tau(\sqrt{c}s+\sqrt{q-c}t))(\mathbb{E}_{r\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\tau(\sqrt{c}s+\sqrt{q-c}r))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}(\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\tau(\sqrt{c}s+\sqrt{q-c}t))^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,c)}(\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q-c)}\tau(s+t))^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{B}_{\tau}(q,c)

∎

Proposition
18
.

Assume
\tau
is piecewise 5-differentiable. Consider
\mathfrak{n}_{\tau}(c)
defined on
[0,1)
. Then

1.

\mathfrak{n}_{\tau}(c)=\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)(1-c)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}}=\sqrt{\frac{\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)(1-c)}{1-\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c)}}

2.

\mathfrak{n}_{\tau}
is decreasing

3.

\lim_{c\rightarrow 1}\mathfrak{n}_{\tau}(c)=1

4.

\mathfrak{n}_{\tau}(c)\geq 1

Proof.

Since
\tau
is piecewise 5-differentiable, we can use theorem
7
in this proof. By definition,
\mathfrak{n}_{\tau}(c)=\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(1)(1-c)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}}
. By theorem
7
, we have
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(1)=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)
. This yields the first part of claim 1. The second part is obtained when dividing both numerator and denominator by
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)
.

Let
1>c^{\prime}>c\geq 0
. Then
\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}{1-c}
is the gradient of the chord from
(c,\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c))
to
(1,\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1))
and
\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c^{\prime})}{1-c^{\prime}}
is the gradient of the chord from
(c^{\prime},\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c^{\prime}))
to
(1,\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1))
. By theorem
7
,
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
is convex and so
(c^{\prime},\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c^{\prime}))
lies on or below the chord from
(c,\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c))
to
(1,\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1))
. Hence, the chord corresponding to
c^{\prime}
has at least as large a gradient as the chord corresponding to
c
. So
\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}{1-c}\leq\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c^{\prime})}{1-c^{\prime}}
, so
\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(1)(1-c)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}}\geq\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(1)(1-c^{\prime})}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c^{\prime})}}
, which yields claim 2.

\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)=\lim_{c\rightarrow 1}\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}{1-c}
by the definition of the derivative. Hence,
\lim_{c\rightarrow 1}\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)(1-c)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}=1
, which yields claim 3.

Claim 4 follows from claims 2 and 3.

∎

Proposition
19
.

Let
f
be an A-architecture where each activation function used is piecewise 5-differentiable and let
q>c\geq 0
. If
f
does not contain batch normalization but can contain layer normalization layers, we have

\mathfrak{n}(f,q,c)=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}(q,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}(q-c)}{\mathfrak{C}(q,q)-\mathfrak{C}(q,c)}}

If
f
does not contain layer normalization but can contain batch normalization layers, an analogous statement holds. See section
11.6
for details.

Proof.

Since the activation functions used are piecewise 5-differentiable, we can use theorem
7
in this proof. All denominators that arise in this proof are non-zero by proposition
15
. Denote by
\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,c)
the value of
\mathfrak{c}_{l}
obtained from table
5.3
when starting the recursion with
q
and
c
. Then
\mathfrak{C}_{L}(q,c)=\mathfrak{C}(q,c)
. Note that this is different from
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}
. We will prove the more general statement

\mathfrak{n}_{l,0}(f,q,c)=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}(q-c)}{\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,q)-\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,c)}}

Denote the right-hand side of this equation by
RHS_{l}
. It is easy to check that
\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,q)=\mathfrak{q}_{l}
. So the left-hand side of the equation is
\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{0}-\mathfrak{c}_{0})}{\mathfrak{g}_{0}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}
and the right-hand side is
