\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\sigma_{l}^{2}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}=\sigma_{l}^{2}\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
as required.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\sigma_{l}^{2}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}
. If
n^{-}\neq n^{+}
,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}=0
, so
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=0
as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is a bias layer.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
as required.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}
. If
n^{-}\neq n^{+}
,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}=0
, so
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=0
as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an LN.

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\epsilon_{l}}-2\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{(\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\epsilon_{l})^{2}}+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}{(\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\epsilon_{l})^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}}{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\epsilon_{l}}-2\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{(\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\epsilon_{l})^{2}}

\displaystyle+\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}{(\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\epsilon_{l})^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}\mathfrak{q}_{k}}-2\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{q}_{k}^{2}}+\frac{\mathfrak{q}_{k}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{q}_{k}^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}-\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{q}_{k}^{2}}

If
n^{-}\neq n^{+}
,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}=0
, so
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
as required.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\epsilon_{l}}{(\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\epsilon_{l})^{2}}=0
as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an addition layer.

\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa];k[\kappa]}^{-;-}=\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k[\kappa]}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

as required.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa];k[\kappa]}^{-;+}=\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa];k[\kappa]}^{-;+}
If
n^{-}\neq n^{+}
, the
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa];k[\kappa]}^{-;+}
are zero, so
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=0
as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an activation layer. As before, let
u\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathfrak{c}_{k;k})
and
v\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{\det\Sigma_{k}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}})
. Then

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathbb{E}_{t,s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{k})}t^{2}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(s)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathbb{E}_{v,u}\Big(v+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}u\Big)^{2}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\Big(\mathbb{E}_{v}v^{2}\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{v}v\mathbb{E}_{u}u\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}u^{2}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\Big(\frac{\det\Sigma_{k}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}u^{2}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\Big(\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}u^{2}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}\Big)

\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}>0
. Also, since
\tau^{\prime}_{l}
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{\text{E2}}
, so is
\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}
and
u^{2}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}
. So we can apply lemma
15
and obtain

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{q}_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathfrak{q}_{k})}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(s)^{2}

\displaystyle+\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{q}_{k}\mathfrak{q}_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathfrak{q}_{k})}s^{2}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(s)^{2}

Is
n^{-}\neq n^{+}
, we further have
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}=0
, so then

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathfrak{q}_{k})}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(s)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}\mathbb{E}_{s,t\sim\mathcal{N}\Big(0,\begin{pmatrix}\mathfrak{q}_{k}&\mathfrak{q}_{k}\\
\mathfrak{q}_{k}&\mathfrak{q}_{k}\end{pmatrix}\Big)}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(s)\tau^{\prime}_{l}(t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

as required. We also have

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathbb{E}_{t,s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{k})}t\tau^{\prime}_{l}(s)\tau_{l}(s)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathbb{E}_{v,u}\Big(v+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}u\Big)\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)\tau_{l}(u)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}u\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)\tau_{l}(u)

As before,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}>0
and
u\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)\tau_{l}(u)
is controlled by
\mathcal{C}^{\text{E2}}
, so
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{q}_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathfrak{q}_{k})}s\tau^{\prime}_{l}(s)\tau_{l}(s)
. When
n^{-}\neq n^{+}
,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}=0
, so
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=0
as required.

This completes the induction and hence stage 4.

Stage 5
: statement (
5.10
)

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}NLC(f_{l}(f_{m}),f_{m}(\mathcal{D}^{(N)}))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\sqrt{\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr(\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{f_{m}}\mathcal{J}_{l,m}^{T}(x))}{\Tr(\mathrm{Cov}_{f_{l}})}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\sqrt{\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr(\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{f_{m}}\mathcal{J}_{l,m}^{T}(x))}{||\mathbb{S}_{x}f_{l}(x)||_{2}^{2}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr(\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{f_{m}}\mathcal{J}_{l,m}^{T}(x))}{\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathbb{S}_{x}f_{l}(x)||_{2}^{2}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}\mathbb{E}_{x}\Tr(\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x)\mathrm{Cov}_{f_{m}}\mathcal{J}_{l,m}^{T}(x))}{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathbb{S}_{x}f_{l}(x)||_{2}^{2}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{m}-\mathfrak{c}_{m})}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}

The denominator is positive by proposition
15
.

Stage 6
: statement (
5.4
)

The case
l=m
is trivial. For
l>m
, as in stage 4, we will treat the cases
m>0
and
m=0
somewhat separately.

Case:
m>0
. We will show
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})u||_{2}^{2}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
, where randomness is induced by
\theta
,
x^{(1)}
and the unit Gaussian vector
u
. From lemma
17
, we then obtain
\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})u||_{2}^{2}=\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})||_{F}^{2}
, and hence
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})||_{F}^{2}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
as required.

We have
\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})u||_{2}^{2}=\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\overline{(u\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})^{T})^{.2}}
. This is the same expression we investigated in stage 4 as
p_{l}^{(n^{-},n^{+})}
with
n^{+}=1
, except that
f_{m}(x^{(n^{-})})-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}f_{m}(x^{(n)})
is replaced by
u
. In fact, if we let
p^{(n^{-},1)}_{l}
refer to
u\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})^{T}
, we can proceed almost exactly as in stage 4 until the point where we take the limit with respect to
N
and
\vec{\epsilon}
. The following differences arise.

•

F^{\text{MN}}
is an input layer. It corresponds to
u
. Because
u
is unit Gaussian, we add a diagonal entry of 1 and off-diagonal entries of zero to the covariance matrix of
\mathcal{G}
. Distribution equality is obvious. The limits become
\tilde{\mathfrak{m}}^{\text{MN}}=0
,
\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;MN}}=1
and
\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;(n)}}_{;m}=0
. In terms of rank stability to start off the induction, we have
\det\begin{pmatrix}\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;MN}}&\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;(n)}}_{;m}\\
\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;(n)}}_{;m}&\mathfrak{c}_{m;m}\end{pmatrix}=\mathfrak{c}_{m;m}>0
.

•

The recursive expansion of
\rho_{l}^{-}
halts at
\rho^{\text{MN}}
, as this is now a dummy multi-activation function. All relevant properties that follow from the expansion are preserved. Specifically, we use that
e^{\text{MN}}
is independent of all other
e
terms for input and FC layers in
F
and that
\tilde{\mathfrak{m}}^{\text{MN}}=0
.

•

The case where
f_{l}
is a readin layer does not appear in the induction step as
l>m>0
and
f_{m}
is a bottleneck for
f_{l}
.

Case:
m=0
. We have

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})||_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}\Big|\Big|\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}\mathcal{J}_{l^{\prime},0}(x^{(1)})^{T}\mathcal{J}_{l,l^{\prime}}(x^{(1)})^{T}\Big|\Big|_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}\Big|\Big|\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}W_{l^{\prime}}\mathcal{J}_{l,l^{\prime}}(x^{(1)})^{T}\Big|\Big|_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}\sum_{i=0}^{d_{\text{in}}-1}\Big|\Big|\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}W_{l^{\prime}}[i,:]\mathcal{J}_{l,l^{\prime}}(x^{(1)})^{T}\Big|\Big|_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}d_{\text{in}}\Big|\Big|\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}W_{l^{\prime}}[0,:]\mathcal{J}_{l,l^{\prime}}(x^{(1)})^{T}\Big|\Big|_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\overline{\Big(\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}\sqrt{d_{\text{in}}}W_{l^{\prime}}[0,:]\mathcal{J}_{l,l^{\prime}}(x^{(1)})^{T}\Big)^{.2}}

Here,
W_{l^{\prime}}[i,0]
denotes the
i
’th row of
W_{l^{\prime}}
and
\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}
is over all readin layers. We use that, by construction, the rows of each
W_{l^{\prime}}
have the same distribution.

Again, we proceed almost exactly as in stage 4 until the point where we take the limit with respect to
N
and
\vec{\epsilon}
, where we now let
p_{l}^{(n^{-},1)}
refer to
\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}\sqrt{d_{\text{in}}}W_{l^{\prime}}[0,:]\mathcal{J}_{l,l^{\prime}}(x^{(1)})^{T}
. The induction step for non-readin layers
f_{l}
is unaltered, as we still have
p_{l}^{(n^{-},1)}=p_{k}^{(n^{-},1)}\mathcal{J}_{l,k}(x^{(1)})^{T}
when
f_{l}
is not an addition layer and
p_{l}^{(n^{-},1)}=\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}p_{k[\kappa]}^{(n^{-},1)}
when
f_{l}
is an addition layer. Having
\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}
be part of the definition of
p_{l}^{(n^{-},1)}
does not affect our arguments. When
f_{l}
is a readin layer, the distribution of
p_{l}^{(n^{-},1)}
is that of
\sqrt{d_{\text{in}}}W_{l}[0,:]
, which is elementwise, has a Gaussian generator with mean zero and variance
\sigma_{l}^{2}
, and is independent of the analogous distributions for other readin layers as there is no weight sharing in
f
. Hence, we add a diagonal entry of
\sigma_{l}^{2}
and off-diagonal entries of zero to
\mathcal{G}
for
F_{l}
. The limits become
\tilde{\mathfrak{m}}_{l}^{-}=0
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\sigma_{l}^{2}
and
\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=0
. Rank stability holds as
\det\Sigma_{l}=\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=q\sigma_{l}^{4}>0
.

Now we return again to the general case where
m
can be zero or non-zero. We are left with taking the limit with respect to
N
and
\vec{\epsilon}
. To do this, we use that we obtained the same recursive calculation rules for
\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}
and
\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}
as in stage 4, except for the readin layer case. Since
\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}
now represents either
\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\overline{(u\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(1)})^{T})^{.2}}
or
\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\overline{\Big(\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ readin}}\sqrt{d_{\text{in}}}W_{l^{\prime}}[0,:]\mathcal{J}_{l,l^{\prime}}(x^{(1)})^{T}\Big)^{.2}}
depending on the value of
m
, showing
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
completes this stage. As part of the induction, we also show
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=0
. Denominators are positive as before. Compared to stage 4, all limit quantities are now also independent of
n^{-}
and
N
.

•

Case:
F^{\text{MF}}
.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN};\text{MN}}=1=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
and
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MF};+}_{;m}=0
. This starts off our induction for the case
m>0
in the required manner.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is a readin layer. If
f_{l}
is a readin layer, we have
m=0
, so
\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}=\frac{\sigma_{l}^{2}}{1}=\sigma_{l}^{2}
. Also,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\sigma_{l}^{2}
and
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=0
as required due to the generator addition described above.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is a fully-connected, non-readin layer.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\sigma_{l}^{2}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}=\sigma_{l}^{2}\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
as required.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\sigma_{l}^{2}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}=0
as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is a bias layer.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
as required.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}=0
as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an LN layer.

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\epsilon_{l}}-2\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{(\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\epsilon_{l})^{2}}+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}{(\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\epsilon_{l})^{3}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}}{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\epsilon_{l}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}\mathfrak{q}_{k}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

as required.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\epsilon_{l}}{(\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}+\epsilon_{l})^{2}}=0
as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an addition layer.

\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa];k[\kappa]}^{-;-}=\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k[\kappa]}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

as required.
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}=\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa];k[\kappa]}^{-;+}=\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k[\kappa];k[\kappa]}^{-;+}=0
as required.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an activation layer. Analogous to stage 4, we have

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\Big(\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}+\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}u^{2}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;-}\mathbb{E}_{u}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}\mathbb{E}_{s,t\sim\mathcal{N}\Big(0,\begin{pmatrix}\mathfrak{q}_{k}&\mathfrak{q}_{k}\\
\mathfrak{q}_{k}&\mathfrak{q}_{k}\end{pmatrix}\Big)}\tau^{\prime}_{l}(s)\tau^{\prime}_{l}(t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{q}_{k})\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

as required.

We also have

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;+}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{u}u\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)\tau_{l}(u)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}^{-;+}}{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\mathfrak{c}_{k;k}}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathfrak{q}_{k})}u\tau^{\prime}_{l}(u)\tau_{l}(u)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

as required.

Stage 7
: statement (
5.8
)

Defining
\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}
as in stage 6, we have

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}\mathbb{E}_{x}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}||^{2}_{F}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(n)})||^{2}_{F}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m}(x^{(n)})||^{2}_{F}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\begin{cases}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}\text{ if }l>m\\
1\text{ else}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon},N}\begin{cases}\mathfrak{c}_{l;l}^{-;-}\text{ if }l>m\\
1\text{ else}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

Stage 8
: statements (a) and (b)

Assume now that
f_{L}
is a readout layer. Fix
N
. Throughout this proof, we have used background theorem
1
. Now, we use theorem
4
and background corollary
2
for statements (a) and (b) respectively.

To apply those results, we construct a mean field architecture
F
with a single finite input layer and readout layer. We proceed as in stage 1 with the following differences.

•

Like
f_{L}
,
F_{L}
is now a readout layer of dimensionality
d_{L}
.

•

F
now has a finite input layer
F_{0}
that is associated with
\mathcal{D}
as well as individual inputs
x^{(n)}
.

•

For a readin layer
f_{l}
in
f
, instead of adding an input layer to
F
and extending
\mathcal{G}
, we add a readin layer
F_{l}
to
F
with the same width and variance parameter as
f_{l}
that does not share weights and has dependency
F_{0}
.

•

\mathcal{G}
now only covers layers derived from bias layers.

It is easy to see that, as in stage 1, we have distribution equality. For (a), this means that
f_{L}
and
F_{L}
have the same meta-distribution. For (b), this means that
(f_{L}(x^{(1)}),..,f_{L}(x^{(N)}))
has the same distribution as
(F_{L}(x^{(1)}),..,F_{L}(x^{(N)}))
for any fixed sample
x^{(1)},..,x^{(N)}
. Note that, as in the statement of background corollary
2
, the surrogate input generated by
\mathcal{G}
does not vary between inputs
x^{(n)}
, as it represents the random initial bias vectors.

Let’s verify the conditions of theorem
4
and background corollary
2
. For (b), we only care about almost all samples, i.e. we can restrict ourselves to a set of samples that has probability 1. So as before, we can assume
\overline{x^{(n)}.x^{(n)}}=\overline{x^{(n^{\prime})}.x^{(n^{\prime})}}=q
and
\overline{x^{(n)}.x^{(n^{\prime})}}=c
for any
1\leq n,n^{\prime}\leq N
,
n\neq n^{\prime}
. Then, the conditions of theorem
4
and background corollary
2
become equivalent as
K_{\text{in}}
becomes
K(N,q,c)
. Further, it turns out that
(\clipout(\clipin(F)),\mathcal{G}(K(N,q,c))\times\mathcal{G}^{N})
is the mean field architecture and generator we constructed early in stage 4 denoted as
(F^{(1)},..,F^{(N)})
for the case
m=L-1
. We denoted the mean field architecture by
(F^{(1)},..,F^{(N)})
. Hence, we showed that the conditions of background theorem
1
hold for
(\clipout(\clipin(F)),\mathcal{G}(K(N,q,c))\times\mathcal{G}^{N})
in stage 4. Hence, the conditions of theorem
4
and background corollary
2
hold.

So we have that (i) the meta-distribution of
F
expansion-converges as
d_{\text{MF}}\rightarrow\infty
to the elementwise meta-distribution with generator
\mathcal{MN}(\mathfrak{c}_{L;L},\mathfrak{c}_{L;L}^{\prime;\prime\prime})
and (ii) for almost all samples
(F(x^{(1)}),..,F(x^{(N)}))
converges in distribution as
d_{\text{MF}}\rightarrow\infty
to a Gaussian that is elementwise over output vectors where the generator has mean zero and covariance matrix
K(N,\mathfrak{c}_{L;L},\mathfrak{c}_{L;L}^{\prime;\prime\prime})
. By distribution equality, the same holds for
f
. And, as we showed in stage 1 and 2,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\mathfrak{c}_{L;L}=\mathfrak{q}_{L}
and
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\mathfrak{c}_{L;L}^{\prime;\prime\prime}=\mathfrak{c}_{L}
. (The limit over
N
was not used in stages 1 and 2.)

Finally, we note that when
f_{L}
is a readout layer, statements (
5.1
) through (
5.10
) still hold when
l<L
as
(f_{0},..,f_{L-1})
is a valid A-architecture without finite output layer.

∎

11.5.3
Theorem
6
: properties of the length kernel
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)

Theorem
6
.

For any
\tau
we have

1.

If
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)\neq 0
for some
\lambda>0
, then for all
\lambda>0
we have

(a)

\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)>0

(b)

\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}
is differentiable at
\lambda
with
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{\prime}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}(s^{2}\lambda^{-3}-\lambda^{-1})

(c)

\frac{\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{\prime}(\lambda)\lambda}{\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)}>-\frac{1}{2}

(d)

(\sqrt{\lambda}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda))^{\prime}>0

2.

If
\tau
is continuous and not zero everywhere, then
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)>0
for all
\lambda>0
.

3.

If
\tau
is continuous at zero,
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}
is continuous at zero.

4.

If
\tau
is directionally differentiable at zero, then
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}
is differentiable at zero with
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{\prime}(0)=\sqrt{\frac{\tau^{-}(0)^{2}+\tau^{+}(0)^{2}}{2}}
if
\tau(0)=0
and
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{\prime}(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sign(\tau(0))(\tau^{+}(0)-\tau^{-}(0))
if
\tau(0)\neq 0
. The + and - superscripts indicate the right and left derivative respectively.

5.

If
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)\neq 0
for some
\lambda>0
, then for all
\lambda>0
the sequence
(\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{n}(\lambda))_{n}
either (i) is strictly increasing and diverges to infinity or (ii) converges.

Proof.

We prove the claims in turn.

Claim
1
(a): We argue by contradiction. Assume we have a
\lambda>0
such that
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)\neq 0
and a
\lambda^{\prime}>0
such that
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda^{\prime})\leq 0
. Then

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle<

\displaystyle\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}n(\lambda^{2},s)d\mu_{1}

We write
\nu(\lambda,s)
for
n(\lambda^{2},s)
. By the definition of the integral, there exists
S>0
such that
0<\int_{-S}^{S}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}
. Hence

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle<

\displaystyle\Big(\max\Big(\frac{\nu(\lambda,0)}{\nu(\lambda^{\prime},0)},\frac{\nu(\lambda,S)}{\nu(\lambda^{\prime},S)}\Big)\Big)^{-1}\int_{-S}^{S}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int_{-S}^{S}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda^{\prime},s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{\prime 2})}\tau(s)^{2}

Since
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda^{\prime})=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{\prime 2})}\tau(s)^{2}}
, we have
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda^{\prime})>0
. Contradiction. Hence, claim
1
(a) holds.

Claim
1
(b): Fix
\lambda>0
.
\nu(\lambda,s)
is twice differentiable with respect to
\lambda
for
s\in\mathbb{R}
. Using the Taylor expansion with the Lagrange form of the remainder, for some
\delta
with
\lambda>\delta>0
, we have
\nu(\lambda+\epsilon,s)=\nu(\lambda,s)+\epsilon\frac{d}{d\lambda}\nu(\lambda,s)+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{2}\frac{d^{2}}{d\lambda^{2}}\nu(\lambda^{+}(s),s)
for all
s\in\mathbb{R}
,
|\epsilon|<\delta
where
\lambda^{+}(s)\in[\lambda-\delta,\lambda+\delta]
. We have

\displaystyle\Big|\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\frac{d^{2}}{d\lambda^{2}}\nu(\lambda^{+}(s),s)d\mu_{1}\Big|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big|\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda^{+},s)(s^{4}(\lambda^{+})^{-6}-5s^{2}(\lambda^{+})^{-4}+2(\lambda^{+})^{-2})d\mu_{1}\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda^{+},s)s^{4}(\lambda^{+})^{-6}d\mu_{1}+5\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda^{+},s)s^{2}(\lambda^{+})^{-4}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle+2\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda^{+},s)(\lambda^{+})^{-2}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\frac{\lambda+\delta}{\lambda-\delta}\nu(\lambda+\delta,s)s^{4}(\lambda-\delta)^{-6}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle+5\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\frac{\lambda+\delta}{\lambda-\delta}\nu(\lambda+\delta,s)s^{2}(\lambda-\delta)^{-4}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle+2\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\frac{\lambda+\delta}{\lambda-\delta}\nu(\lambda+\delta,s)(\lambda-\delta)^{-2}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\lambda+\delta)(\lambda-\delta)^{-7}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda+\delta)}s^{4}\tau(s)^{2}+5(\lambda+\delta)(\lambda-\delta)^{-5}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda+\delta)}s^{2}\tau(s)^{2}

\displaystyle+2(\lambda+\delta)(\lambda-\delta)^{-3}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda+\delta)}\tau(s)^{2}

\displaystyle<

\displaystyle\infty

Hence

\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\epsilon}(\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda+\epsilon)^{2}-\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\epsilon}\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda+\epsilon,s)-\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\epsilon}\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\Big(\epsilon\nu(\lambda,s)(s^{2}\lambda^{-3}-\lambda^{-1})+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{2}\frac{d^{2}}{d\lambda^{2}}\nu(\lambda^{+}(s),s)\Big)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)(s^{2}\lambda^{-3}-\lambda^{-1})+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\tau(s)^{2}\frac{d^{2}}{d\lambda^{2}}\nu(\lambda^{+}(s),s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)(s^{2}\lambda^{-3}-\lambda^{-1})d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}(s^{2}\lambda^{-3}-\lambda^{-1})

Let
L(\lambda)=\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}
. We showed that
L
is differentiable with
L^{\prime}(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}(s^{2}\lambda^{-3}-\lambda^{-1})
. As
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)>0
by claim
1
(a),
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}
is then differentiable with
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{\prime}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{2}\frac{L^{\prime}(\lambda)}{\sqrt{L(\lambda)}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}(s^{2}\lambda^{-3}-\lambda^{-1})
as required.

Claim
1
(c): Fix
\lambda>0
. By claim
1
(a), we have
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)>0
. So
\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}>0
so there exists an
\epsilon>0
with
\int_{s\in\mathbb{R},s\not\in[-\epsilon,\epsilon]}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)>0
, so

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle<

\displaystyle\epsilon^{2}\int_{s\in\mathbb{R},s\not\in[-\epsilon,\epsilon]}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int_{s\in\mathbb{R},s\not\in[-\epsilon,\epsilon]}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)s^{2}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\tau(s)^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)s^{2}d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}s^{2}

So we have

\displaystyle\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{\prime}(\lambda)\lambda

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}(s^{2}\lambda^{-2}-1)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{-1}(\lambda^{-2}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}s^{2}-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2})

\displaystyle>

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{-1}(-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{-1}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)

as required.

Claim
1
(d): Fix
\lambda>0
. We have

\displaystyle(\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)\lambda^{\frac{1}{2}})^{\prime}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{\prime}(\lambda)\lambda)\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}

\displaystyle>

\displaystyle\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)\Big)\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

as required.

Claim
2
: Fix
\lambda>0
. We have

\mathfrak{L}(\lambda)^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda^{2})}\tau(s)^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\nu(\lambda,s)\tau(s)^{2}d\mu_{1}

Since
\tau
is not the zero function and is continuous, so is
\nu(\lambda,s)\tau(s)^{2}
. Hence, by lemma
8
, the integral is positive, so
\mathfrak{L}(\lambda)
is as well.

Claim
3
: Let
\lambda>0
. We have
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}=\int_{0}^{\infty}(\tau(s)^{2}+\tau(-s)^{2})\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}
. If
\tau(s)
is continuous at zero, so is
\tau(s)^{2}+\tau(-s)^{2}
. Hence we can apply lemma
9
using
F(s)=\tau(s)^{2}+\tau(-s)^{2}
and
p=0
to obtain
\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow 0}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}=2\tau(0)^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}=\tau(0)^{2}=\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(0)^{2}
. Since
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}
is non-negative,
\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow 0}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)=\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(0)
as required.

Claim
4
: Let
\lambda>0
. Because
\tau
is directionally differentiable at 0, we have
\tau(s)=\tau(0)+s\tau^{+}(0)+sh(s)
when
s\geq 0
and
\tau(s)=\tau(0)+s\tau^{-}(0)+sh(s)
when
s\leq 0
where
\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}h(s)=h(0)=0
.

Case 1:
\tau(0)=0
. Then we have

\displaystyle\lambda^{-2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lambda^{-2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\big((s\tau^{+}(0)+sh(s))^{2}+(-s\tau^{-}(0)-sh(-s))^{2}\big)\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lambda^{-2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\big((\tau^{+}(0)+h(s))^{2}+(\tau^{-}(0)+h(-s))^{2}\big)s^{2}\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}

(\tau^{+}(0)+h(s))^{2}+(\tau^{-}(0)+h(-s))^{2}
is continuous at zero, so we can apply lemma
9
with this expression as
F
and
p=2
to obtain

\displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow 0}\lambda^{-2}\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\tau^{+}(0)^{2}+\tau^{-}(0)^{2})\int_{0}^{\infty}s^{2}\nu(1,s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\tau^{+}(0)^{2}+\tau^{-}(0)^{2})\frac{1}{2}

As
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(0)=|\tau(0)|=0
, we have
\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow 0}\lambda^{-1}(\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)-\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(0))=\sqrt{\frac{\tau^{-}(0)^{2}+\tau^{+}(0)^{2}}{2}}
as required.

Case 2:
\tau(0)\neq 0
. Then we have

\displaystyle\lambda^{-1}(\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}-\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(0)^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lambda^{-1}\int_{0}^{\infty}\big((\tau(0)+s\tau^{+}(0)+sh(s))^{2}+(\tau(0)-s\tau^{-}(0)-sh(-s))^{2}-2\tau(0)^{2}\big)\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lambda^{-1}\int_{0}^{\infty}\Big(2\tau(0)(\tau^{+}(0)+h(s)-\tau^{-}(0)-h(-s))

\displaystyle+s(\tau^{+}(0)+h(s))^{2}+s(\tau^{-}(0)+h(-s))^{2}\Big)s\nu(\lambda,s)d\mu_{1}

The expression inside the large brackets is continuous at zero, so we can apply lemma
9
with this expression as
F
and
p=1
to obtain

\displaystyle\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow 0}\lambda^{-1}(\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}-\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(0)^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\tau(0)(\tau^{+}(0)-\tau^{-}(0))\int_{0}^{\infty}s\nu(1,s)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\tau(0)(\tau^{+}(0)-\tau^{-}(0))

Let
L(\lambda)=\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(\lambda)^{2}
. We showed
L^{\prime}(0)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\tau(0)(\tau^{+}(0)-\tau^{-}(0))
. Hence
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{\prime}(0)=\frac{1}{2}\frac{L^{\prime}(0)}{\sqrt{L(0)}}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\tau(0)(\tau^{+}(0)-\tau^{-}(0))}{|\tau(0)|}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sign(\tau(0))(\tau^{+}(0)-\tau^{-}(0))
as required.

Claim
5
: The condition of claim
1
holds, so claim
1
holds. Fix
\lambda
. Denote the sequence
(\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}^{n}(\lambda))_{n}
by
S_{n}
. If
S_{n}
is increasing, then it either diverges to infinity or it converges, so (i) or (ii) hold. If there is an
n
such that
S_{n}=S_{n+1}
, the sequence converges, so (ii) holds. So going forward assume there is an
n
such that
S_{n}>S_{n+1}
.

Case 1: There are finitely many
n
such that
S_{n}>S_{n+1}
.

Let
n
now be the largest such value. We prove by induction that for all
n^{\prime}>n
we have
S_{n+1}\leq S_{n^{\prime}}<\sqrt{S_{n}S_{n+1}}
. The statement trivially holds for
n^{\prime}=n+1
. Assume it holds for some
n^{\prime}>n
. Because
n
is the largest value with
S_{n}>S_{n+1}
, we have
S_{n^{\prime}+1}\geq S_{n^{\prime}}\geq S_{n+1}
. Further, by claim
1
(d), we have
\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(S_{n^{\prime}})<\mathfrak{L}_{\tau}(S_{n})\sqrt{\frac{S_{n}}{S_{n^{\prime}}}}=S_{n+1}\sqrt{\frac{S_{n}}{S_{n^{\prime}}}}\leq\sqrt{S_{n}S_{n+1}}
. This completes the induction. So eventually
S_{n}
is increasing and bounded above, so (ii) holds.

Case 2: There are infinitely many
n
such that
S_{n}>S_{n+1}
.

Let the sequence of such values
n
be denoted by
S_{n_{d}}
. Assume there is some
d
such that
S_{n_{d}}\leq S_{n_{d+1}}
. Then we can’t have
n_{d+1}=n_{d}+1
because
S_{n_{d}}>S_{n_{d}+1}
by definition. So
n_{d+1}>n_{d}+1
. Then from the induction under case 1 we obtain
S_{n_{d}+1}\leq S_{n_{d+1}-1}<\sqrt{S_{n_{d}}S_{n_{d}+1}}
and finally
S_{n_{d+1}}<\sqrt{S_{n_{d}}S_{n_{d}+1}}
. Contradiction. So
S_{n_{d}}
is strictly decreasing, so it converges. Again, using the induction from case 1, we obtain that
\sqrt{S_{n_{d}}S_{n_{d}+1}}>S_{n}
for all
n_{d}<n<n_{d+1}
and hence
S_{n_{d}}>S_{n}
for all
n>n_{d}
. So if
S_{n_{d}}
converges to zero, so does
S_{n}
, so (ii) holds. So going forward assume that
S_{n_{d}}
converges to a positive value. Call it
L
. Assume
S_{n}
does not converge to
L
. Then there is a
\delta
such that for arbitrarily large
n
we have
|S_{n}-L|>\delta
. Since there is an
S_{n_{d}}
with
S_{n_{d}}<L+\delta
, eventually
S_{n}<L+\delta
. Hence for arbitrarily large
n
we have
S_{n}<L-\delta
. Because
S_{n_{d}+1},..,S_{n_{d+1}}
is strictly increasing for each
d
, there are arbitrarily large
d
such that
S_{n_{d}+1}<L-\delta
. But then
S_{n_{d+1}}<\sqrt{S_{n_{d}}S_{n_{d}+1}}
and
S_{n_{d+1}}>L
yields
S_{n_{d}}>L+\delta
. So there are arbitrarily large
d
such that
S_{n_{d}}>L+\delta
, so
S_{n_{d}}
does not converge to
L
. Contradiction. So
S_{n}
does converge to
L
, so (ii) holds, as required.

∎

11.5.4
Theorem
7
: properties of the covariance kernel
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)

Theorem
7
.

Assume
\tau
is piecewise 5-differentiable. Consider
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)
defined on
[0,1]
. Let
a_{\tau}s+b_{\tau}
be the least squares linear fit to
\tau
under
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
and let
\tilde{\tau}=\tau-a_{\tau}s-b_{\tau}
. Then

(a)

\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
is differentiable and
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}
.

(b)

\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
is increasing, convex and for all
c>0
,
\epsilon>0
with
c+3\epsilon\leq 1
we have
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c+3\epsilon)-3\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c+2\epsilon)+3\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c+\epsilon)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)\geq 0
.

(c)

(i)
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)=\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}(c)+a_{\tau}^{2}c+b_{\tau}^{2}
, (ii)
\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}(0)=0
, (iii)
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(0)=b_{\tau}^{2}
, (iv)
\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}^{\prime}(0)=0
, (v)
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(0)=a_{\tau}^{2}
, (vi)
CAR(\tau,\mathcal{N}(0,1))=\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(0)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)}
, (vii)
LAR(\tau,\mathcal{N}(0,1))=\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(0)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)}
and (viii)
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
is linear if and only if
\tau
is linear.

Now also assume
\tau
is not linear. Then, for the normalized covariance kernel
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c)=\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)}
exactly one of three cases hold on
[0,1]
.

1.

There is a stable fixed point at
c^{\text{lim}}=1
with exponential convergence rate and no other fixed point.
0<\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)<1
holds.

2.

There is a stable fixed point at
c^{\text{lim}}=1
with sub-exponential convergence rate and no other fixed point.
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)=1
holds.

3.

There is an unstable fixed point at 1 and there is exactly one other fixed point
c^{\text{lim}}
in
[0,1)
, which is stable.
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)>1
and
1>\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(c^{\text{lim}})\geq 0
hold. The convergence rate is super-exponential or exponential depending on whether
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(c^{\text{lim}})=0
holds.

In particular, there exists exactly one stable fixed point
c^{\text{lim}}
and iterating
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
will lead to convergence towards
c^{\text{lim}}
from any starting point.

Proof.

Like the proof of theorem
2
, this proof proceeds in a number of stages, where each stage builds upon the results of previous stages. It is easy to check that an alternative definition for
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)
is
\mathbb{E}_{s,t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\tau(s)\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)
. Throughout this proof, let
s
and
t
be independent unit Gaussians.

Stage 1
: Assume
\tau
is twice differentiable. Then for
1>c\geq 0
,
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
is differentiable at
c
and
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(c)=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(c)
.

Throughout stage 1, consider
1>c\geq 0
fixed and consider
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
defined on
[-1,1]
. Let
|\epsilon|<\frac{1}{2}(1-c)
and let

\gamma=\frac{2c\epsilon-\epsilon^{2}}{1-c^{2}}

and

\delta=-\epsilon s-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t+\sqrt{1-(c-\epsilon)^{2}}t

Then we have

\delta=-\epsilon s+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t(\sqrt{1+\gamma}-1)=-\epsilon s+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t(\frac{1}{2}\gamma+r(\gamma)\gamma^{2})

where
r(\gamma)
is derived from the Taylor expansion of the square root about 1. All values between
1
and
1+\gamma
are contained in the interval
[\frac{1-\frac{1}{4}(1+c)^{2}}{1-c^{2}},\frac{1}{1-c^{2}}]
. Because the square root is twice differentiable in that interval with a bounded second derivative, the Lagrange form of the remainder yields that
|r(\gamma)|
is bounded. Let the bound be
R
. Then

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c-\epsilon)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\tau((c-\epsilon)s+\sqrt{1-(c-\epsilon)^{2}}t)-\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\Big(\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t+\delta)-\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\Big(\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+\delta\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\delta^{2}h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta)-\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\Big((-\epsilon s+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t(\frac{1}{2}\gamma+r(\gamma)\gamma^{2}))\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}(-\epsilon s+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t(\frac{1}{2}\gamma+r(\gamma)\gamma^{2}))^{2}h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta)\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\epsilon(-s+\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}t)\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle+\epsilon^{2}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta))\Big)

Here,
h
is derived from the Taylor expansion of
\tau
about
cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t
. Because
\tau
is twice differentiable, the Lagrange form of the remainder yields
h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta)=\tau^{\prime\prime}(s^{\prime})
for some
s^{\prime}
with
cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t\leq s^{\prime}\leq cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t+\delta
. This in turn yields
|h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta)|\leq T_{2}(|s|+|t|)
, where
T_{2}
is defined as in section
11.1.3
.

Here,
P_{0}
and
P_{1}
can be considered low-order polynomials of
s
,
t
,
\epsilon
,
r
,
\tau(s)
and
\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)
terms. (Remember that
c
is a constant.)

First consider
\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta))
, the coefficient of
\epsilon^{2}
. Let
P_{0}^{+}
and
P_{1}^{+}
be the polynomials that are equal to
P_{0}
and
P_{1}
, except each term has a positive sign. Then

\displaystyle\Big|\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(P_{0}(s,t,\epsilon,r,\tau(s),\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t))

\displaystyle+P_{1}(s,t,\epsilon,r,\tau(s),\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t))h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta)\Big)\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(P_{0}^{+}(|s|,|t|,\frac{1}{2}(1-c),R,|\tau(s)|,|\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|)

\displaystyle+P_{1}^{+}(|s|,|t|,\frac{1}{2}(1-c),R,|\tau(s)|,|\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|)T_{2}(|s|+|t|)\Big)

Using the “full force” of assumption
6
, this bound is finite. Since it is also independent of
\epsilon
, we have
\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\epsilon|\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(P_{0}+P_{1}h)|=0
, so
\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\epsilon\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(P_{0}+P_{1}h)=0
.

Now consider
\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(-s+\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}t)\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)
, the coefficient of
\epsilon
. Let
u
be a 2-dimensional unit Gaussian column vector. Then we can rewrite the coefficient using vector notation as

\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}-1&\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\end{pmatrix}u\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}u\Big)\tau^{\prime}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}c&\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}u\Big)

Because the distribution of
u
is spherically symmetric, it is invariant under multiplication with an orthogonal matrix. Let

A=\begin{pmatrix}c&-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\\
\sqrt{1-c^{2}}&c\end{pmatrix}

It is easy to check that
A
is orthogonal. Therefore we can continue transforming the coefficient as follows.

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}-1&\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\end{pmatrix}Au\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}Au\Big)\tau^{\prime}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}c&\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}Au\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\end{pmatrix}u\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}c&-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}u\Big)\tau^{\prime}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}u\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}t\tau(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\tau^{\prime}(s)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\mathbb{E}_{s}\big(\tau^{\prime}(s)\mathbb{E}_{t}t\tau(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\big)

We further have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{t=-\infty}^{\infty}\tau^{\prime}(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)n(t)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\tau(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)n(t)]_{-\infty}^{\infty}

\displaystyle-\int_{t=-\infty}^{\infty}\Big(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\tau(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\Big)(-tn(t))d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\mathbb{E}_{t}t\tau(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

Here, we use integration by parts. This is allowed because
n(t)
is absolutely continuous and
\tau^{\prime}
is integrable. Continuing the previous chain of equations, we have

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\mathbb{E}_{s}\big(\tau^{\prime}(s)\mathbb{E}_{t}t\tau(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}\mathbb{E}_{s}\big(\tau^{\prime}(s)(-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{t}\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t))\big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau^{\prime}(s)\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

Putting everything together, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(c)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau^{\prime}(s)\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(-s+\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}t)\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle-\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\epsilon\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\epsilon(-s+\frac{c}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}}t)\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle+\epsilon^{2}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t,\delta))\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c-\epsilon)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)}{\epsilon}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(c)

as required.

Stage 2
: Assume
\tau
is thrice differentiable. Then
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
is differentiable at 1 and
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(1)
.

Let
1\geq\epsilon>0
and let
\delta=-\epsilon s+\sqrt{\epsilon}\sqrt{2-\epsilon}t
. Then we have

\delta=-\epsilon s+\sqrt{2}\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}t-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\epsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}t+r(\epsilon)\epsilon^{\frac{5}{2}}t

where
r(\epsilon)
is derived from the Taylor expansion of the square root about 2. All values between
2-\epsilon
and
2
are contained in the interval
[1,2]
. Because the square root is twice differentiable in that interval with a bounded second derivative, the Lagrange form of the derivative yields that
|r(\epsilon)|
is bounded. Let the bound be
R
. Then

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1-\epsilon)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\Big(\tau((1-\epsilon)s+\sqrt{\epsilon}\sqrt{2-\epsilon}t)-\tau(s)\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\Big(\tau(s+\delta)-\tau(s)\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\Big(\tau(s)+\delta\tau^{\prime}(s)+\frac{1}{2}\delta^{2}\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)+\frac{1}{6}\delta^{3}h(s,\delta)-\tau(s)\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\Big((-\epsilon s+\sqrt{2}\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}t-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\epsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}t+r(\epsilon)\epsilon^{\frac{5}{2}}t)\tau^{\prime}(s)

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}(-\epsilon s+\sqrt{2}\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}t-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\epsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}t+r(\epsilon)\epsilon^{\frac{5}{2}}t)^{2}\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{6}(-\epsilon s+\sqrt{2}\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}t-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\epsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}t+r(\epsilon)\epsilon^{\frac{5}{2}}t)^{3}h(s,\delta)\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\sqrt{2}\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}t\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(s)-\epsilon s\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(s)

\displaystyle+\epsilon t^{2}\tau(s)\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)+\epsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(s,\delta))\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\epsilon(-s\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(s)+\tau(s)\tau^{\prime\prime}(s))+\epsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(s,\delta))\Big)

The last step uses
\mathbb{E}t=0
and
\mathbb{E}t^{2}=1
.

Here,
h
is derived from the Taylor expansion of
\tau
about
s
. Because
\tau
is thrice differentiable, the Lagrange form of the remainder yields
h(s,\delta)=\tau^{\prime\prime\prime}(s^{\prime})
for some
s^{\prime}
with
s\leq s^{\prime}\leq s+\delta
. This in turn yields
|h(s,\delta)|\leq T_{3}(|s|+|t|)
, where
T_{3}
is defined as in section
11.1.3
.

Here,
P_{0}
and
P_{1}
are low-order polynomials of
s
,
t
,
\sqrt{\epsilon}
,
r
,
\tau(s)
,
\tau^{\prime}(s)
and
\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)
terms. (Remember that
c
is a constant.)

First consider
\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(s,\delta))
, the coefficient of
\epsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}
. Let
P_{0}^{+}
and
P_{1}^{+}
be the polynomials that are equal to
P_{0}
and
P_{1}
, except each term has a positive sign. Then

\displaystyle\Big|\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(P_{0}(s,t,\sqrt{\epsilon},r,\tau(s),\tau^{\prime}(s),\tau^{\prime\prime}(s))+

\displaystyle P_{1}(s,t,\sqrt{\epsilon},r,\tau(s),\tau^{\prime}(s),\tau^{\prime\prime}(s))h(s,\delta)\Big)\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(P_{0}^{+}(|s|,|t|,1,R,|\tau(s)|,|\tau^{\prime}(s)|,|\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)|)

\displaystyle+P_{1}^{+}(|s|,|t|,1,R,|\tau(s)|,|\tau^{\prime}(s)|,|\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)|)T_{3}(|s|+|t|)\Big)

Again, by assumption
6
, this bound is finite. So
\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\sqrt{\epsilon}|\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(P_{0}+P_{1}h)|=0
, so
\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\sqrt{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(P_{0}+P_{1}h)=0
.

Now consider
\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(-s\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(s)+\tau(s)\tau^{\prime\prime}(s))
, the coefficient of
\epsilon
. Using integration by parts, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau^{\prime}(s)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{s=-\infty}^{\infty}\tau^{\prime}(s)\big(\tau^{\prime}(s)n(s)\big)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle[\tau(s)\big(\tau^{\prime}(s)n(s)\big)]_{-\infty}^{\infty}-\int_{s=-\infty}^{\infty}\tau(s)\big(\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)n(s)-\tau^{\prime}(s)sn(s)\big)d\mu_{1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s}s\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(s)-\tau(s)\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)

This is allowed because
\tau^{\prime}
is integrable and
\tau(s)n(s)
is absolutely continuous. The latter follows from assumption
6
applied to
(\tau(s)n(s))^{\prime}=\tau^{\prime\prime}(s)n(s)-\tau^{\prime}(s)sn(s)
. This yields that
(\tau(s)n(s))^{\prime}
converges to zero as
s\rightarrow\infty
and
s\rightarrow-\infty
. Since
(\tau(s)n(s))^{\prime}
is also continuous, it is bounded. Hence,
\tau(s)n(s)
is indeed absolutely continuous.

Putting everything together, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(1)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau^{\prime}(s)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s}(s\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(s)-\tau(s)\tau^{\prime\prime}(s))-\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\sqrt{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(s,\delta))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\epsilon}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\epsilon(-s\tau(s)\tau^{\prime}(s)+\tau(s)\tau^{\prime\prime}(s))+\epsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}(P_{0}+P_{1}h(s,\delta))\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1-\epsilon)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)}{\epsilon}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)

as required.

Stage 3
: Assume
\tau
is 5-differentiable. Then
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
is thrice differentiable and
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}\geq 0
,
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime\prime}=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime\prime}}\geq 0
and
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime\prime\prime}=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime\prime\prime}}\geq 0
.

Stages 1 and 2 together yield
\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}_{\tau}=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}
for all
c
. Since both
\tau^{\prime}
and
\tau^{\prime\prime}
are thrice differentiable, we can apply those stages to these functions to obtain
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime\prime}}=\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}_{\tau^{\prime}}=(\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}})^{\prime}=(\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}_{\tau})^{\prime}=\mathfrak{C}^{\prime\prime}_{\tau}
and
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime\prime\prime}}=\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}_{\tau^{\prime\prime}}=(\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime\prime}})^{\prime}=(\mathfrak{C}^{\prime\prime}_{\tau})^{\prime}=\mathfrak{C}^{\prime\prime\prime}_{\tau}
as required. Applying proposition
13
to
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}
,
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime\prime}}
and
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime\prime}}
, we obtain that they are non-negative.

Stage 4
: (a) and (b) hold under the conditions of the theorem.

Throughout the remainder of this proof, we will continue to use the
\tau^{\prime}
notation even though
\tau
is not differentiable everywhere. The following rules apply:

•

In the context of integration,
\tau^{\prime}
may be chosen to refer to either the left or right derivative at any point where
\tau
is not differentiable. Since expressions involving either or both the left and right derivative are assumed to be integrable by assumption
6
, and valid Lebesgue integrals are not affected when altering the value of the integrand at a finite number of points, this choice is immaterial.

•

In the context of bounding
\tau^{\prime}
, any bound has to apply to both the left and right derivative.

If
\tau
is piecewise 5-differentiable with a single piece encompassing
\mathbb{R}
, stage 4 follows directly from stage 3. So now assume there are two or more pieces. Denote the boundaries of the intervals corresponding to the pieces by
s_{1},..,s_{D}
where
D\geq 1
. These intervals are then
(\infty,s_{1}],[s_{1},s_{2}],..,[s_{D-1},s_{D}],[s_{D},\infty)
and there are
D+1
of them. Let
(\epsilon)_{n}
,
n\geq 0
be a positive decreasing sequence that converges to zero, where also
\epsilon_{0}<\frac{1}{2}(s_{d+1}-s_{d})
for all
1\leq d\leq D-1
. Then for any
n
the intervals
[s_{d}-\epsilon_{n},s_{d}+\epsilon_{n}]
,
1\leq d\leq D
are all disjoint. Denote the union of those intervals by
I_{n}
. Then each of the
I_{n}
is contained in
I_{0}
. Since
\tau
is continuous and
I_{0}
is bounded, there is a bound
V
for
|\tau|
across
I_{0}
. Since
\tau
is continuously differentiable on each of
[s_{d}-\epsilon_{0},s_{d}]
,
1\leq d\leq D
and
[s_{d},s_{d}+\epsilon_{0}]
,
1\leq d\leq D
,
\tau^{\prime}
is bounded on each of those intervals. Since there are a finite number of such intervals, we can let some
G
be an upper bound for
|\tau^{\prime}|
across
I_{0}
.

For each
n
, we want to choose an activation function
\tau_{n}
that is equal to
\tau
everywhere except on
I_{n}
and 5-differentiable everywhere. We can choose such a
\tau_{n}
by simply matching the function value and first five derivatives of
\tau
at the boundary points of
I_{n}
. Because
|\tau|
is bounded by
V
on
I_{n}
, we can choose a
\tau_{n}
such that
|\tau_{n}|
is bounded by, say,
2V
on
I_{n}
. Since
|\tau^{\prime}|
is bounded by
G
on the
[s_{d}-\epsilon_{n},s_{d}]
and the
[s_{d},s_{d}+\epsilon_{n}]
, by the intermediate value principle, we have that
|\tau(s_{d})-\tau(s_{d}-\epsilon_{n})|\leq G\epsilon_{n}
and
|\tau(s_{d}+\epsilon_{n})-\tau(s_{d})|\leq G\epsilon_{n}
, so the absolute value of the slope of the line segment from
(s_{d}-\epsilon_{n},\tau(s_{d}-\epsilon_{n}))
to
(s_{d}+\epsilon_{n},\tau(s_{d}+\epsilon_{n}))
is at most
G
. Therefore we can choose
\tau_{n}
so that
|\tau_{n}^{\prime}|
is bounded by, say,
2G
on
I_{n}
. Bounding
\tau_{n}
also means that it is integrable with respect to any Gaussian measure.

Let
\mu_{n}=\int_{s\in I_{n}}n(s)d\mu_{1}
. Then we have
\mu_{n}<2D\epsilon_{n}
. We have

\displaystyle|\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{n}}(c)|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big|\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\tau(s)\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)-\tau_{n}(s)\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\Big)\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big|\tau(s)\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)-\tau_{n}(s)\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big|\tau(s)\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)-\tau_{n}(s)\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\Big|

\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big|\tau_{n}(s)\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)-\tau_{n}(s)\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\Big|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)||\tau(s)-\tau_{n}(s)|

\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{s,t}|\tau_{n}(s)||\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)-\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)||\tau(s)-\tau_{n}(s)|

\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(|\tau(s)|+|\tau(s)-\tau_{n}(s)|)|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)-\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)||\tau(s)-\tau_{n}(s)|

\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t\in I_{n}}|\tau(s)||\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)-\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|

\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}\text{ and }cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t\in I_{n}}|\tau(s)-\tau_{n}(s)||\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)-\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|(|\tau(s)|+|\tau_{n}(s)|)

\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t\in I_{n}}|\tau(s)|(|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|+|\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|)

\displaystyle+\text{\scalebox{0.98}{$\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}\text{ and }cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t\in I_{n}}(|\tau(s)|+|\tau_{n}(s)|)(|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|+|\tau_{n}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|)$}}

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle 3V\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|+3V\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t\in I_{n}}|\tau(s)|+9V^{2}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}

Let
u
be a 2-dimensional unit Gaussian column vector. Because the distribution of
u
is spherically symmetric, it is invariant under multiplication with an orthogonal matrix. Let

A=\begin{pmatrix}c&-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\\
\sqrt{1-c^{2}}&c\end{pmatrix}

It is easy to check that
A
is orthogonal. Then using vector notation we obtain

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t\in I_{n}}|\tau(s)|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{pmatrix}c&\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}u\in I_{n}}|\tau(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}u)|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{pmatrix}c&\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}Au\in I_{n}}|\tau(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}Au)|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\mathbbm{1}_{\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}u\in I_{n}}|\tau(\begin{pmatrix}c&-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}u)|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}|\tau(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|

The last step uses that the distribution of
t
is symmetric about zero. Continuing the long chain of equations from above we have

\displaystyle 3V\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|+3V\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t\in I_{n}}|\tau(s)|+9V^{2}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 6V\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\mathbbm{1}_{s\in I_{n}}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|+9V^{2}\mu_{n}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 6V\int_{s\in I_{n}}\Big(\mathbb{E}_{t}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|\Big)n(s)d\mu_{1}+9V^{2}\mu_{n}

We have
\mathbb{E}_{t}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|=\mathbb{E}_{z}|\tau(z)|
, where
z
has mean
cs
and standard deviation
\sqrt{1-c^{2}}
. So the standard deviation of
z
is bounded by
1
. Further,
|cs|
is bounded by
\max(|s_{1}-\epsilon_{0}|,|s_{D}+\epsilon_{0}|)
. Further,
|\tau|
is continuous, so it is bounded on any bounded interval. So by lemma
10
, we have that
\mathbb{E}_{z}|\tau(z)|
is bounded across
c
and
s
. Let that bound be
B
. Then

6V\int_{s\in I_{n}}\Big(\mathbb{E}_{t}|\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)|\Big)n(s)d\mu_{1}+9V^{2}\mu_{n}\leq 6VB\mu_{n}+9V^{2}\mu_{n}\leq 12VBD\epsilon_{n}+18V^{2}D\epsilon_{n}

So in summary, we have
|\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{n}}(c)|\leq 12VBD\epsilon_{n}+18V^{2}D\epsilon_{n}
. Analogously, we obtain
|\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(c)-\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{n}^{\prime}}(c)|\leq 12GBD\epsilon_{n}+18G^{2}D\epsilon_{n}
. The only difference in the derivation is that
|\tau^{\prime}|
is not continuous. However,
|\tau^{\prime}|
is continuous on each of a finite set of pieces, so
|\tau^{\prime}|
is still bounded on any bounded interval via the maximum of the piecewise bounds. So lemma
10
still applies.

Both
12VBD\epsilon_{n}+18V^{2}D\epsilon_{n}
and
12GBD\epsilon_{n}+18G^{2}D\epsilon_{n}
are independent of
c
, so
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{n}}
converges uniformly to
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
and
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{n}^{\prime}}
converges uniformly to
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}
. Since also
\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}_{\tau_{n}}=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{n}^{\prime}}
by stage 4, we have
\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}_{\tau}=\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}
. This is (a).

By stage 3, all the
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{n}}
have the properties in (b). It is easy to check that these properties are also preserved under uniform function convergence.

Stage 5
: (c) holds under the conditions of the theorem.

Using lemma
11
, we have

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tau(s)\tau(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(\tilde{\tau}(s)+a_{\tau}s+b_{\tau})(\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+b_{\tau})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\Big(\tilde{\tau}(s)\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+\tilde{\tau}(s)a_{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle+\tilde{\tau}(s)b_{\tau}+a_{\tau}s\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}^{2}s(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}b_{\tau}s

\displaystyle+b_{\tau}\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}b_{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+b_{\tau}^{2}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big(\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(s)\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}c\mathbb{E}_{s}s\tilde{\tau}(s)+a_{\tau}\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{s}\tilde{\tau}(s)\mathbb{E}_{t}t

\displaystyle+b_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s}\tilde{\tau}(s)+a_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}s\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}^{2}c\mathbb{E}_{s}s^{2}+a_{\tau}^{2}\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{s}s\mathbb{E}_{t}t+a_{\tau}b_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s}s

\displaystyle+b_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}b_{\tau}c\mathbb{E}_{s}s+a_{\tau}b_{\tau}\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{t}t+b_{\tau}^{2}\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big(\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(s)\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}s\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle+a_{\tau}^{2}c+b_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+b_{\tau}^{2}\Big)

cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t
is unit Gaussian just as
s
, so
\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)=\mathbb{E}_{s}\tilde{\tau}(s)=0
.

Let
u
be a 2-dimensional unit Gaussian column vector. Because the distribution of
u
is spherically symmetric, it is invariant under multiplication with an orthogonal matrix. Let

A=\begin{pmatrix}c&-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\\
\sqrt{1-c^{2}}&c\end{pmatrix}

It is easy to check that
A
is orthogonal. Using vector notation, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}s\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}u\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}c&\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}u\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}Au\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}c&\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}Au\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{u}\Big(\begin{pmatrix}c&-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\end{pmatrix}u\Big)\tau\Big(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}u\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}(cs-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)\tilde{\tau}(s)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c\mathbb{E}_{s}s\tilde{\tau}(s)-\sqrt{1-c^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{s}\tilde{\tau}(s)\mathbb{E}_{t}t

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

So we obtain

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(s)\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}s\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)

\displaystyle+a_{\tau}^{2}c+b_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+b_{\tau}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(s)\tilde{\tau}(cs+\sqrt{1-c^{2}}t)+a_{\tau}^{2}c+b_{\tau}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}(c)+a_{\tau}^{2}c+b_{\tau}^{2}

This is (i). Throughout the rest of this stage, we will repeatedly use lemma
11
. We have

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}(s)\tilde{\tau}(t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{s}\tilde{\tau}(s))^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

This is (ii).

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}(0)+0a_{\tau}^{2}+b_{\tau}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle b_{\tau}^{2}

This is (iii).

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}^{\prime}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}^{\prime}}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s,t}\tilde{\tau}^{\prime}(s)\tilde{\tau}^{\prime}(t)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{s}\tilde{\tau}^{\prime}(s))^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tilde{\tau}^{\prime}(s)n(s)d\mu_{1}\Big)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big([\tilde{\tau}(s)n(s)]_{-\infty}^{\infty}-\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tilde{\tau}(s)(-sn(s))d\mu_{1}\Big)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}}s\tilde{\tau}(s)n(s)d\mu_{1}\Big)^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{s}s\tilde{\tau}(s))^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

Here, we use integration by parts, which is allowed because
\tau^{\prime}
, and hence
\tilde{\tau}^{\prime}
, is integrable and
n(s)
is uniformly continuous. We also use that
\tilde{\tau}
is piecewise 5-differentiable since
\tau
is. Thus, we obtain (iv).

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}^{\prime}_{\tau}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{\tau^{\prime}}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau^{\prime}(s))^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{s}s\tau(s))^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle a_{\tau}^{2}

This is (v). We use integration by parts as above.

\displaystyle CAR(\tau,\mathcal{N}(0,1))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{(b_{\tau}+a_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{s}s)^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau(s)^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{b_{\tau}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau(s)^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(0)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)}

This is (vi).

\displaystyle LAR(\tau,\mathcal{N}(0,1))

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{s}((s-\mathbb{E}_{s}s)a_{\tau})^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau(s)^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{a_{\tau}^{2}\mathbb{E}_{s}s^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau(s)^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}^{\prime}(0)}{\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)}

This is (vii). If
\tau
is linear, then
\tilde{\tau}
is the zero function and so
\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}
is the zero function. Hence,
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(c)=a_{\tau}^{2}c+b_{\tau}^{2}
, which is linear. Conversely, if
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}
is linear, then so is
\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}
. Since
\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}(0)=\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}^{\prime}(0)=0
,
\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}
is the zero function, and so
\mathfrak{C}_{\tilde{\tau}}(1)=\mathbb{E}\tilde{\tau}(s)^{2}=0
. Since
\tilde{\tau}(s)n(s)
is continuous, by the contrapositive of lemma
8
,
\tilde{\tau}
is the zero function, and so
\tau
is linear. This yields (viii), which completes the stage.

Stage 6
: The second part of the theorem holds.

We have
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)=\mathbb{E}_{s}\tau(s)^{2}
. Because
\tau
is not linear, it is not zero everywhere. Hence we can apply lemma
8
to
\tau(s)^{2}n(s)
to obtain
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau}(1)>0
. Hence,
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is valid. Also, theorem statement (b) clearly holds for
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
and theorem statement (a) implies that
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is differentiable.

It is obvious that no two of the three convergence cases can hold simultaneously. We will now show that at least one of them holds. Clearly, 1 is a fixed point of
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
. We will now consider three distinct possibilities based on the number of other fixed points.

Possibility 1:
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c)
has no fixed points apart from
c=1
.

Because
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is increasing, we have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}^{\prime}_{\tau}(1)\geq 0
. Because
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is convex and increasing,
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)=0
implies that
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is constant. This would contradict proposition
12
since
\tau
is non-constant. Hence,
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}^{\prime}_{\tau}(1)>0
.

If
1>\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}^{\prime}_{\tau}(1)>0
, convergence case 1 holds. If
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}^{\prime}_{\tau}(1)=1
, convergence case 2 holds. Finally, assume that
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}^{\prime}_{\tau}(1)>1
. Then there is a
c
such that
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c)<c
. But we also have that
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(0)\geq 0
by proposition
13
, that
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is continuous and that there is no fixed point besides 1. Contradiction.

Possibility 2:
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c)
has exactly one fixed point apart from
c=1
.

Let this fixed point be
c^{\text{lim}}<1
. Because
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is continuous, it is either above or below the diagonal in
[c^{\text{lim}},1]
. It cannot lie above the diagonal, else the chord from
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c^{\text{lim}})
to
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(1)
lies below
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
. So
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
lies below the diagonal. Let
1>c_{2}>c^{\text{lim}}
. Then
\frac{\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(1)-\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{2})}{1-c_{2}}>1
and
\frac{\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{2})-\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c^{\text{lim}})}{c_{2}-c^{\text{lim}}}<1
. By the intermediate value principle and because
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is convex, we have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(1)>1
and
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(c^{\text{lim}})<1
. Because
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is increasing,
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}^{\prime}(c^{\text{lim}})\geq 0
, so convergence case 3 holds.

Possibility 3:
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c)
has more than one fixed point apart from
c=1
.

Let
c_{1}
be the infimum of all fixed points. Because
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}
is continuous,
c_{1}
is itself a fixed point. Under possibility 3, there exists an additional fixed point
c_{2}
such that
1>c_{2}>c_{1}
. Consider some
c_{2}>c_{3}>c_{1}
. Because the chord from
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{1})
to
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{2})
cannot lie below
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})
, we must have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})\leq c_{3}
. Because the chord from
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})
to
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(1)
cannot lie below
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{2})
, we must have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})\geq c_{3}
. Hence,
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})=c_{3}
. Now consider some
c_{3}>c_{2}
. Because the chord from
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{2})
to
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(1)
cannot lie below
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})
, we must have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})\leq c_{3}
. Because the chord from
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{1})
to
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})
cannot lie below
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{2})
, we must have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})\geq c_{3}
. Hence,
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{3})=c_{3}
. In summary, we have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c)=c
for all
c\geq c_{1}
. Assume
c_{1}=0
. Then
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c)=c
for all
c
and so
\mathfrak{C}
is linear. So by stage 5,
\tau
is linear. Contradiction. So
c_{1}>0
. Let
\epsilon<\min(\frac{1}{2}(1-c_{1}),c_{1})
and let
c_{4}=c_{1}-\epsilon
. It is easy to check that
c_{4}
,
c_{4}+\epsilon
,
c_{4}+2\epsilon
and
c_{4}+3\epsilon
are in
[0,1]
. Since the chord from
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{4})
to
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(1)
cannot lie below
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{1})
, we have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{4})\geq c_{4}
. Because
c_{4}
is not a fixed point, we further have
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{4})>c_{4}
. But then
\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{4}+3\epsilon)-3\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{4}+2\epsilon)+3\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{4}+\epsilon)-\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{4})=c_{4}-\tilde{\mathfrak{C}}_{\tau}(c_{4})<0
. Contradiction. So possibility 3 is invalid. This completes the proof.

∎

11.6
Mean field theory of batch normalization

There are two theoretical results covered in this chapter that do not straightforwardly extend to the case where an A-architecture contains batch normalization layers: theorem
5
and proposition
19
. As throughout most of this work, as discussed in section
2.4.1.1
, we relegate the BN case to its own section so that we can present the BN-free case without the additional conceptual and notational complexity that BN brings with it. As usual, we conceptualize an architecture with BN as a function that takes not an individual input, but a batch of inputs in addition to a parameter. We formalize our notation, terminology and conventions for this situation in subsection
11.6.1
. In subsection
11.6.2
, we give a single lemma that is used to model the limit of expectation operators as the batch size converges to infinity. Finally, we give and prove generalizations of theorem
5
and proposition
19
to the BN case in subsections
11.6.3
and
11.6.4
respectively.

Both results rely on taking the limit of batch size to infinity. To our knowledge, this is a novel approach in mean field theory. For layer normalization, taking the width of layers to infinity means that the moments used for normalization are taken over an infinite sample. This allows us to replace these random moments with their almost sure limit, which yields the very simple calculation rules in table
5.3
. For batch normalization, the strategy is analogous. When taking the batch size to infinity, the random moments taken across the batch can also be replaced by their almost sure limit, which yields equally simple calculation rules. Conditional on these limits, the propagation of individual inputs and their gradients becomes effectively independent of the batch. Considering this similarity, the form of theorem
5
for the BN case is ultimately analogous to the LN case, except that three limit operators are present instead of two.

The generalization of proposition
19
is less intuitive. Table
5.3
implies that
\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}(q,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}
, the derivative of the covariance kernel used in section
5.4.5
, is zero if there is no directed path from input to output layer in the layer graph not containing a BN layer. To explain this, we must consider the elem-like
(q,c)
condition on the input distribution. It implies that the
q
and
c
parameter affect not only the square mean and co-mean of one or two inputs, but of almost all inputs. Varying the
c
parameter changes the co-mean of
f(x)
and
f(x^{\prime})
as the co-mean of
x
and
x^{\prime}
varies, and as the co-mean of
x
and
x^{\prime}
with other inputs varies as well. Varying the co-mean with other inputs is immaterial if the architecture does not contain BN as those other inputs do not affect the value of
f(x)
and
f(x^{\prime})
. However, if the architecture does contain BN, varying
c
effectively varies not just the co-mean of
x
and
x^{\prime}
, but the function
f
itself via its dependence on the batch. In order to eliminate this side effect, we need to allow the co-mean of
x
and
x^{\prime}
to differ from all other co-means. We call this “special” co-mean the
r
parameter. Based on this insight, we prove an extension to theorem
5
that establishes calculation rules for the mean field limit of the co-mean of
f_{l}(x)
and
f_{l}(x^{\prime})
, which we term
\mathfrak{r}_{l}
. Finally, we replace
\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}(q,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}
by a covariance kernel derivative that represents
\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{L}}{dr}|_{r=q}
, and we obtain the desired result.

11.6.1
Additional notation, terminology and conventions

The following notation, terminology and conventions (NTCs) apply throughout the remainder of this section, and hence throughout the remainder of this chapter. We say a ‘batch input’ or simply ‘batch’
X
is a tuple
(x^{(1)},..,x^{(B)})
of ‘individual inputs’ or simply ‘inputs’, which are vectors of dimensionality
d_{\text{in}}
.
B
denotes batch size. An A-architecture
f
is a function that given a parameter
\theta
and batch input
X
returns a ‘batch output’
f(X)
. We say it is composed of ‘big layers’
f_{l}
,
0\leq l\leq L
that form a ‘big layer graph’. A big layer
f_{l}
is composed of ‘small layers’
f_{l,b}
,
1\leq b\leq B
. We refer to
l
as the ‘big layer index’ and
b
as the ‘batch index’. When propagating
X
forward, a small layer represents the value obtained for an individual input and a big layer represents the value obtained jointly for all individual inputs. We use the terms ‘FC layer’, ‘BN layer’, etc. to refer to both big and small layers.
