\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\lim_{B,N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\frac{1}{d_{l}^{\text{MF}}}||\mathcal{J}_{l,m,1}(X^{(1)})||_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\lim_{B,N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\overline{p^{(n^{-},1)}_{l,1}.p^{(n^{-},1)}_{l,1}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\lim_{B,N}\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}\overline{F^{-}_{l,1}.F^{-}_{l,1}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

The major difference is the form of the recursive expansion as it arises in the BN and activation layer cases of the induction, which we dive into below. The following minor differences also arise.

•

The
F^{\text{MN}}_{b}
are input layers. Each of them corresponds to a segment of
u
of dimensionality
d_{m}^{\text{MF}}
. Because
u
is unit Gaussian, we add a diagonal entry of 1 and off-diagonal entries of zero to the covariance matrix of
\mathcal{G}
for each
F^{\text{MN}}_{b}
. Distribution equality is obvious. The
\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\text{ a.s.}}
quantities become
\tilde{\mathfrak{m}}^{\text{MN}}_{1}=0
,
\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;MN}}_{1;1}=1
and
\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;MN}}_{1;2}=\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;(n)}}_{1;m,1}=\mathfrak{c}^{\text{MN;(n)}}_{1;m,2}=0
. The same holds for the
\lim_{B,N}
quantities. Finally,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}^{\text{MN;MN}}_{1;1}=1=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
. This is required to start off the induction.

•

n^{-}
does not arise in the construction of
F
and all limit quantities are independent of
n^{-}
and
N
. The
n^{-}\neq n^{+}
case becomes the general case.

•

The case where
f_{l}
is a readin layer does not appear in the induction step as
l>m>0
and
f_{m}
is a bottleneck for
f_{l}
. We can ignore all associated arguments.

•

When
f_{l}
is an addition layer, the recursive expansion of
\rho_{l}^{-}
halts at the
\rho^{\text{MN}}_{b}
, as these are now dummy multi-activation functions. The same arguments apply as the
e^{\text{MN}}_{b}
are independent of all other
e
terms for input and FC layers in
F
and as
\tilde{\mathfrak{m}}^{\text{MN}}_{1}=0
.

•

If
f_{l}
is an FC, bias or addition layer, we obtain
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}^{-;-}_{l,1;l,1}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
as required, as the induction hypothesis now yields
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}^{-;-}_{k,1;k,1}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
.

Let’s look at the BN layer case. The “first expansion” becomes

\displaystyle\rho_{l,1}^{-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}}c_{l^{\prime}}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{l^{\prime},l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)(e_{l^{\prime},1}^{-}-\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}^{-}})

\displaystyle+\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}}\sum_{\mathcal{L}\in\mathsf{indpow}(P_{l^{\prime},l}),Z=|\mathcal{L}|>0}c_{l^{\prime}}(-1)^{|Z|}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{l^{\prime},l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)...

\displaystyle...\frac{(\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}^{-}\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[1]}}^{+}}-\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}^{-}}\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[1]}}^{+}})(\rho^{+}_{k_{\mathcal{L}[Z]},1}-\widehat{\rho^{+}_{k_{\mathcal{L}[Z]}}})}{\nu_{\mathcal{L}[Z]}^{+}}\prod_{z=1}^{|Z|-1}\frac{\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z]}}^{+}\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z+1]}}^{+}}-\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z]}}^{+}}\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z+1]}}^{+}}}{\nu_{\mathcal{L}[z]}^{+}}

\displaystyle+\sum_{f_{m}}c_{m}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{m,l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)(e_{1}^{\text{MN}}-\widehat{e^{\text{MN}}})

\displaystyle+\sum_{f_{m}}\sum_{\mathcal{L}\in\mathsf{indpow}(P_{m,l}),Z=|\mathcal{L}|>0}c_{m}(-1)^{|Z|}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{m,l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)...

\displaystyle...\frac{(\widehat{e^{\text{MN}}\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[1]}}^{+}}-\widehat{e^{\text{MN}}}\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[1]}}^{+}})(\rho^{+}_{k_{\mathcal{L}[Z]},1}-\widehat{\rho^{+}_{k_{\mathcal{L}[Z]}}})}{\nu_{\mathcal{L}[Z]}^{+}}\prod_{z=1}^{|Z|-1}\frac{\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z]}}^{+}\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z+1]}}^{+}}-\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z]}}^{+}}\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z+1]}}^{+}}}{\nu_{\mathcal{L}[z]}^{+}}

Here, for consistency of notation, we write
\sum_{f_{m}}
for the sum over only layer
f_{m}
if that layer is touched by the recursive expansion and a sum over no layers otherwise. (Note again that the recursive expansion halts at the
\rho^{\text{MN}}_{b}
.) The difference between this first expansion and that for the BN layer case of stage 12 is that super terms 3 and 4 have been replaced by copies of super terms 1 and 2 where
l^{\prime}
is replaced by

. Control holds as in stage 12.

We can decompose
(e_{1}^{\text{MN}},..,e_{B}^{\text{MN}})
as
u^{\text{MN}}+c^{\{9\}}s^{\text{MN}}
where
u^{\text{MN}}
is a Gaussian vector with mean zero and covariance matrix as our other
u
vectors,

is a unit Gaussian scalar and

. We use this to derive the “second expansion”. It contains minus terms, minus plus terms, short plus terms and long plus terms as in the BN layer case of stage 12. We no longer obtain n-terms and n-plus terms, but we obtain similar terms where some
u^{(n)}
components are replaced by
u^{\text{MN}}
components, and the N-sum, N-frequency and part of the normalizer are removed. For example, an n-term becomes

c_{m}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{m,l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)u^{\text{MN}}[1]

Note that no such term is present if
\sum_{f_{m}}
is the empty sum. Again,
\rho_{l,1}
is a sum over a fixed number of six kinds of pure terms of standard form. Compared to the BN layer case of stage 12, standard form terms now do not contain N-sums and N-frequencies, but we allow them to contain
u^{\text{MN}}
components. The application of lemma
18
is as in the BN layer case of stage 12. Since no N-sums are present, each product of a pure term and a pure or co-term has standard form. Since now no
c^{\{4\}}
terms or
c^{\{6\}}
terms are present, we immediately obtain that
\ddot{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,1}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;+}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;+}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;-}
and
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;-}
are valid.
\ddot{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,1}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;-}=0
holds again by symmetry. To determine the value of
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;+}
and
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;-}
, we again consider individual products of pure terms and pure terms or co-terms and find that most of them become zero because of the multiplier converging to zero, the presence of a single
u
component, or the B-frequency converging to zero. We obtain
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;+}=0
and when we endow

\displaystyle\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}}\Bigg(\frac{\lim_{B,N}c_{l^{\prime}}^{2}c^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}c^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}}{\lim_{B\text{ a.s.}}\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{l^{\prime},l}}\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}\Bigg)\mathbb{E}_{u}u_{l^{\prime}}^{-}[1]^{2}+\sum_{f_{m}}\Bigg(\frac{\lim_{B,N}c_{m}^{2}}{\lim_{B\text{ a.s.}}\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{m,l}}\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}\Bigg)\mathbb{E}_{u}u^{\text{MN}}[1]^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}}\frac{c_{l^{\prime}}^{2}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;-}}{\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{l^{\prime},l}}\ddot{\nu}_{l^{\prime\prime}}}+\sum_{f_{m}}\frac{c_{m}^{2}}{\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{m,l}}\ddot{\nu}_{l^{\prime\prime}}}

Again, using the recursive calculation rules for bias, addition and BN layers, it is easy to check that this is equivalent to
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;-}=\frac{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{k,1;k,1}^{-;-}}{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{k,1;k,1}-\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{k,1;k,2}+\epsilon_{l}}
. Hence
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;-}=\frac{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{k,1;k,1}^{-;-}}{\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{k,1;k,1}-\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{k,1;k,2}+\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\epsilon_{l}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}{(\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k})\mathfrak{g}_{m}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}
as required.

Finally, let’s turn to the activation layer case. The first recursive expansion becomes

\displaystyle\rho_{l,1}^{-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ normed}}c_{l^{\prime}}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{l^{\prime},l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)(e_{l^{\prime},1}^{-}-\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}^{-}})\tau_{l}^{\prime}(\rho_{k,1}^{+})

\displaystyle+\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ normed}}\sum_{\mathcal{L}\in\mathsf{indpow}(P_{l^{\prime},l}),Z=|\mathcal{L}|>0}c_{l^{\prime}}(-1)^{|Z|}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{l^{\prime},l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)...

\displaystyle...\frac{(\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}^{-}\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[1]}}^{+}}-\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}^{-}}\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[1]}}^{+}})(\rho^{+}_{k_{\mathcal{L}[Z]},1}-\widehat{\rho^{+}_{k_{\mathcal{L}[Z]}}})}{\nu_{\mathcal{L}[Z]}^{+}}\Bigg(\prod_{z=1}^{|Z|-1}\frac{\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z]}}^{+}\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z+1]}}^{+}}-\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z]}}^{+}}\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z+1]}}^{+}}}{\nu_{\mathcal{L}[z]}^{+}}\Bigg)\tau_{l}^{\prime}(\rho_{k,1}^{+})

\displaystyle+\sum_{f_{m}\text{ normed}}c_{m}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{m,l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)(e_{1}^{\text{MN}}-\widehat{e^{\text{MN}}})\tau_{l}^{\prime}(\rho_{k,1}^{+})

\displaystyle+\sum_{f_{m}\text{ normed}}\sum_{\mathcal{L}\in\mathsf{indpow}(P_{m,l}),Z=|\mathcal{L}|>0}c_{m}(-1)^{|Z|}\Bigg(\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{m,l}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}}\Bigg)...

\displaystyle...\frac{(\widehat{e^{\text{MN}}\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[1]}}^{+}}-\widehat{e^{\text{MN}}}\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[1]}}^{+}})(\rho^{+}_{k_{\mathcal{L}[Z]},1}-\widehat{\rho^{+}_{k_{\mathcal{L}[Z]}}})}{\nu_{\mathcal{L}[Z]}^{+}}...

\displaystyle...\Bigg(\prod_{z=1}^{|Z|-1}\frac{\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z]}}^{+}\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z+1]}}^{+}}-\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z]}}^{+}}\widehat{\rho_{k_{\mathcal{L}[z+1]}}^{+}}}{\nu_{\mathcal{L}[z]}^{+}}\Bigg)\tau_{l}^{\prime}(\rho_{k,1}^{+})

\displaystyle+\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}\text{ unnormed}}c_{l^{\prime}}e_{l^{\prime},1}^{-}\tau_{l}^{\prime}(\rho_{k,1}^{+})+\sum_{f_{m}\text{ unnormed}}c_{m}e_{1}^{\text{MN}}\tau_{l}^{\prime}(\rho_{k,1}^{+})

The difference between this first expansion and that for the activation layer case of stage 12 is that super terms 3, 4 and 6 have been replaced by copies of super terms 1, 2 and 5 where

. Control holds as in stage 12. Again, we derive the second expansion. It contains minus terms, minus plus terms, short plus terms and long plus terms as in the activation layer case of stage 12. We no longer obtain n-terms and n-plus terms, but we obtain similar terms where some

Again,

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{f_{l^{\prime}}}\Bigg(\frac{\lim_{B,N}c_{l^{\prime}}^{2}c^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}c^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}}{\lim_{B\text{ a.s.}}\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{l^{\prime},l}}\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}\Bigg)\mathbb{E}_{u,s,v}u_{l^{\prime}}^{-}[1]^{2}\tau_{l}^{\prime}(\ddot{\mathsf{exp}}_{l,1})^{2}

\displaystyle+\sum_{f_{m}}\Bigg(\frac{\lim_{B,N}c_{m}^{2}}{\lim_{B\text{ a.s.}}\prod_{f_{l^{\prime\prime}}\in P_{m,l}}\nu_{l^{\prime\prime}}^{+}}\Bigg)\mathbb{E}_{u,s,v}u^{\text{MN}}[1]^{2}\tau_{l}^{\prime}(\ddot{\mathsf{exp}}_{l,1})^{2}

Again, using the recursive calculation rules for bias, addition and BN layers, it is easy to check that we have

Again, we proceed along the lines of stage 12, where we now let

We will have to show that the expression on the last line is

Let’s start by looking at the readin layers. If
f_{l}
if a readin big layer, the distribution of the

is the distribution of the segments of

are zero, except the diagonal entry added for

. While distribution equality is clear, the major consequence of this is that there is no symmetry between the batch index value 1 and other batch index values for any quantity that depends directly or indirectly on the distribution of the
F^{-}_{l,b}
or the
\rho^{-}_{l,b}(e)

\tilde{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,1}^{-}
,

,
\tilde{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,1}^{+}=\tilde{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,1}

,
\mathfrak{c}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;-}

\mathfrak{c}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;-}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l,2;l,3}^{-;-}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;+}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;+}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l,2;l,1}^{-;+}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;+}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l,2;l,3}^{-;+}

and

is not affected by the distribution of the layers in

This wider range of limit quantities will unfortunately complicate our limit analysis for BN and activation big layers. Before we go ahead with this analysis, we again document “minor” differences to the analysis in stage 12, just as for the case
m>0
above.

•

The
F^{\text{MN}}_{b}
do not arise, as they pertain only to the case

•

n^{-}
does not arise in the construction of

and all limit quantities are independent of

and

case becomes the general case.

•

The induction is now used to show the following with regards to limits: (i)
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;-}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;-}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,3}^{-;-}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,1}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,3}^{-;+}=0
; (ii)

; (iii)

. From this we obtain

as required. When

is a readin, FC, bias or addition layer, (i) through (iv) carry over easily from the dependencies or the generator, as in stage 12. For an addition layer, as we have

Joint distribution of inputs
Compared to the BN layer case of stage 12, the inputs of

\displaystyle e_{l^{\prime},1}^{+}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c^{\{1\}}_{l^{\prime}}z_{l^{\prime}}^{+}

\displaystyle e_{l^{\prime},1}^{-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c^{\{2\}}_{l^{\prime}}z_{l^{\prime}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l^{\prime}}z_{l^{\prime}}^{-}

\displaystyle e_{l^{\prime},b}^{+}

\displaystyle e_{l^{\prime},b}^{-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle c^{\{7\}}_{l^{\prime}}z_{l^{\prime}}^{+}+c^{\{8\}}_{l^{\prime}}z_{l^{\prime}}^{-}+c^{\{9\}}_{l^{\prime}}s_{l^{\prime}}^{+}+c^{\{10\}}_{l^{\prime}}s_{l^{\prime}}^{-}+c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}u_{l^{\prime}}^{+}[b]+c^{\{13\}}_{l^{\prime}}u_{l^{\prime}}^{-}[b]\text{ for }b\geq 2

. To start with, we obtain

c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{11\}}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{e}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{+}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{+}-\mathbb{E}_{e}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{+}e_{l^{\prime},3}^{+}}=\sqrt{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}}

c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{12\}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{e}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{-}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{+}-\mathbb{E}_{e}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{-}e_{l^{\prime},3}^{+}}{c^{\{11\}}_{l^{\prime}}}=\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;+}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;+}}{\sqrt{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}}}

c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{13\}}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{e}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{-}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{-}-\mathbb{E}_{e}e_{l^{\prime},2}^{-}e_{l^{\prime},3}^{-}-c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}}

=\sqrt{\frac{(\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-})(\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2})-(\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;+}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;+})^{2}}{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}}}

This is reminiscent of
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{1\}}
,
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{3\}}
and
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{5\}}
from the BN layer case of stage 12. Let’s look at the square roots that arise in the formulas above. Because
Q_{l^{\prime}}
is positive semi-definite, the quadratic form defined by
Q_{l^{\prime}}
applied to any vector is non-negative. Using this principle on
(0\times B,1,-1,0\times(B-2))
yields
\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}\geq 0
. Here,
\times
refers to the repetition of a vector component. Going forward, we use
\widetilde{\mathsf{expr}}
to refer to the mean of
\mathsf{expr}
over batch index values 2 through
B
, i.e.
\widetilde{\mathsf{expr}}=\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{b^{\prime}=2}^{B}\mathsf{expr}|_{b=b^{\prime}}
. The Cauchy-Schwartz inequality yields
\frac{(B-1)^{2}}{(B-2)^{2}}\Big(\mathbb{E}_{e}(e_{l^{\prime},2}^{-}-\widetilde{e_{l^{\prime}}^{-}})^{2}\mathbb{E}_{e}(e_{l^{\prime},2}^{+}-\widetilde{e_{l^{\prime}}^{+}})^{2}-(\mathbb{E}_{e}(e_{l^{\prime},2}^{-}-\widetilde{e_{l^{\prime}}^{-}})(e_{l^{\prime},2}^{+}-\widetilde{e_{l^{\prime}}^{+}}))^{2}\Big)=(\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-})(\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2})-(\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{+;-}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{+;-})^{2}\geq 0
. So expressions to which square roots are applied are indeed non-negative.

Let’s look at denominators that arise in the formulas above. When
\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}=0
, the Cauchy-Schwartz-derived relationship above yields
\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{+;-}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{+;-}=0
, and hence we can remove
u_{l^{\prime}}^{+}
from the decomposition, which corresponds to setting
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{11\}}=c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{12\}}=0
and
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{13\}}=\sqrt{\mathfrak{c}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;-}-\mathfrak{c}_{l,2;l,3}^{-;-}}
. So we never have to divide by zero.

Let’s look at the limits of
c^{\{11\}}_{l^{\prime}}
,
c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}
and
c^{\{13\}}_{l^{\prime}}
with respect to
N
and
B
. From the induction hypothesis, we have that the individual
\mathfrak{c}^{-;-}_{l^{\prime},.;l^{\prime},.}
and
\mathfrak{c}^{+;-}_{l^{\prime},.;l^{\prime},.}
have valid limits. By non-singularity from stage 9, we have
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}>0
. So we obtain that
\ddot{c}^{\{11\}}_{l^{\prime}}
,
\ddot{c}^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}
and
\ddot{c}^{\{13\}}_{l^{\prime}}
have identical formulas to
c^{\{11\}}_{l^{\prime}}
,
c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}
and
c^{\{13\}}_{l^{\prime}}
above except that two dots are placed above each
\mathfrak{c}
term. So, by the induction hypothesis, we further have
\ddot{c}_{l^{\prime}}^{\{11\}}=\sqrt{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}}
and
\ddot{c}_{l^{\prime}}^{\{12\}}=\ddot{c}_{l^{\prime}}^{\{13\}}=0
. Using the principle of the non-negative quadratic form on
(0,1,-1,0\times(2B-3))
yields
\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}\geq 0
. Using the principle of the non-negative quadratic form on
(0,1,1,0\times(2B-3))
yields
\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}+\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}\geq 0
. Combining those results yields
|\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}|\geq|\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}|\geq 0
. Since the induction hypothesis yields
\lim_{B,N}B\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}=0
, we also have
\lim_{B,N}B\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}=0
. Finally, since
c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}+c^{\{13\}}_{l^{\prime}}c^{\{13\}}_{l^{\prime}}=\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}
, we have
\lim_{B,N}\sqrt{B}c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}=\lim_{B,N}\sqrt{B}c^{\{13\}}_{l^{\prime}}=0
.

Knowing the value of
c^{\{11\}}_{l^{\prime}}
,
c^{\{12\}}_{l^{\prime}}
and
c^{\{13\}}_{l^{\prime}}
, an assignment to the other 10
c^{\{.\}}_{l^{\prime}}
terms is valid if they satisfy the following system.

\begin{pmatrix}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}&\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}&\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}&\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}\\
\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}&\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;-}&\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}^{-;+}&\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}\\
\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}&\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}^{-;+}&\frac{B-2}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}+\frac{1}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}&\frac{B-2}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;+}+\frac{1}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;+}\\
\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}&\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}&\frac{B-2}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;+}+\frac{1}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;+}&\frac{B-2}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}+\frac{1}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}\end{pmatrix}=A_{l^{\prime}}A_{l^{\prime}}^{T}

where

A_{l^{\prime}}=\begin{pmatrix}c^{\{1\}}_{l^{\prime}}&0&0&0\\
c^{\{2\}}_{l^{\prime}}&c^{\{3\}}_{l^{\prime}}&0&0\\
c^{\{4\}}_{l^{\prime}}&c^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}&c^{\{6\}}_{l^{\prime}}&0\\
c^{\{7\}}_{l^{\prime}}&c^{\{8\}}_{l^{\prime}}&c^{\{9\}}_{l^{\prime}}&c^{\{10\}}_{l^{\prime}}\\
\end{pmatrix}

In other words,
A_{l^{\prime}}A_{l^{\prime}}^{T}
must be the Cholesky decomposition of a matrix. Call it
R_{l^{\prime}}
. Let
v
be an arbitrary 4-dimensional row vector. Then

vR_{l^{\prime}}v^{T}=v^{*}Q_{l^{\prime}}(v^{*})^{T}\geq 0\text{ where }v^{*}=(v[2],\frac{v[4]}{B-1}\times(B-1),v[1],\frac{v[3]}{B-1}\times(B-1))

as
Q_{l^{\prime}}
is positive semi-definite. So
R_{l^{\prime}}
is itself positive semi-definite. So we can set unique valid values for
c^{\{1\}}_{l^{\prime}}
through
c^{\{10\}}_{l^{\prime}}
by letting
A_{l^{\prime}}A_{l^{\prime}}^{T}
be the Cholesky decomposition where the number of columns that are not all zero equals the rank of
R_{l^{\prime}}
.

What remains is to investigate the limits of
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{1\}}
through
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{10\}}
. We have
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{7\}}c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{7\}}+c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{8\}}c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{8\}}+c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{9\}}c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{9\}}+c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{10\}}c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{10\}}=\frac{B-2}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}+\frac{1}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}
.
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}=0
so
\ddot{c}_{l^{\prime}}^{\{7\}}=\ddot{c}_{l^{\prime}}^{\{8\}}=\ddot{c}_{l^{\prime}}^{\{9\}}=\ddot{c}_{l^{\prime}}^{\{10\}}=0
. Since
\lim_{B,N}B\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},2}^{-;-}=\lim_{B,N}B\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},2;l^{\prime},3}^{-;-}=0
, we also have
\lim_{B,N}\sqrt{B}c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{7\}}=\lim_{B,N}\sqrt{B}c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{8\}}=\lim_{B,N}\sqrt{B}c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{9\}}=\lim_{B,N}\sqrt{B}c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{10\}}=0
. For
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{1\}}
through
c_{l^{\prime}}^{\{6\}}
, we need to use explicit formulas. We obtain

\displaystyle c^{\{1\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}}

\displaystyle c^{\{2\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}}{\sqrt{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}}}

\displaystyle c^{\{3\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;-}-\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}}{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}}}

\displaystyle c^{\{4\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}}{\sqrt{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}}}

\displaystyle c^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}}{\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}c^{\{3\}}_{l^{\prime}}}

\displaystyle c^{\{6\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{B-2}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}+\frac{1}{B-1}\mathfrak{c}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-c^{\{4\}}_{l^{\prime}}c^{\{4\}}_{l^{\prime}}-c^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}c^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}}

Stage 9 yields
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}>0
and the induction hypothesis of this stage yields
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;-}>0
as well as
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;+}=0
. So
\ddot{c}^{\{3\}}_{l^{\prime}}=\sqrt{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;-}}>0
, so all denominators in the above formulas have positive limits, so all limits are straightforward and we obtain

\displaystyle\ddot{c}^{\{1\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}}

\displaystyle\ddot{c}^{\{2\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle\ddot{c}^{\{3\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}^{-;-}}

\displaystyle\ddot{c}^{\{4\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}}{\sqrt{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}}}

\displaystyle\ddot{c}^{\{5\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle\ddot{c}^{\{6\}}_{l^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2}(\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}-\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},2})}{\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l^{\prime},1;l^{\prime},1}}}

Recursive expansion
The first expansion is given above. Replacing the remaining
\rho^{+}
terms (not inside a
\nu^{+}
) with
e^{+}
and
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu^{+}}}
terms is as for super terms 1 and 2 in the BN layer case of stage 12. However, the second expansion in terms of
u
components and
s
and
z
terms is more complex. For now, we simply replace the
e
terms (not inside a
\nu^{+}
) with their decomposition in terms of
u
components and
s
and
z
terms. We do not further simplify the resulting expression for now. We thus obtain two kinds of pure terms. “Short terms” originate from super term 1 and “long terms” originate from super term 2. Pure terms are an instance of the expression inside the leading sum(s) as in stage 12. So the second expansion is a sum over a fixed number of 2 kinds of pure terms. Again, they contain a multiplier, normalizer and polynomial. N-sums and N-frequencies are not present. The polynomial can now also contain
s
,
z
and
c^{\{.\}}
terms that stem from the replacement of the
e
terms by their decomposition. In this context, we consider a standard form term to be defined by those conditions.

Expectation limits of standard form terms
Relative to the BN layer case of stage 12, multiplying out the polynomial results in a sum of “chains” that can now contain
s
,
z
and
c^{\{.\}}
terms in addition to
u
components. Nonetheless, aggregation works as before except that chains are only considered equivalent if the same
s
,
z
and
c^{\{.\}}
terms are present, of which there is a bounded number. The B-frequencies converge. After aggregation, the
c^{\{.\}}
terms in the aggregated chain can be absorbed into the multiplier, which causes the multiplier to differ from aggregated chain to aggregated chain. Nonetheless, applying lemma
18
works as before.
\chi_{d}
has one component for each distinct
u
component or
s
or
z
term that arises in the aggregated chain.
\hat{\Sigma}
is still the identity. The valid limit of the expectation of the product of B-frequency, (chain-specific) multiplier, normalizer and (
c^{\{.\}}
-free) aggregated chain is equal to the product of the limit of the B-frequency, the limit of the multiplier, the almost sure limit of the normalizer and the expectation of the aggregated chain with respect to the unit Gaussian.

When investigating limit quantities such as
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;+}=\lim_{B,N}\mathbb{E}_{e}\rho_{l,1}^{-}\rho_{l,1}^{+}
, the recursive expansion of the
\rho_{l,b}^{+}
is as in the BN layer case of stage 9 / 12, except that the decomposition of the
e
terms differs, which yields co-terms that can contain
s
,
z
and
c^{\{.\}}
terms in their polynomial in addition to
u
components. Nonetheless, they are standard form terms in this context, and products of a pure term and a pure term or co-term are standard form terms. This yields that all
\lim_{B,N}
quantities of interest are valid as long as the additional
B
factor in
\lim_{B,N}B\mathfrak{c}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;-}
does not cause divergence, which we show below.

Specific expectation limits
Let’s look at
\ddot{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,1}^{-}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,2}^{-}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;+}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;+}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,1}^{-;+}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;+}
and
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,3}^{-;+}
. For each of these, each aggregated chain contains exactly one copy of exactly one of
c^{\{2\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}
,
c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}
,
c^{\{7\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}
,
c^{\{8\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}
,
c_{l_{1}}^{\{9\}}s_{l_{1}}^{+}
,
c^{\{10\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{-}
,
c^{\{12\}}_{l_{1}}u_{l_{1}}^{+}[b]
or
c^{\{13\}}_{l_{1}}u_{l_{1}}^{-}[b]
for some
l_{1}<l
. The expectation limit of a product of multiplier, normalizer and aggregated chain is zero if the chain contains any of the above except
c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}
, due to the chain-specific multiplier becoming zero. If the aggregated chain contains
c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}
and it does not contain another
z_{l_{1}}^{-}
term, the expectation limit is zero due to the single
z_{l_{1}}^{-}
term. Finally, if the aggregated chain contains
c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}
and it does contain another
z_{l_{1}}^{-}
term, it must also contain a
c^{\{5\}}_{l_{1}}
term, which has limit zero. So overall we have
\ddot{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,1}^{-}=\ddot{\mathfrak{m}}_{l,2}^{-}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,1}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;+}=\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,3}^{-;+}=0
as required.

Let’s look at
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;-}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,1;l,2}^{-;-}
,
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,2}^{-;-}
and
\ddot{\mathfrak{c}}_{l,2;l,3}^{-;-}
. Each of
\rho_{l,1}^{-}\rho_{l,1}^{-}
,
\rho_{l,1}^{-}\rho_{l,2}^{-}
,
\rho_{l,2}^{-}\rho_{l,2}^{-}
and
\rho_{l,2}^{-}\rho_{l,3}^{-}
is a sum of products of two pure terms. As usual, we consider the expectation limit of individual products by pure term type. A product of a short term and a long term as well as a product of a long term and another long term contains in its polynomial a factor stemming from
\widehat{e_{l_{1}}^{-}e_{l_{2}}^{+}}-\widehat{e_{l_{1}}^{-}}\widehat{e_{l_{2}}^{+}}
, where
l_{1}<l
and
l_{2}<l
are not necessarily different. We have

\displaystyle\widehat{e_{l_{1}}^{-}e_{l_{2}}^{+}}-\widehat{e_{l_{1}}^{-}}\widehat{e_{l_{2}}^{+}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{B^{2}}\Big(B(c^{\{2\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-})c^{\{1\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}+B\sum_{b=2}^{B}(c^{\{7\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{8\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}+c^{\{9\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{10\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{-}

\displaystyle+c^{\{12\}}_{l_{1}}u_{l_{1}}^{+}[b]+c^{\{13\}}_{l_{1}}u_{l_{1}}^{-}[b])(c^{\{4\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}+c^{\{5\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{-}+c^{\{6\}}_{l_{2}}s_{l_{2}}^{+}+c^{\{11\}}_{l_{2}}u_{l_{2}}^{+}[b])

\displaystyle-(c^{\{2\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}+\sum_{b=2}^{B}(c^{\{7\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{8\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}+c^{\{9\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{10\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{-}

\displaystyle+c^{\{12\}}_{l_{1}}u_{l_{1}}^{+}[b]+c^{\{13\}}_{l_{1}}u_{l_{1}}^{-}[b]))(c^{\{1\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}+\sum_{b=2}^{B}(c^{\{4\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}+c^{\{5\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{-}+c^{\{6\}}_{l_{2}}s_{l_{2}}^{+}+c^{\{11\}}_{l_{2}}u_{l_{2}}^{+}[b]))\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{B-1}{B^{2}}(c^{\{2\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}-c^{\{7\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}-c^{\{8\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}-c^{\{9\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{+}-c^{\{10\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{-})(c^{\{1\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}-c^{\{4\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}

\displaystyle-c^{\{5\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{-}-c^{\{6\}}_{l_{2}}s_{l_{2}}^{+})+\frac{B-1}{B}c^{\{12\}}_{l_{1}}c^{\{11\}}_{l_{2}}\widetilde{u_{l_{1}}^{+}u_{l_{2}}^{+}}+\frac{B-1}{B}c^{\{13\}}_{l_{1}}c^{\{11\}}_{l_{2}}\widetilde{u_{l_{1}}^{-}u_{l_{2}}^{+}}

Here we use that
\widetilde{u}=0
for all
u
vectors. Now we form aggregated chains in a 3-step process. First, we aggregate the “partial chains” obtained from multiplying out all of the polynomial except for the factor stemming from
\widehat{e_{l_{1}}^{-}e_{l_{2}}^{+}}-\widehat{e_{l_{1}}^{-}}\widehat{e_{l_{2}}^{+}}
. Second, we multiply a copy of each aggregated partial chain with
\frac{B-1}{B^{2}}(c^{\{2\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}-c^{\{7\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}-c^{\{8\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}-c^{\{9\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{+}-c^{\{10\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{-})(c^{\{1\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}-c^{\{4\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}-c^{\{5\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{-}-c^{\{6\}}_{l_{2}}s_{l_{2}}^{+})
, a copy of each aggregated partial chain with
\frac{B-1}{B}c^{\{12\}}_{l_{1}}c^{\{11\}}_{l_{2}}\widetilde{u_{l_{1}}^{+}u_{l_{2}}^{+}}
and a copy of each aggregated partial chain with
\frac{B-1}{B}c^{\{13\}}_{l_{1}}c^{\{11\}}_{l_{2}}\widetilde{u_{l_{1}}^{-}u_{l_{2}}^{+}}
. Third, we form aggregated chains from each copy. Since the B-frequencies of aggregated partial chains are convergent, the B-frequencies of aggregated chains stemming from the first copy converge to zero. Aggregated chains stemming from the second and third copy contain
c^{\{12\}}_{l_{1}}
and
c^{\{13\}}_{l_{1}}
respectively, which converge to zero. So for any type of aggregated chain, the expectation limit is zero.

This leaves products of a short term and another short term. If the big layer indices from the leading sum are different, all aggregated chains contain two single
u
components or
s
or
z
terms, one each for the two big layer indices. The expectation limit is zero. If the big layer indices are both equal to some
l^{\prime}
, the polynomial stems from
(e_{l^{\prime},b}-\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}})(e_{l^{\prime},b^{\prime}}-\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}})
, where
(b,b^{\prime})
is one of
(1,1)
,
(1,2)
,
(2,2)
and
(2,3)
depending on the limit quantity considered. We have

\displaystyle e_{l^{\prime},b}-\widehat{e_{l^{\prime}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\mathbbm{1}_{b=1}-\frac{1}{B})c^{\{2\}}_{l^{\prime}}z_{l^{\prime}}^{+}+(\mathbbm{1}_{b=1}-\frac{1}{B})c^{\{3\}}_{l^{\prime}}z_{l^{\prime}}^{-}+(\mathbbm{1}_{b\neq 1}-\frac{B-1}{B})c^{\{7\}}_{l^{\prime}}z_{l^{\prime}}^{+}

Finally, let’s look at

A product of a long term and another long term contains in its polynomial two factors stemming from
\widehat{e_{l_{1}}^{-}e_{l_{2}}^{+}}-\widehat{e_{l_{1}}^{-}}\widehat{e_{l_{2}}^{+}}

\frac{B-1}{B^{2}}(c^{\{2\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}-c^{\{7\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}-c^{\{8\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}-c^{\{9\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{+}-c^{\{10\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{-})(c^{\{1\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}-c^{\{4\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{+}-c^{\{5\}}_{l_{2}}z_{l_{2}}^{-}-c^{\{6\}}_{l_{2}}s_{l_{2}}^{+})...

...\frac{B-1}{B^{2}}(c^{\{2\}}_{l_{3}}z_{l_{3}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l_{3}}z_{l_{3}}^{-}-c^{\{7\}}_{l_{3}}z_{l_{3}}^{+}-c^{\{8\}}_{l_{3}}z_{l_{3}}^{-}-c^{\{9\}}_{l_{3}}s_{l_{3}}^{+}-c^{\{10\}}_{l_{3}}s_{l_{3}}^{-})(c^{\{1\}}_{l_{4}}z_{l_{4}}^{+}-c^{\{4\}}_{l_{4}}z_{l_{4}}^{+}-c^{\{5\}}_{l_{4}}z_{l_{4}}^{-}-c^{\{6\}}_{l_{4}}s_{l_{4}}^{+})

and a copy of each aggregated partial chain with

\frac{B-1}{B^{2}}(c^{\{2\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}-c^{\{7\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{+}-c^{\{8\}}_{l_{1}}z_{l_{1}}^{-}-c^{\{9\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{+}-c^{\{10\}}_{l_{1}}s_{l_{1}}^{-})...

...(c^{\{2\}}_{l_{3}}z_{l_{3}}^{+}+c^{\{3\}}_{l_{3}}z_{l_{3}}^{-}-c^{\{7\}}_{l_{3}}z_{l_{3}}^{+}-c^{\{8\}}_{l_{3}}z_{l_{3}}^{-}-c^{\{9\}}_{l_{3}}s_{l_{3}}^{+}-c^{\{10\}}_{l_{3}}s_{l_{3}}^{-})(c^{\{1\}}_{l_{4}}z_{l_{4}}^{+}-c^{\{4\}}_{l_{4}}z_{l_{4}}^{+}-c^{\{5\}}_{l_{4}}z_{l_{4}}^{-}-c^{\{6\}}_{l_{4}}s_{l_{4}}^{+})

Third, we form aggregated chains from each copy. Since aggregated partial chains have convergent B-frequency, aggregated chains stemming from the first copy have a B-frequency that when multiplied with
B
converges to zero, because of the two
\frac{B-1}{B^{2}}
factors. Aggregated chains stemming from the second or third copy have a B-frequency that when multiplied with

\frac{B-1}{B^{2}}
factor. Further, the chain-specific multiplier for those chains contains either a
c^{\{12\}}
or
c^{\{13\}}
term, so it converges to zero. Aggregated chains stemming from the fourth copy contain two
c^{\{12\}}
terms, two
c^{\{13\}}
terms or both terms. Hence, the multiplier for those chains times
B
converges to zero. So no matter the copy, the expectation limit of the product of B-frequency, multiplier, normalizer and aggregated chain is zero.

A product of a short term and a long term contains in its polynomial a factor stemming from

1\text{ else}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\lim_{B,N}\begin{cases}\mathfrak{c}_{l,1;l,1}^{-;-}\text{ if }l>m\\
1\text{ else}\end{cases}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{m}}

Stage 16
: statements (c) and (d)

Assume now that
f_{L,1}
is a readout layer. Fix
N
. As in stage 8, we construct a mean field architecture
F
with a single readout layer. The difference is that now we require multiple finite input layers. We proceed as in stage 9 with the following differences.

•

Like
f_{L,1}
,
F_{L,1}
is now a readout layer of dimensionality
d_{L}
. The
F_{L,b}
for
b\geq 2
are removed from
F
.

•

F
now has finite input layers
F_{0,b}
which are jointly associated with
\mathcal{D}^{B}
and the batch inputs
X^{(n)}
.

•

For a readin layer
f_{l}
in
f
, instead of adding input layers
F_{l,b}
to
F
and extending
\mathcal{G}
, we add readin layers
F_{l,b}
with the same width and variance parameter as the
f_{l,b}
that share weights with each other but not other readin layers in
F
and have dependency
F_{0,b}
respectively.

•

\mathcal{G}
now only covers layers derived from bias big layers.

It is easy to see that, as in stage 9, we have distribution equality. For (c), this means that
f_{L,1}
and
F_{L,1}
have the same meta-distribution. For (b), this means that
(f_{L,1}(X^{(1)}),..,f_{L,1}(X^{(N)}))
has the same distribution as
(F_{L,1}(X^{(1)}),..,F_{L,1}(X^{(N)}))
for any fixed sample
X^{(1)},..,X^{(N)}
. Note that as in the statement of background corollary
2
, the surrogate input generated by
\mathcal{G}
does not vary between batch inputs
X^{(n)}
, as it represents the random initial bias vectors.

In stage 8, we used theorem
4
and background corollary
2
for statements (a) and (b) respectively. Now we require generalized versions that handle the case where there is more than one finite input layer. It is easy to obtain such generalizations. For background corollary
2
, we simply need to replace
\mathcal{G}(K_{\text{in}})
with the proper generator for the wider set of readin layers. The value of the covariance kernel for a pair
(X^{(n)},X^{(n^{\prime})})
then depends on all the square means and co-means of the individual inputs in
X^{(n)}
and
X^{(n^{\prime})}
. In the context of this stage,
\clipout(\clipin(F))^{N}
has
NBI
input layers that stem from readin layers in
F
, where
I
is the number of readin big layers in
f
. The proper generator that yields distribution equality is
\mathcal{G}(K(NB,q,c))
, i.e. a mean zero Gaussian where the covariance matrix entry corresponding to
F_{l,b}^{(n)}
and
F_{l^{\prime},b^{\prime}}^{(n^{\prime})}
is

\sigma_{l}\sigma_{l^{\prime}}(\mathbbm{1}_{b=b^{\prime}\text{ and }n=n^{\prime}}q+\mathbbm{1}_{b\neq b^{\prime}\text{ or }n\neq n^{\prime}}c)\mathbbm{1}_{\text{$l=m$ or $f_{l}$ and $f_{m}$ share weights}}

Here, we use
n
and
n^{\prime}
to represent duplex indices. As (d) only requires considering almost all samples, we can assume that all square means of individual inputs are
q
and all co-means of individual inputs are
c
. As opposed to the general case, we can thus define a covariance kernel over only those two parameters.

We base the generalized theorem
4
on the generalized background corollary. We associate the finite input layers with
\mathcal{D}^{B}
and replace
\mathcal{G}(K(N,q,c))
with
\mathcal{G}(K(NB,q,c))
. The proof goes through as before. The conditions of the generalizations hold because
(\clipout(\clipin(F))^{N},\mathcal{G}(K(NB,q,c))\times\mathcal{G}^{N})
is the mean field architecture and generator we constructed early in stage 12 denoted as
(F^{(1)},..,F^{(N)})
for the case
m=L-1
. We proved the conditions in that stage.

So we have that (i) the meta-distribution of
F_{L,1}
expansion-converges as
d_{\text{MF}}\rightarrow\infty
to the elementwise meta-distribution with generator
\mathcal{MN}(\mathfrak{c}_{L,1;L,1},\mathfrak{c}_{L,1;L,1}^{\prime;\prime\prime})
and (ii) for almost all samples
(F_{L,1}(X^{(1)}),..,F_{L,1}(X^{(N)}))
converges in distribution as
d_{\text{MF}}\rightarrow\infty
to a Gaussian that is elementwise over output vectors where the generator has mean zero and covariance matrix
K(N,\mathfrak{c}_{L,1;L,1},\mathfrak{c}_{L,1;L,1}^{\prime;\prime\prime})
. By distribution equality, the same holds for
f_{L,1}
. And, as we showed in stage 9 and 10,
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\lim_{B}\mathfrak{c}_{L,1;L,1}=\mathfrak{q}_{L}
and
\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}}\lim_{B}\mathfrak{c}_{L,1;L,1}^{\prime;\prime\prime}=\mathfrak{c}_{L}
. (The limit over
N
was not used in stages 9 and 10.)

Finally, we note that when
f_{L,1}
is a readout layer, statements (
11.1
) through (
11.11
) still hold when
l<L
as
(f_{0},..,f_{L-1})
is a valid A-architecture without finite output layer.

∎

11.6.4
Proposition
19
part 2

Proposition
19
.

(part 2; see section
11.4
for part 1)

Let
f
be an A-architecture and let
X^{(1)}=(x^{(1,1)},..,x^{(1,B)})
and
X^{(2)}=(x^{(2,1)},..,x^{(2,B)})
be two batch inputs. Assume:

•

\mathbb{E}_{i}x^{(n,b)}[i]x^{(n,b)}[i]=q
for some
q
and all
1\leq n\leq 2
and
1\leq b\leq B

•

\mathbb{E}_{i}x^{(n,b)}[i]x^{(n^{\prime},b^{\prime})}[i]=c
for some
c
and all
1\leq n,n^{\prime},\leq 2
,
1\leq b,b^{\prime}\leq B
, except when
(n,b)=(n^{\prime},b^{\prime})
or
(n,n^{\prime},b,b^{\prime})=(1,2,1,1)

•

\mathbb{E}_{i}x^{(1,1)}[i]x^{(2,1)}[i]=r
for some
r

•

q>r\geq c\geq 0

•

The activation functions used in
f
are piecewise 5-differentiable.

If
f
does not contain layer normalization but can contain batch normalization layers, we have

\lim_{\vec{\epsilon}\rightarrow 0}\Big(\lim_{B\rightarrow\infty}\big(\lim_{d_{\text{MF}}\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}_{i}f_{l,1}(X^{(1)})[i]f_{l,1}(X^{(2)})[i]=\mathfrak{r}_{l}\text{ a.s.}\big)\Big)

where…

•

…
\vec{\epsilon}
is the vector of all regularizers used by normalization layers in
f
.

•

…
0\leq l\leq L

•

…
\mathfrak{r}_{l}=\begin{cases}r\text{ parameter of inputs if $f_{l}$ is an input layer}\\
\sigma_{l}^{2}\mathfrak{r}_{k}\text{ if $f_{l}$ is an FC layer}\\
\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},\mathfrak{r}_{k})\text{ if $f_{l}$ is an activation layer}\\
\mathfrak{r}_{k}+\sigma_{l}^{2}\text{ if $f_{l}$ is a bias layer}\\
\frac{\mathfrak{r}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k}}{\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k}}\text{ if $f_{l}$ is a BN layer}\\
\sum_{\kappa_{l}=1}^{K_{l}}w_{l,\kappa_{l}}^{2}\mathfrak{r}_{k_{l}[\kappa_{l}]}\text{ if $f_{l}$ is an addition layer}\end{cases}

•

… randomness is induced by
\theta
and the
X^{(n)}
.

Define the covariance kernel
\mathfrak{C}(q,c,r)
as the function that returns
\mathfrak{r}_{L}
given
q
,
c
and
r
. Then we further have

\mathfrak{n}(f,q,c)=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}(q,c,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}(q-c)}{\mathfrak{C}(q,c,q)-\mathfrak{C}(q,c,c)}}

Remark

While we phrase part 2 of this proposition entirely in terms of the three-argument covariance kernel
\mathfrak{C}(q,c,r)
for simplicity, it is worth noting that
\mathfrak{C}(q,c,q)
and
\mathfrak{C}(q,c,c)
are identical to
\mathfrak{C}(q,q)
and
\mathfrak{C}(q,c)
respectively, as used in part 1 of the proposition.

It is worth noting that the co-means stipulated by the proposition are achievable. Let
v^{\text{all}}
,
v^{\text{1}}
,
v^{\text{(1,1)}}
, ..,
v^{\text{(1,B)}}
,
v^{\text{(2,1)}}
, ..,
v^{\text{(2,B)}}
be a set of orthonormal vectors. Then letting
x^{(n,b)}=\sqrt{c}v^{\text{all}}+\sqrt{r-c}v^{\text{1}}+\sqrt{q-r}v^{(n,b)}
when
b=1
and
x^{(n,b)}=\sqrt{c}v^{\text{all}}+\sqrt{q-c}v^{(n,b)}
otherwise, we obtain the desired co-means.

Proof.

Like the statement of the proposition, the proof has two parts. The first part is a continuation of the proof of theorem
5
for the BN case given in section
11.6.3
, i.e. it can be viewed as another stage. The second part of the proof proceeds along the lines of the proof of the first part of this proposition given in section
11.4
, and is based only on the calculation rules for the
\mathfrak{r}_{l}
,
\mathfrak{q}_{l}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{l}
and
\mathfrak{g}_{l}
given above and in table

. Because activation functions used are piecewise 5-differentiable, we can use theorem
7
in this proof.

Part 1
: We proceed along the lines of stage 10. The statement trivially holds for
l=0
.
F
is constructed as in that stage, where again

corresponds to
f_{l,b}(X^{(1)})
and

corresponds to
f_{l,b}(X^{(2)})
.
\mathcal{G}
is similar. It is a Gaussian with mean zero and covariance matrix as follows. An entry corresponding to layers

and is otherwise

,

or

depending on how

matches up with the conditions of this proposition. An entry corresponding to

and

otherwise. An entry corresponding to

and

and (iv)

. We also use proposition
15
and non-singularity from stage 9.

Part 2
: All denominators that arise in this part are non-zero by proposition

. Denote by

Denote the right-hand side of this equation by
RHS_{l}
. It is easy to check that
\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,c,q)=\mathfrak{q}_{l}
and that
\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,c,c)=\mathfrak{c}_{l}
. So the left-hand side of the equation is
\sqrt{\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}(\mathfrak{q}_{0}-\mathfrak{c}_{0})}{\mathfrak{g}_{0}(\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l})}}
and the right-hand side is
\sqrt{\frac{\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,c,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}(\mathfrak{q}_{0}-\mathfrak{c}_{0})}{\mathfrak{q}_{l}-\mathfrak{c}_{l}}}
. Also
\mathfrak{g}_{0}=1
. So we simply need to show

\mathfrak{g}_{l}=\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,c,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}

Again, we proceed by induction on
l
based on layer operation. The base case of our induction is
l=0
, where
\mathfrak{C}_{l}
is the identity so both sides are equal to 1. For the induction step, we have
l>0
so
f_{l}
is not an input layer.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an FC, bias, BN or activation layer. We have

\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,c,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}=\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{dr}|_{r=q}=\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{d\mathfrak{r}_{k}}|_{\mathfrak{r}_{k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}}\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{k}}{dr}|_{r=q}

=\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{d\mathfrak{r}_{k}}|_{\mathfrak{r}_{k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}}\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}_{k}(q,c,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}=\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{d\mathfrak{r}_{k}}|_{\mathfrak{r}_{k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}}\mathfrak{g}_{k}

So we must show that

\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}=\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{d\mathfrak{r}_{k}}|_{\mathfrak{r}_{k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}}

The
\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{d\mathfrak{r}_{k}}|_{\mathfrak{r}_{k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}}
term is
\sigma_{l}^{2}
for FC, 1 for bias, and
\frac{1}{\mathfrak{q}_{k}-\mathfrak{c}_{k}}
for BN. It is easy to check that this equals
\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}
. If
f_{l}
is an activation layer, we have
\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{d\mathfrak{r}_{k}}|_{\mathfrak{r}_{k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}}=\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}_{\tau_{l}}(\mathfrak{q}_{k},q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}}
. This is the same expression we encountered in the proof of the first part of proposition
19
and so again we have
\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{d\mathfrak{r}_{k}}|_{\mathfrak{r}_{k}=\mathfrak{q}_{k}}=\frac{\mathfrak{g}_{l}}{\mathfrak{g}_{k}}
.

•

Case:
f_{l}
is an addition layer. We have

\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}_{l}(q,c,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}=\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{dr}|_{r=q}=\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{l}}{d\mathfrak{r}_{k[\kappa]}}|_{\mathfrak{r}_{k[\kappa]}=\mathfrak{q}_{k[\kappa]}}\frac{d\mathfrak{r}_{k[\kappa]}}{dr}|_{r=q}

=\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\frac{d}{dq^{\prime}}\mathfrak{C}_{k[\kappa]}(q,c,q^{\prime})|_{q^{\prime}=q}=\sum_{\kappa=1}^{K}w_{\kappa}^{2}\mathfrak{g}_{k[\kappa]}=\mathfrak{g}_{l}

∎
